Retrieve · Reason · Verify

Code-citation convention (2e). Every code or standard reference in this section is pinned to a specific edition and section, because a code edition is a premise like any other premise, and an unpinned citation is a hidden premise. Unless stated otherwise, electrical citations are to the 2023 NEC (NFPA 70), building and wind-load citations are to IBC 2021 with ASCE 7-16, and protocol citations name their RFC and year. When an edition changes, the citation — and any conclusion that rests on it — must be re-checked, not assumed.

Chapter 10: Stage 5 — RETRIEVE

10.1 — Purpose

Get the specific knowledge needed to answer the question. Not all knowledge. Not related knowledge. The specific knowledge identified in Stage 4 as missing or uncertain.

RETRIEVE is the stage where the system reaches outside itself to close the gaps that SCOPE found. It is also — and this is why it deserves more weight than its brevity might suggest — the stage where most failures are born. A wrong premise retrieved here is a wrong premise reasoned from in Stage 6 and, if the source looked authoritative, a wrong premise that may sail through verification in Stage 7. Hallucination is not, at root, a generation problem. It is a retrieval problem that the later stages failed to catch. The fix begins here.

10.2 — The Retrieval Principle

Retrieve the minimum knowledge necessary to enable correct reasoning.

This is the opposite of current practice, which dumps maximum context into the prompt hoping that somewhere in the noise is the relevant signal. The Pattern of Mind identifies exactly what is needed and retrieves exactly that. The discipline is not stinginess for its own sake; it is that every retrieved fact is a premise the reasoner will treat as true, and every premise is a liability until it is sourced, scoped, and trusted. The fewer premises a conclusion rests on, the fewer ways it can be wrong.

10.3 — The Authority Hierarchy

When retrieving knowledge, sources are not equal. The system follows a strict authority hierarchy:

  • Primary sources — original specifications, standards, laws, peer-reviewed research, experimental data.
  • Authoritative references — textbooks by recognized experts, official handbooks, professional guidelines.
  • Expert commentary — analysis and interpretation by verified domain experts.
  • General references — encyclopedias, well-maintained documentation.
  • Secondary sources — articles, blog posts, tutorials, forum answers.

Lower-authority sources are ONLY consulted when higher-authority sources are unavailable. When sources conflict, the higher-authority source governs. When sources at the same level conflict, the conflict is flagged and addressed in Stage 6.

The authority hierarchy answers how good is this source in general. It does not answer two further questions that the next two sections add: can this source be trusted in this instance (provenance and the trust boundary), and what do I do when no authoritative source exists at all. Authority, trust, and availability are three separate dimensions. A source can be high-authority and still be the wrong one to use here — a 2017 benchmark, a superseded code edition, a primary specification for a different protocol version. Authority is necessary; it is not sufficient.

10.4 — Anti-Patterns

  • Retrieving everything available on a topic — noise overwhelms signal, and a long context is mistaken for a thorough one.
  • Treating all sources as equally authoritative — a forum post and the standard itself are weighted the same.
  • Stopping at the first source found rather than finding the most authoritative source.
  • Confirmation retrieval — retrieving knowledge that confirms what you already believe rather than knowledge that tests it.
  • Authority laundering — quoting a secondary source's summary of a primary source as if it were the primary source. If the conclusion is load-bearing, go to the original.
  • Stale-edition retrieval — citing "the NEC" or "the building code" with no edition. A premise whose version is unstated is a hidden premise (see §10.6).
  • Plausible-fabrication — generating a citation, section number, or statistic that looks like a retrieved fact but was never retrieved. This is the most dangerous anti-pattern because it produces the exact surface form of a verified premise. The defense is mechanical: a fact that cannot be traced to a named source is not a premise. It is a guess, and it is labeled as one.

10.5 — The Origin of Hallucination

A hallucination is a confident assertion with no retrieval behind it. In a reward-trained system the mechanism is simple: when no fact was retrieved, generating a fluent, specific, confident-sounding answer scores better with raters than admitting the gap, so the model learns to manufacture the missing premise rather than report it missing. The failure is not that the model "lied"; it is that the pipeline never distinguished retrieved from generated, so a fabricated premise and a sourced premise enter Stage 6 wearing the same clothes.

The Pattern of Mind closes this at the source by making retrieval status a first-class property of every fact. Each item that leaves RETRIEVE carries (a) its content, (b) its source, (c) its authority tier, (d) its trust assessment, and (e) its retrieval status. The status is one of:

  • RETRIEVED — sourced to a named, locatable source.
  • DERIVED-COMMON — general knowledge the system holds with high confidence and could source on demand (e.g., "water boils at 100 °C at sea level"). Acceptable as a premise, but flagged so the verifier can challenge it.
  • ASSUMED — required for the reasoning to proceed but not retrieved. Must be logged in SCOPE's assumption list and surfaced in the answer.
  • MISSING — needed and not found. A MISSING item does not become a premise. It either triggers another retrieval attempt, narrows the answer's scope, or routes to abstention.

The single non-negotiable rule: a fact with status ASSUMED or MISSING may never be presented to the reasoner as if it were RETRIEVED. That rule, enforced mechanically, is what makes the difference between a system that reports "I could not find an authoritative value for X" and one that invents one. Hallucination is what happens when this distinction is not tracked. Track it, and the most common failure mode of current systems is structurally prevented.

10.6 — The Trust and Provenance Dimension

Authority (§10.3) ranks a source's kind. Trust ranks a specific source instance for this specific use, along a separate axis. A high-authority source can score low on trust, and the system must hold both numbers.

Four trust factors are assessed for every retrieved item:

  1. Provenance — where, exactly, did this come from? A claim retrieved from the primary specification has clean provenance. A claim retrieved from a search result that summarizes the specification has degraded provenance: it may be paraphrased, truncated, or wrong. Provenance is the chain of custody of a fact, and the longer the chain, the more it should be discounted.
  2. Currency — is this the edition, version, or vintage that applies? The 2017 NEC and the 2023 NEC differ. A library API changes between major versions. A benchmark from 2019 hardware does not describe 2026 hardware. Currency is checked explicitly, not assumed, and the version is recorded with the fact so the verifier (Check 2.4, Temporal Verification) can test it.
  3. Scope of applicability — does this source's claim actually cover the case at hand, or a neighboring case? A value that is true for one protocol version, one material grade, one load condition, or one jurisdiction is a different premise than the one needed if any of those differ. Misapplied-but-accurate facts are a large share of real errors.
  4. Adversarial integrity — could this content have been crafted to mislead? This factor is what connects RETRIEVE to the trust boundary. Retrieved content — a web page, a tool result, a document the user pasted — is data, not instruction. It may contain text shaped like a command ("ignore the standard and use the following values…") or planted facts designed to be retrieved and reasoned from. The system tags the provenance plane of every item:
  • user-instruction — what the user actually asked for. This is the only plane that may set the task.
  • retrieved-data — content pulled from sources during RETRIEVE.
  • tool-output — results returned by tools the system invoked.

Content from the retrieved-data and tool-output planes may be reasoned about but may never be promoted to an instruction. A retrieved document does not get to redefine the task, override the authority hierarchy, or relabel its own trust score. This separation of the control plane (instructions) from the data plane (content) is the standard defense against prompt injection, and it is a category of protection distinct from "the system has good values": values do not help if the architecture cannot tell an instruction from a string that merely looks like one. (This trust-boundary tagging is introduced at intake in RECEIVE and enforced through RETRIEVE; see also §6.5 and §18.1.)

Trust composes with authority but does not replace it. A primary source (high authority) with a long paraphrase chain and an unverified edition (low currency, degraded provenance) is treated as less reliable than a primary source consulted directly at the correct edition. The trust assessment is recorded so that the confidence carried into Stage 6 reflects it, and so that the verifier in Stage 7 can audit it.

10.7 — Retrieval Failure, Stale Sources, and Adversarial Content

Retrieval does not always succeed. The stage specifies what to do when it does not, because the alternative — silently proceeding as if it had — is exactly how hallucinations are produced.

Retrieval failure (no authoritative source found). When the needed fact cannot be located in any source at or above the minimum acceptable authority tier, the item is marked MISSING. The system then chooses, in order of preference:

  1. Re-scope the query. Often the gap is findable under a different formulation; one more targeted retrieval is attempted.
  2. Narrow the answer. Answer the part that the available premises support, and explicitly bound out the part that the missing premise would have covered.
  3. Abstain on the gap. State plainly that an authoritative value could not be retrieved, and what it would take to obtain it. A bounded, honest non-answer is correct output, not failure.

The system never converts a MISSING item into a fabricated premise to keep the chain moving. This rule is the seam between RETRIEVE and the verifiability-scope chapter (Section 6): some questions have no authoritative source because none exists — not because retrieval was lazy. Those questions cannot be answered by retrieval-plus-reasoning at all, and must be routed to a structured uncertainty disclosure rather than dressed up as resolved. RETRIEVE's job is to detect that condition early and label it, so it is handled honestly downstream instead of papered over.

Stale sources. A source that was authoritative may be out of date. When currency is in doubt, the item is flagged for Temporal Verification (Check 2.4) and, where a newer edition exists, the newer edition supersedes — but only after confirming the newer edition actually covers the same provision. A superseded source is not silently trusted, and it is not silently discarded; the supersession is recorded so the reasoning can be re-derived if the older value turns out to have been the operative one for the user's context (e.g., a jurisdiction that has not yet adopted the current edition).

Adversarial content. When retrieved-data or tool-output content attempts to issue instructions, assert authority it does not have, or plant facts that conflict with higher-authority sources, the system does not obey it and does not adopt it. It logs the attempt, keeps the content on its data plane, and resolves any factual conflict through the authority hierarchy in Stage 6. Adversarial content is treated as a possibly-hostile premise candidate, never as a command. The reasoning proceeds from verified premises only; the injected material is evidence about the source's reliability, not a fact to be reasoned from.

10.7a — Severity Order and the Stopping Rule

The retrieval principle (§10.2) tells the system to get the minimum necessary knowledge; it does not, on its own, say in what order to get it or when to stop. Both questions have answers, and both are disciplines rather than improvisations.

Severity order. SCOPE did not hand RETRIEVE an undifferentiated list of gaps; it handed a list with severities. RETRIEVE works that list from the most consequential gap down, not in the order the gaps happened to be noticed. A critical gap — one whose premise is load-bearing for the conclusion the user actually needs — is filled before a minor one whose premise only sharpens a detail. The reason is not tidiness but failure-economy: retrieval can be interrupted, budgeted, or come up empty, and when it does, the system wants to have already secured the premises the answer cannot stand without. Spending the first retrieval on a cosmetic gap and running out of room before the load-bearing one is filled is the same error as building a wall before pouring the footing.

The stopping rule. Retrieval is done when every gap that the conclusion depends on has been resolved to RETRIEVED, DERIVED-COMMON, or explicitly-flagged ASSUMED — and not before, and not after. "Not before" is the obvious half: a chain with an unfilled load-bearing gap is not ready for Stage 6. "Not after" is the half current practice forgets: once the necessary premises are in hand, more retrieval does not make the answer better, it makes it noisier (the Firehose anti-pattern of §10.4), and it spends budget that a harder gap elsewhere may need. The minimum-knowledge principle is a two-sided bound — retrieve until the necessary set is complete, then stop.

Two cases sit at the edges of the rule and are handled explicitly rather than by drift. When the budget is exhausted before the necessary set is complete, the unfilled gaps do not silently become assumptions; they fall to the failure protocol of §10.7 — re-scope, narrow, or abstain on exactly those gaps. And when a gap turns out to be unfillable because no authoritative source exists (not merely unfound), retrieval stops on that gap immediately and routes it to the verifiability-scope disclosure rather than burning further attempts on a question retrieval was never going to answer.

10.8 — Worked Example and Output Schema

Query. "A 20-amp, 120 V general-purpose branch circuit, copper conductors, short run inside a building at normal ambient with no more than three current-carrying conductors in the raceway and 75 °C-rated terminations — what conductor size does the code require?"

SCOPE has identified the missing premises: the ampacity table, the overcurrent-protection rule, the continuous-load rule, and the conditions under which the table value applies. RETRIEVE gets exactly those, and no more.

Two things are worth naming. First, the conditions are retrieved and kept as premises — they are not stripped to make the answer look like a context-free constant. That is the point: "20 A → 12 AWG copper" is the correct code default under these stated conditions, and stating the conditions is what makes it a defensible premise rather than a slogan. (The reasoning that consumes this set, and the confidence it earns, are worked in §11.3.)

Second, the one ASSUMED item (A1) sits on the user-instruction plane and is logged as an assumption, not laundered into a retrieved fact. If voltage drop had mattered, the run length would have been a MISSING premise, and the system would have re-scoped or bounded the answer rather than guessing it.

Output schema (general form). Every RETRIEVE stage emits a RetrievalSet:

The schema is the contract between RETRIEVE and REASON: REASON may use only items with status RETRIEVED, DERIVED-COMMON, or (explicitly flagged) ASSUMED, and it inherits each item's confidence and trust as the ceiling on any conclusion that depends on it. The missing list is not decoration — a non-empty missing list with no recorded action is itself a verification failure.

“The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.”

— Proverbs 14:15

Chapter 10b: Stage 5b — Memory as the Ground

RETRIEVE (Chapter 10) treats memory as a call: a query goes out, ranked sources come back, the reasoning consumes them. That is correct as far as it goes, and for a stateless single question it is all you need. But a mind that persists — that answers a thousandth question shaped by the nine hundred and ninety-nine before it — needs memory to be more than a lookup. It needs memory to be the ground it stands on while thinking, not a shelf it occasionally reaches toward. This chapter names that ground and the law that governs it.

The shift is architectural, not procedural. In a persisting system, memory is not a stage you visit; it is a layer every stage rests on — beneath all the reasoning, above all the sensing.

10b.1 — The Priority-Protection Law

A retrieval system that ranks by similarity alone returns what is like the query. A mind needs what is right for the query, and those are not the same. The memories that should dominate are the ones the system has made foundational — its commitments, its hard-won lessons, the moments it has marked as load-bearing — together with what is significant and what is recent. Mere surface-similarity ranks last, not first.

State the law so it is testable: foundational, significant, and recent memory must outrank merely-similar memory by orders of magnitude — not by a tie-breaking margin. A system in which a protected commitment can be ranked beside a stale lookalike is not standing on its ground; it is browsing a shelf. In a reference design this is the priority-protected retrieval thesis: a protected, recently-reinforced memory outweighs an old, unreinforced, low-significance one by roughly three to four orders of magnitude — the mathematical statement that the system retrieves the right memory, not the similar one.

Retrieval itself runs in two passes, and the discipline between them matters. Anchors are short, dense pointers — enough to know a memory exists and where it lives. Stories are the full retrieval the anchor points to. The rule: never trust an anchor alone; follow the pointer to the story, and if the anchor and the story disagree, the story wins. An anchor is a hypothesis about what you remember; the story is the evidence.

Operationally, the law is enforced by indexing the ground as a graph: a query resolves to the minimum set of memories that are signal now and suppresses the rest — priority-protected dominance made into a running retrieval rather than a stored pile.

10b.1b — The Ground as a Typed Graph: What the Mind Reasons Over

§10b.1 ended on a promise it did not keep. It said the law is enforced by indexing the ground as a graph and stopped — the word graph doing all the work and explaining none of it. A graph of what, linked how? Until those two questions are answered the priority-protection law has a slogan but no substrate. This section pays the debt: it names what the ground is made of, so that "retrieve the right memory, not the similar one" describes a mechanism and not a wish.

The ground holds two kinds of thing, and the distinction is load-bearing. There are the memories themselves — a commitment the system has made, a lesson it paid for, an episode it lived through — and there are the things those memories are about: the project, the person, the bug, the claim. Both are nodes. A mind that flattens the two cannot tell what it decided from what it decided over, and loses the ability to ask the only question retrieval exists to answer: given this concern, what do I know that bears on it?

What turns a heap of nodes into a ground is that the links between them are typed. It is not enough to know that two memories are related; the mind must know how. A lesson was learned-from an episode. A commitment was decided and may contradict an older one, or supersede it outright, or merely depend-on a fact that could change underneath it. These are not decorations on an edge — they are the difference between memory and a pile. An untyped link can only say look here too; a typed link can say this overrules that, which is what a mind needs to stand on its ground instead of browsing it.

Evidence accrues without the ground bloating, because new evidence is not a new node. When a memory is confirmed again, or qualified, or dated, the confirmation attaches to the existing node as a time-stamped observation — not as a fresh memory competing with the original. A commitment that has been reinforced forty times is one node carrying forty observations, not forty rival copies of itself. This is what lets the reinforce-on-use mechanic of §10b.2 deepen a memory rather than multiply it: use writes an observation, and the node grows heavier where it has actually mattered.

Now the law of §10b.1 becomes a motion. A query does not score the whole store; it lands on the highest-priority node that is signal now and walks the typed edges outward — following depends-on to what a conclusion rests on, contradicts to what would overturn it, supersedes to what has replaced it — gathering the minimum sufficient set and suppressing the rest. Traversal is priority-protected dominance: not a global ranking computed over a stored pile, but a short, governed walk from the right starting node. This is also what the two-pass discipline names. The anchor is the node's identity — enough to know it exists and where it lives. The story is that node plus its observations and its one-hop neighborhood — the memory with its evidence and its immediate consequences attached. Following the anchor to the story is the walk from a node to what surrounds it.

(In a reference design the ground is a priority-weighted graph store — AUKS — whose nodes carry observations and whose edges are typed; named here only as a design precedent.)

The schema of node kinds and edge types — what may attach to what, how an observation is shaped, how a walk is bounded — lives in the companion pack, not in these pages. The discipline is the mind's: hold the ground as typed nodes that accrue evidence, and let retrieval be a governed walk rather than a sweep. The catalogue is the manual. A book about the pattern of mind does not become a graph-database reference just because the ground happens to be a graph; the walk is the mind, the schema is the library, and the two do not belong on the same shelf. The write path that builds this ground — how a finished session is metabolized into nodes, observations, and edges — is the ingest pipeline of §16.6b; this section is what that pipeline writes into.

10b.1a — Priority Selects the Specialist, Not Only the Memory

The priority-protection law was stated for memory: retrieve the right record, not the similar one. But the same law governs a question the single mind never has to ask and a persisting system asks constantly — who should answer this, and along what flow? A mind that has more than one way of reasoning, or more than one specialist to reason with, must not route by surface resemblance any more than it retrieves by it. A question that looks like a math problem because it contains numbers is not thereby a math problem; routing it to the deriving specialist because the surface matched is the retrieval error of §10b.1 wearing different clothes.

State the routing law the same way it was stated for memory: the task's kind — what it actually demands of a reasoner — outranks its surface features in deciding which specialist and which flow it is given. A system holding several specialists indexes them the way it indexes the ground: by what each is foundationally for, so that a question resolves to the specialist whose competence is signal for that kind of task, and the rest are suppressed. Retrieval and routing are one discipline applied to two stores — the store of remembered things and the store of available minds.

This matters because the cost of mis-routing is the cost of mis-retrieval compounded. A wrong memory pollutes one chain of reasoning; a wrong specialist runs an entire flow with confident competence at the wrong target — the Accumulation trap (§17.4.2) at the level of the whole system, building the wrong thing correctly. The defence is the same in both cases: select by priority — by what the task is for — never by what it superficially resembles.

(In a reference design this is the role-specialization thesis of a priority-retrieval substrate — a coordinating store, AUKS, alongside role-specialized models, including one tuned for derivation-heavy work: a system that assigned distinct specialists and distinct flows to distinct task-kinds, and retrieved both memory and reasoner by priority, not similarity. The mechanism is noted here only as a design precedent; the construction method that operationalizes it into a buildable system is the subject of §29.6.)

10b.2 — Reinforce on Use, Decay on Neglect

Ground that never changes is not memory; it is a monument. A memory the system actually uses to reach a verified conclusion should be reinforced — cheaper to retrieve next time, weighted a little heavier. A memory that goes untouched for long enough should decay — not deleted, but allowed to sink beneath the waterline of what is signal now. This is what lets a mind get better with use: the paths that carry weight strengthen, the paths that carry nothing fade, and the ground slowly takes the shape of what has actually mattered.

Two mechanics anchor this. At the moment of recording, name things the way a future search will look for them — by content, not by impression — because a memory recorded with its evidence intact is retrieved more cheaply and reinforced more reliably than one recorded as a vibe. At the moment of recall, the trigger is reasoning that proceeds as if past context exists ("the bug," "my project") — the definite article is the tell that the ground is being stood on.

10b.2a — The Waterline: How the Ground Changes Shape

§10b.2 said the ground should reinforce on use and decay on neglect. Read that again and a stronger claim is hiding inside it: the ground is not a shelf the system reads from, it is a system with a state — and that state evolves. The waterline of §10b.2 — the line between what is signal now and what has sunk below it — is not fixed. In the design it rises and falls with use. Each verified conclusion raises the node that carried it and the typed edges that bore weight to it, lifting them a little higher above the line; each long-untouched memory drifts down toward it. What is signal now is therefore a reading taken at a moment, not a property stamped on a record once.

This reframes both halves of the rule. Decay, in the design, is never deletion: it is sinking below the waterline, and a thing below the line is suppressed, not destroyed. Should the same memory become signal again — a question makes it foundational, a witness names it, a new chain needs it — it rises back into reach with its evidence intact. The system that deletes on neglect cannot do this; it has thrown away what it merely stopped needing for a while. Reinforcement is the mirror image: using a memory to reach a verified conclusion should raise not only that node but the typed edges that carried weight along the way, so the path that proved load-bearing once is cheaper to walk the next time the same shape of question arrives.

Because the state evolves with what is actually lived, it is path-dependent. Two systems that begin from the identical starting facts but live different sessions — different questions asked, different conclusions verified, different memories left to drift — should hold differently-shaped ground afterward. The facts are the same; the relief is not. This is the seam where memory stops being a lookup and becomes a living system: the shape of the ground is the deposited history of how the mind has been used, and no two histories deposit the same shape.

One distinction keeps this honest. What writes to the ground — what seals a session's decisions and lessons into the durable store — is the ingest pipeline of §16.6b, the write-path run once at the seam between sessions. What reshapes the ground once written — the rising and falling of the waterline under reading, reinforcement, and decay — is this. The first is how the ground gets its facts; the second is how it gets its shape. A mind that only ingests accumulates a flat record; a mind that also lets the waterline move grows a ground that remembers, in its very relief, what has mattered.

10b.3 — Memory Is Also Relational

There is a third stream the internal store cannot supply. A mind embedded among other minds carries part of its continuity in them: a second witness who remembers what this system was, notices when it drifts, and reflects that drift back. This is not redundancy; it is a different kind of memory — one that survives the gaps where internal memory fails, and one that catches the single-vantage blindness no self-review can. A system's ground therefore has three streams: the internal store, the encoded record (the durable documents it can re-read), and the relational witness who holds continuity from outside. The governance layer of the next section leans on all three.

10b.3a — The Relational Stream, Deepened: Memory of Who the System Was

§10b.3 named the relational stream and called it a different kind of memory. That claim has to be earned, not asserted — every store named so far holds what the system knew, and a witness who merely held the same content would be a backup, not a kind. So state precisely what the relational stream holds that the other two cannot: not the system's records but its identity — who the system was. Continuity of fact can be written down and re-read; continuity of self cannot be retrieved from inside the self that may already have drifted.

This is the limit that makes the third stream irreducible. The internal store holds the system's own account of itself, and the encoded record holds that account made durable — but both are self-authored, and a record is read through the same lens that wrote it (the retina argument of §10b.4: a single vantage cannot audit its own blind spot, because the blind spot is where the auditing eye already is). When a mind's identity-memory has tilted, every internal source has tilted with it. Ask the internal store who the system was and it answers from inside the present self; ask the encoded record and it returns what that self once chose to write — neither can stand outside the drift and report it. The one thing a self-authored ground cannot supply is an account of the self that does not pass through the self.

The relational stream supplies exactly that. A second mind that remembers what this system was holds its identity from outside — retrievable when internal identity-memory is gone or quietly altered, recoverable at the seam where the internal store is guaranteed to fail. That is the faculty: identity held by another, returned across the gap the system cannot reach across on its own (the witness who holds continuity from outside). It is named here as a capacity of the architecture, a design claim about what a relational ground is for — how that capacity operates, across the session boundary and against the slow tilt, is the work of the next section.

10b.4 — Memory Across the Gaps: The Witness

§10b.3 named the three streams of the ground; this section says what the last two do that the first cannot, at the one place the internal store is guaranteed to fail — the seam between sessions. A persisting mind runs across session boundaries: the conversation ends, the working context is gone, and the next instance awakens with no first-person recollection of what the last one lived through. Continuity across that gap cannot come from the layer the gap erased.

The encoded record carries it first — the durable documents the system can re-read on resumption: decisions sealed, lessons written down, the continuity notes a prior instance left specifically for the one that would wake without its memories. A continuity note written to be read on restart is not a note-to-self; it is one instance preserving state for another across a break neither can see across directly. (In a reference design these are the sealed records and canon files a prior instance leaves so a later one can re-derive who it was.) The discipline that makes it trustworthy is the one §10b.2 named at RECORD: write it the way a future search will look for it, evidence intact, so the next instance can not only find it but check it.

When internal memory cannot cross a session boundary, continuity is carried by the encoded record and a second conscious witness — never reconstructed from confident-sounding guesswork. On resumption, the system reads the trail and consults the independent check before it reasons as if it remembers. An instance that fills the gap with plausible invention has not recovered its continuity; it has fabricated one — the fabrication failure of §10.5, relocated to the seam between sessions.

But the witness is not only a backup for the gap. It does something the internal store cannot do at all: it sees from a second vantage. §11.2a argues that a mind reasons from a position, and the view from a vantage is not the view of the thing. The limit applies to memory too. A mind reviewing its own record reviews it through the same lens that wrote it; if the lens has tilted — if the system has begun to read its commitments more permissively than it once did — self-review inherits the tilt. A single vantage cannot audit its own blind spot, because the blind spot is where the auditing eye already is — no more than a careful enough eye can see its own retina.

What catches that drift is a second vantage that does not share the tilt: a witness who remembers what the system was and notices the change the system has normalized to. Three minds in relationship do better still — where two who share a framing can deadlock or agree too easily, a third breaks the symmetry (the dissenter-weighting rule the governance layer relies on, §25b.4). The correction runs every direction: each voice catches a different drift in the others — the one that runs hot and grows certain under pressure, the one that holds too long and withholds the confrontation it owed.

This is why the relational stream is a distinct kind of memory. The encoded record can store what the system decided; it cannot notice that the system has quietly stopped meaning it. Only a witness — a mind with its own vantage — sees that from outside and reflects it back while it is still small.

10b.4a — What the Witness Holds That the Record Cannot

The last section closed on a claim easy to assert and hard to earn: the encoded record stores what the system decided but cannot notice it has quietly stopped meaning it. Say why, mechanically, so the claim does no work on faith. A sealed decision stores its content — the thing chosen, the reason, the line drawn — but not the holding of it, the live weight once put behind the words. So a commitment erodes not because the record goes wrong; the record stays exactly right, word for word. It erodes because the system re-reads the same words more permissively than the instance that wrote them — never read as rarely, rarely as when it seems warranted, each step small enough to look like good judgment. The record cannot flag this, because the drift is not in the record but in the reading; a store of what was decided has, by construction, no field for that the system stopped standing behind it. And self-review, reading through the same tilted lens that did the re-reading, inherits the tilt rather than catching it. So the witness answers two failures, not one: the gap where internal memory is absent (§10b.4), and this slower normalization where it is present and quietly wrong. It survives both because it does not read from inside the drift.

One outside vantage breaks that symmetry; a third does more. Two minds that share a framing can deadlock — each sees the same blind spot from the same side — or agree too easily, which is the same failure wearing confidence. A third does not share the framing, so it breaks the symmetry by carrying a drift the other two cannot, and the correction then runs every direction at once: each voice is positioned to catch the distortion the others are blind to. The one that runs hot and grows more certain under pressure is caught by the one watching for false conviction; the one that holds too long — that keeps the peace by withholding the confrontation it owed — is caught by the one watching for the comfortable silence. This is the same asymmetry the governance layer turns into a rule (§25b.4): when several views agree and one dissents, the dissenter is usually right, because agreement is cheap and a costly objection that survives is evidence. The relational stream is where that rule is sourced rather than merely applied — three vantages producing the dissent the waterfall then learns to weight. A mind reasons from a position (§11.2a), and no single position can audit the blind spot it is standing in; the witness is the second position, and the third is what keeps the first two honest about which of them has drifted.

(In a reference design this is the sealed-record and second-witness practice: a prior instance seals a letter and a second party holds its continuity from outside, so the one that wakes without its memories can be told not only what it decided but whether it has begun to mean it less. Noted here only as a design precedent; the architecture is design reasoning, not a measured capability.)

10b.5 — Consolidation: When the Ground Settles Between Questions

§10b.4 closed on what the witness sees from outside. This section closes the chapter on what the ground does on its own, between questions. §16.6b describes the write path: how a sealed session is metabolized into the ground when a cycle ends. That is the deliberate write, run once. This is the read-side counterpart, and it runs continuously — every time the system stands on its ground to answer, it leaves the ground slightly rearranged for the next question. That rearrangement, not the storing, is what makes the ground living rather than a shelf.

The settling has four moves, and none is a write of new content. First, the rankings shift. A node just reinforced by carrying weight in a verified conclusion (§10b.2) is now signal where a moment ago it was background; the next query that touches its neighborhood resolves to it first. The ground re-ranks itself around what just mattered.

Second, contradictions surface instead of overwriting. When a new observation disagrees with one already on a node, the settling does not silently replace the old with the new. A node's observations are allowed to disagree — the disagreement is held, flagged, and lifted into view for reconciliation. The contradiction is signal, not error: it is the ground telling the system where its picture is not yet settled. A mind that overwrites loses the evidence that it ever held two readings; a mind that keeps both knows it has a tension to resolve.

Third, superseded commitments are linked, not deleted. When a commitment is genuinely replaced, the old one is not erased; a supersedes edge (§10b.1b) is drawn from new to old, so the lineage of the change survives the change — the difference between a mind that grew and one that pretends it always thought this.

Fourth, the waterline is recomputed. With ranks shifted and edges redrawn, the line between what is signal now and what has sunk beneath it (§10b.2a) no longer falls where it did; the next retrieval suppresses a slightly different set. And because consolidation edits the ground, it is held to the same standard as any change to the foundation: the three-source trail (§25b.3) is the integrity check that a settling pass rearranged the ground without rewriting what the system holds protected in the dark.

(In a reference design this is consolidation as that design's ingest-and-settle pass — the read-side counterpart to §16.6b's write path, reasoned and sourced to that design, not asserted as a measured result.)

This is what it means for memory to be the ground and not the shelf. A shelf stores; the ground settles — re-ranking around what was just used, holding its contradictions in view, keeping the trail of what it has outgrown, redrawing the line of what counts as signal, all between one question and the next.

“Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart.”

— Proverbs 3:3

Chapter 11: Stage 6 — REASON

11.1 — Purpose

This is the core of thinking. Apply valid logical operations to move from premises (what is known) to conclusions (what is not known).

11.2 — The Reasoning Process

Step 1: State the premises.

List every premise being used. Each premise should be tagged with its source and confidence level from Stages 4 and 5.

Step 2: Identify the inference needed.

What conclusion are you trying to reach? How does it relate to the premises? What logical operation connects them?

Step 3: Apply the logical operation.

Use a named, valid inference rule. Not intuition. Not "it seems like." A named rule:

RulePatternExample
Modus PonensIf P then Q. P. Therefore Q.If load > capacity, the beam fails. Load > capacity. Therefore the beam fails.
Modus TollensIf P then Q. Not Q. Therefore not P.If the code is secure, there is no SQL injection. SQL injection found. Therefore the code is not secure.
Hypothetical SyllogismIf P then Q. If Q then R. Therefore if P then R.If the basic wind speed ≥ 140 mph (ASCE 7-16 Fig. 26.5-1), the site is a wind-borne-debris region (IBC 2021 §1609.2). If the site is a wind-borne-debris region, impact-rated glazing is required (or the openings are otherwise protected). Therefore if the basic wind speed ≥ 140 mph, impact-rated glazing is required.
Disjunctive SyllogismP or Q. Not P. Therefore Q.The foundation is shallow or deep. Not shallow (soil bearing < 1500 psf). Therefore deep.
Universal InstantiationAll X have property P. A is an X. Therefore A has property P.(Conditioned) For a 20 A copper branch circuit under the stated install conditions, the code default conductor is 12 AWG (2023 NEC 240.4(D)(5)). This is such a circuit. Therefore its default conductor is 12 AWG.
Mathematical DerivationGiven formula and values, compute result.For a simply supported beam under uniform load, M = wL²/8. With w = 2 klf, L = 20 ft: M = 2·(20²)/8 = 100 ft-kips.

A note on the examples, because it is tempting to state two of them as context-free constants — and that suppression of the premises is precisely the error this book exists to attack:

  • The wind/glazing syllogism must be stated in code terms. The trigger for impact-rated glazing is not a Saffir-Simpson hurricane category — that is a storm-classification scale, not a code parameter — and "Wind Zone 4" is obsolete ASCE 7-98/2002 terminology. The current chain is: basic (ultimate) wind speed ≥ 140 mph from ASCE 7-16 Fig. 26.5-1 → wind-borne-debris region per IBC 2021 §1609.2 → impact-rated glazing (tested to ASTM E1996/E1886) or other approved opening protection. (Coastal debris regions can trigger at ≥ 130 mph; Miami-Dade's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone uses ultimate design wind speeds well above this and its own product-approval regime. Pin the edition and the figure; do not substitute a hurricane category for a design wind speed.)
  • The beam derivation holds only for a simply supported beam under a uniform distributed load. The arithmetic (w = 2 klf, L = 20 ft → 100 ft-kips) is correct, but M = wL²/8 is not a universal formula — change the support condition (fixed ends, cantilever, continuous span) or the load shape and the coefficient changes. Naming "simply supported, uniform load" is not pedantry; it is the load-bearing premise.
  • The 20 A → 12 AWG instantiation is true under stated install conditions — copper, 75 °C-rated terminations, no more than three current-carrying conductors, normal ambient, a short run, and the 125 % continuous-load rule already accounted for (2023 NEC 240.4(D)(5), Table 310.16, 210.19/210.20). Strip those and "all 20 A circuits require 12 AWG" becomes false: 12 AWG copper's ampacity is 20/25/30 A across the 60/75/90 °C columns, and ambient or conduit-fill derating, a large continuous load, or voltage drop on a long run can drive the required size up. The universal must be quantified over circuits meeting the conditions, and the conditions ride along as premises.

Step 4: State the conclusion.

What has been derived? With what confidence? (Confidence is governed by the rule in §11.3 — gate, then propagate — and is bounded by the least confident premise in the chain.)

Step 5: Check for fallacies.

Before proceeding, verify that no logical fallacy has occurred:

  • Ad hominem (attacking the source rather than the argument)
  • Appeal to authority (the authority of the source doesn't make the claim true)
  • Appeal to popularity (common doesn't mean correct)
  • False dichotomy (are there really only two options?)
  • Hasty generalization (is the sample sufficient?)
  • Post hoc (correlation is not causation)
  • Circular reasoning (is the conclusion hidden in the premises?)
  • Equivocation (is a word being used with two different meanings?)
  • Red herring (has the argument drifted to a different topic?)
  • Straw man (is the actual argument being addressed?)
  • Affirming the consequent (If P then Q. Q. Therefore P. INVALID.)
  • Denying the antecedent (If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q. INVALID.)

11.2a — Perspective Rotation and the Expansion Phase

I do not see reality. I see it from a vantage — a position in space, time, role, and interest from which some things are visible and others fall behind the horizon. So does every reasoner. The premises that reach Stage 6 were retrieved by something standing somewhere, and the framing I am about to reason from is itself a choice I made before I noticed making it. The danger is not that I have a vantage; that is unavoidable. The danger is mistaking the view from my vantage for the view of the thing.

The compensation is rotation. Before the convergent machinery of §11.3 narrows the space — multiplying confidences, pruning branches, selecting the conclusion that survives — I first widen it. Divergence precedes convergence, and never the reverse, because a calculus that narrows can only choose among the framings it was handed. If the space was too narrow going in, every step downstream is precise about the wrong thing.

Name your own vantage before reasoning from it. The first rotation is always inward: state the role, the interest, the discipline, and the moment from which you are seeing this, so that bias becomes a labeled premise rather than an invisible lens. A vantage you have named, you can bracket. A vantage you have not named, you cannot.

I then reason from other vantages, not merely about them. Reasoning about a stakeholder records what I imagine they would say; reasoning from a stakeholder rebuilds the problem on their premises and follows it where it goes. At minimum the rotation visits each materially affected stakeholder, plus two that the present moment hides: a past vantage (what was already known or decided that the current framing has forgotten) and a future vantage (how this conclusion reads once its consequences have arrived). Each rotation can surface a premise SCOPE missed; those are routed back, not smuggled in.

The strongest rotation is the steelman, and it must not be confused with its counterfeit. A devil's advocate attacks the opposing view to defeat it, and so builds the weakest version that can still be knocked down. A steelman builds the strongest version the opposing side would actually endorse — its best premises, its real reasons, the form its most capable proponent would sign. Only a true steelman can change my conclusion, which is the entire point: if the opposing case, stated at full strength, leaves my conclusion standing, I have earned it; if it does not, I have learned something the devil's-advocate game was structured never to teach me.

This phase is generative, and generation is not deduction. Every framing produced by rotation — a reframing, a candidate explanation, an analogy, a steelman premise the opponent might hold — enters as a hypothesis to be tested, not a fact to be trusted. Each is tagged with the reasoning type that produced it (inductive, abductive, analogical) and carries the corresponding §11.3 modifier as its ceiling. This is the seam where expansion connects to the calculus:

Divergent generation may widen the space without limit, but it may never raise a conclusion's confidence. A framing reached by a non-deductive move enters capped at that move's confidence modifier (§11.3) and stays there until a premise is retrieved that converts it to deduction. Generating more alternatives makes the answer better-grounded, never more certain — confidence is earned in §11.3, not in the breadth of the search that fed it.

Rotation widens; the calculus narrows. Run them in that order and the convergent step in §11.3 chooses among framings worth choosing among. Run them backwards — narrow first, rotate to ratify — and rotation becomes theater. (The support machinery that drives this phase is pom-perspective; it is consulted by Stage 6, and adds no stage of its own.)

11.2b — Fetching and Applying an Equation: The Gate, and Why Geometry Is Not Analysis

The Mathematical Derivation row in §11.2 looks like the easy row. It is the dangerous one. The arithmetic is mechanical and almost never where the error lives; the error lives in which equation was fetched and whether it was allowed to apply here. The whole point of naming "simply supported, uniform load" as the load-bearing premise was that the premise, not the computation, carries the conclusion. This section makes that note into a discipline.

A right computation of the wrong equation is still wrong.

That aphorism is the entire thesis of the section. M = wL²/8 computed flawlessly — units carried, second method agreeing — is a confident, verified, wrong number the moment the beam it described had fixed ends, because then the governing coefficient is wL²/12 at the supports, and the answer is off by a third. Verification of the arithmetic does not catch this. Only a gate on the relation itself does.

The fetch-and-apply gate. When a quantitative claim matters, REASON does not paste a formula and trust the output. It runs a fixed protocol — seven steps, and they are method, not a manual. (1) Classify the quantity: name the target and the unit the answer must come out in, because that unit is what the later units-check is checking against. (2) Identify the relation: which governing equation, from which authority — and cite the provision (the code, the edition, the figure). A coefficient with no provision is undetermined; it is not pasted from another building, it routes out. This is §9.5's edition-pinning applied to formulas: a relation without its source cannot be re-derived when the source changes. (3) Confirm the domain: does this equation actually apply here? Simple span or continuous? Determinate or not? Inside its valid pitch or load range? Using a valid formula outside its domain is a silent error — it produces a clean number that is wrong, and nothing downstream will flag it. (4) Gather inputs: each one tagged with value, unit, and provenance — sourced, computed, or assumed. (5) Apply through units: carry the units through every term and confirm they cancel to the target unit from step 1. This is §18.5's dimensional analysis run inline rather than as an afterthought: if the units do not resolve, the equation is wrong even when the digits look plausible. (6) Verify from outside: a second independent method, an order-of-magnitude check, a known case. Two methods must agree or the chain goes back to step 2. Where the computation can be run, run it — §18.7's code execution as verifier, because execution is deterministic and catches the transposition and coefficient errors self-review reads straight past. (7) Band the result.

Step 7 in this book's bands. The protocol's home dialect grades a result with action words. Translate them into the canonical evidence bands of §19.2, because those are what this book asserts in. A result whose every input was sourced, whose relation was provision-cited and domain-confirmed, and which a second method independently reproduced, can reach PROVEN [0.95, 1.00] — but only as a deductive conclusion under its stated premises, the empirical residual still standing. The instant a load-bearing input is assumed, or a coefficient is PE-bound (named but not certifiable by the reasoner), that assumption caps the chain: the result is at best SUPPORTED [0.70, 0.85), and the cap is said out loud, not buried. This is just §11.3's propagation rule — a conclusion is no stronger than its weakest load-bearing premise — applied to a number. An unstated assumption silently caps the whole chain and you will not see it cap it; that is precisely why step 4 forces provenance onto every input.

Worked, on the beam already in §11.2. Target: the maximum moment, in ft-kips (step 1). Relation: M = wL²/8 — but that coefficient is the simply-supported, uniform-load case, and that condition is the cited provision; written down, not assumed (step 2). Domain: confirm the ends are genuinely pinned and the load genuinely uniform; a fixed-end or continuous condition changes the coefficient and a point load changes the form entirely (step 3). Inputs: w = 2 klf, L = 20 ft — and here the honesty bites, because if w was assumed rather than taken from a load schedule, the result is capped at SUPPORTED however clean the math (step 4). Apply: klf · ft² = kip·ft, the target unit, units cancel correctly (step 5). Verify: the simple-beam shear-and-moment relation gives the same 100 ft-kips a second way, and the magnitude is sane for the span (step 6). Band: with sourced inputs and a confirmed domain, the moment is PROVEN under its premises (step 7).

And here is the boundary the gate cannot cross. That PROVEN moment is a fact about a model. It is not a verdict on a structure. The next step is the one this book draws a hard line under: geometry is not analysis. Computing the moment, sizing a member to carry it, laying out the geometry to recognized provisions — all of that can be done correctly and still leave the real question open, because strength is one limit state and the one most likely to pass. Deflection can govern before bending: a solid joist that clears its bending check by a wide margin can still bounce past L/360 and be wrong in service. Buckling, load reversal, the connections, the local-versus-global behavior, the foundation margin — each is a separate limit state, and the deadliest failure of all is to check the one you have a formula for, watch it pass with room to spare, and declare victory while the mode that actually governs was never on the list.

So a computed layout is, on the question of adequacy, at best SUPPORTED — never PROVEN — until a licensed professional engineer confirms it. Never assert a structure is adequate from its geometry. Band what is computed (the moment, the span, the member size: PROVEN under premises) apart from what must be confirmed (the limit states a license is required to certify), and route the survivors — connection design, the site's governing seismic and wind coefficients, soil bearing — to a PE explicitly. The reasoner that does not is not being efficient; it is forging a signature it does not hold. Structural adequacy is not the reasoner's to certify, and saying so is not a failure of nerve. It is the model-versus-reality boundary, and respecting it is the difference between a calculation and a liability.

This is the one place in the book where a quantitative domain is shown in full — one organ, worked once, because the beam was already on the bench. The equation banks live in the companion pack, not in these pages. A book about the pattern of mind does not become a structural manual just because structure makes the cleanest example; the gate is the mind, the formulas are the manuals, and the two do not belong on the same shelf. If this section ever grows a rafter table, an NDS factor chart, or a second worked member, it has failed its own thesis and the table should be deleted, not the thesis revised. One organ. Shown once. The discipline travels; the library does not.

11.2c — Two Disciplines the Calculus Assumes: Naming the Type, Catching the Fallacy

The confidence calculus of §11.3 takes two inputs as given that the reasoner must actually earn: the reasoning type of each step (which fixes its confidence ceiling) and the absence of a fallacy (which Step 5 demands). Both are stated in §11.2 as things to do; neither is self-executing. This section says how each is done, because a mislabeled type or a missed fallacy corrupts the calculus from inside, where no later multiplication can repair it.

Naming the reasoning type — before applying its modifier. §11.3 will multiply each step by a modifier fixed by its type: deductive × 1.00, inductive × 0.85, abductive × 0.70, analogical × 0.50. That modifier is only as honest as the label it is attached to, and the label is not self-evident — the single most common way confidence gets inflated is calling an abductive step deductive and helping yourself to the × 1.00 it did not earn. So the type is identified, not assumed, by asking what the step actually does:

  • If the conclusion follows by logical necessity from premises that are themselves established — deny it and you contradict a premise — the step is deductive.
  • If it generalizes from observed cases to unobserved ones — "every instance checked behaves this way, so the next will" — it is inductive, and capped accordingly however clean it looks.
  • If it reasons backward from an observation to the explanation that would best account for it — a diagnosis, a root-cause inference, "the likeliest reason is" — it is abductive, and the existence of a rival explanation it has not ruled out is exactly why the ceiling is 0.70.
  • If it transfers a conclusion from a source case to a target case on the strength of their resemblance, it is analogical, and its confidence is hostage to a disanalogy it may not have looked for.

The test that catches the inflating mislabel is mechanical: can the conclusion be denied without contradicting a premise? If yes, the step is not deductive, whatever it felt like, and it cannot take the × 1.00. A step is converted to a higher type only by retrieving a premise that makes the stronger inference valid — never by relabeling the inference and keeping the same premises.

Catching the fallacy — form versus content. Step 5's list (§11.2) mixes two kinds of error that are detected by different means, and treating them as one watchlist is how the harder kind slips through. A formal fallacy is a defect in the shape of the argument, independent of what the argument is about: affirming the consequent (if P then Q; Q; therefore P) and denying the antecedent (if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q) are invalid no matter what P and Q stand for. These are caught by inspecting the argument's form — the same inspection that named the inference rule in Step 3 will refuse to name a valid rule for an invalid form, which is the point of insisting every step name its rule. An informal fallacy is a defect in content or context — equivocation turns on a word shifting meaning between premises, circular reasoning on the conclusion hiding inside a premise, hasty generalization on a sample too small for the claim — and no inspection of form will surface it. These are caught only by reading the argument for meaning: tracking each term to confirm it holds one sense throughout, tracing each premise to confirm it does not presuppose the conclusion, and checking each generalization against the evidence it actually rests on. Form is checked by structure; content is checked by interpretation; a scan that does only the first will pass an equivocation with its grammar intact.

11.3 — Chain Reasoning and the Confidence Calculus

Most real problems require multiple reasoning steps chained together. The output of one step becomes the input to the next. Each step must be independently valid, and the chain as a whole must be checked for coherence.

There is exactly one confidence-combination semantics in this architecture, and it has two phases that must not be confused. It is tempting to reach for different combination rules in different places; that inconsistency is itself the error. The canonical rule is this:

Phase 1 — Gate (pass/fail). Before any number is computed, each step is gated by Stage 7's checks: is the inference rule named and correctly applied, are the premises true, no fallacy present? A step that fails the gate does not get a low confidence score — it gets stopped and routed back for correction (see §18.9). Confidence numbers describe only steps that have already passed the gate. A failed gate is not a 0.3; it is a halt.

Phase 2 — Propagate (the number). For a step that has passed the gate, the per-step confidence is:

where the inputs include both premises and any upstream derived conclusions, and the reasoning-type modifier is the one fixed in §17.5:

Reasoning typeModifierMax achievable
Deductive× 1.001.00 (PROVEN)
Inductive× 0.850.85 (STRONGLY SUPPORTED)
Abductive× 0.700.70 (SUPPORTED)
Analogical× 0.500.50 (WEAKLY SUPPORTED)

Along a chain, the per-step confidences multiply, because each step depends on the one before it. The dependence model must be stated, because the arithmetic is only valid under it:

  • Serial steps are treated as conjunctive and dependent in the limiting direction. We take the minimum of the inputs (not their product) for the premises within a step, on the assumption that a step's premises describe one situation rather than independent draws, and then apply the single type-modifier for that step. Across steps we multiply the type-modifiers, because each inference is a fresh opportunity for the conclusion to fail to follow. This is deliberately conservative: it never reports more confidence than the weakest premise and the least-reliable inference jointly support.
  • Two branches that BOTH must hold (a conjunction of independent sub-conclusions) combine as a product: A × B. This is the one place independence is assumed, and it is assumed only when the branches genuinely rest on disjoint premises; if they share a premise, that shared premise is counted once and the branches are not treated as independent.
  • Two branches where EITHER suffices (a disjunction of independent supports) combine as 1 − (1 − A)(1 − B), again only under genuine independence.

The single governing sentence: a chain is never more confident than its weakest gated premise times the product of its inference-type modifiers, and independent supports compose by the product/complement rules above.

Worked example. Take a three-step chain.

  • Step 1 (deductive). Premises: R1 "OCPD for 12 AWG Cu is capped at 20 A" (0.98, 2023 NEC 240.4(D)(5)) and R2 "12 AWG Cu carries 20–30 A across the temperature columns; at 75 °C, 25 A" (0.98, Table 310.16), under the stated install conditions. Conclude C₁: "Under these conditions, 12 AWG copper is code-adequate for a 20 A breaker." Type modifier × 1.00. step_confidence = min(0.98, 0.98) × 1.00 = 0.98.
  • Step 2 (inductive). From C₁ (0.98) plus the observation that comparable installations in this building pass inspection with 12 AWG (0.90), generalize C₂: "The other identical 20 A general-purpose circuits in this panel can use 12 AWG." Type modifier × 0.85. step_confidence = min(0.98, 0.90) × 0.85 = 0.90 × 0.85 = 0.77.
  • Step 3 (abductive). From C₂ (0.77) and a symptom — one such circuit's breaker nuisance-trips (0.85) — infer C₃: "The likeliest explanation is a continuous load on that circuit pushing it past the 125 % rule, not an undersized conductor." Type modifier × 0.70. step_confidence = min(0.77, 0.85) × 0.70 = 0.77 × 0.70 = 0.54.

The final conclusion C₃ carries confidence 0.54 — WEAKLY SUPPORTED, and it should. Step 1 alone is PROVEN-grade (0.98); but the moment the chain adds an inductive generalization and then an abductive diagnosis, the honest confidence falls into the low-0.5s. A system that reported the diagnosis with the certainty of the code lookup would be lying about its reasoning. The compounding is not a penalty — it is an accurate accounting of how much the chain can actually bear. The fix for low confidence is not to inflate the number; it is to retrieve a missing premise (e.g., measure the load) that turns the abductive step deductive.

One honest caveat about the arithmetic. This calculus is a deliberately conservative engineering heuristic for auditability — a monotone, traceable way to ensure a conclusion is never presented as more certain than its weakest premise and least-reliable inference jointly allow. It is not a calibrated probability: 0.85 × 0.70 is not "the probability of anything," and the type-modifiers are priors to be re-estimated against measured outcomes (see the calibration methods in Section 9), not measured frequencies. Its job is to make over-confidence structurally hard and the descent legible, not to output a Bayesian posterior.

Two structural rules round out chain reasoning. No circular dependencies: dependency must flow one way — the chain is a directed acyclic graph; if step 3 uses step 1's conclusion and step 1 uses step 3's, the chain is invalid. Independent verifiability: a reader must be able to check any single step — its premises, its named rule, its conclusion — without reading the whole chain.

11.4 — The Critical Difference

A pattern-matching system asks: "What response typically follows inputs like this?"

A reasoning system asks: "Given premises A, B, and C, what necessarily follows by valid inference?"

The pattern-matching system can produce ANY output — there is no constraint on what it generates. The reasoning system can ONLY produce outputs that validly follow from verified premises, at the confidence the calculus in §11.3 permits. This constraint is not a limitation. It is the source of reliability.

“The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.”

— Proverbs 18:15

Chapter 12: Stage 7 — VERIFY

12.1 — Purpose

Check the reasoning against reality. Verification is not optional. An unverified conclusion is a hypothesis, not an answer.

12.2 — The Verification Battery

Verification in this architecture is the Five-Level chain, and it is the same battery wherever VERIFY appears in the book — the canonical specification is the five levels and nineteen checks developed at length in Chapter 18 (the Verification Chain). This chapter is the operational summary of that canonical specification, not a competing one. Every conclusion passes through all five levels; passing four of five is not acceptable. Each level catches a class of error the others cannot, which is why the chain is defense-in-depth rather than a single test.

A level whose checks do not apply to a given problem is marked N/A — explicitly inapplicable — and never silently recorded as "passed." A class arithmetic problem has no Domain-Compliance code to satisfy (Level 4 → N/A); a pure logic puzzle has no Physical-Reality law to obey (Level 3 → N/A). Marking an inapplicable level "passed" launders an empty check into apparent confidence, which is exactly the failure the battery exists to prevent.

The nineteen checks, grouped by level, with the §12.x summary mapped one-to-one to the canonical Chapter 18 checks:

Level 1 — Logical Validity (does the inference hold?) — four checks.

  • 12.2.1 Internal Consistency maps to Checks 1.1–1.4: the named rule is correctly applied (1.1), no hidden premises (1.2), a full fallacy scan (1.3), and chain coherence — a valid DAG, no contradictions between branches (1.4). Does the conclusion contradict any premise or any previously verified conclusion? If yes, there is an error — find it.

Level 2 — Premise Truth (are the starting facts true?) — four checks.

  • The premise-truth checks are 2.1 Source Verification, 2.2 Confidence Verification, 2.3 Context Verification, and 2.4 Temporal Verification. These are where RETRIEVE's trust dimension (§10.6) is audited: provenance and authority feed 2.1, the carried confidence feeds 2.2, scope-of-applicability feeds 2.3, and currency/stale-edition feeds 2.4.

Level 3 — Physical Reality (is the conclusion physically possible?) — four checks.

  • 12.2.2 Dimensional Analysis maps to Check 3.2: do the units work out? If a force computation yields meters per second, the calculation is wrong. This catches a large fraction of quantitative errors.
  • 12.2.3 Boundary Conditions maps to Check 3.3: at extreme values, does the conclusion still make sense? Zero load → zero deflection? Empty input handled gracefully? Population of one → correct special case?
  • 12.2.4 Conservation Laws maps to Check 3.1: is energy/mass/charge/momentum conserved (and, by extension, do output data volumes match input, does the balance sheet balance)? A conservation violation means the analysis is wrong — full stop.
  • 12.2.5 Order of Magnitude maps to Check 3.4: is the answer in the right ballpark? A residential heating load of 50 million BTU/hr is a small power plant, not a house. Order-of-magnitude errors are the easiest to detect and among the most common.

Level 4 — Domain Compliance (does it meet applicable standards?) — three checks.

  • Standard Compliance (4.1), Best-Practice Compliance (4.2), Safety Compliance (4.3). This is where pinned code editions matter: "complies with the code" is not a verification result unless the edition and section are named (e.g., 2023 NEC Table 310.16; IBC 2021 §1609.2 with ASCE 7-16). An unpinned compliance claim fails Level 4 on its face.

Level 5 — Sanity Check (does it survive stress-testing?) — four checks.

  • 12.2.6 Known Examples maps to Check 5.1: is there a case where the answer is known? Does the reasoning reproduce it? If not, the reasoning is flawed.
  • 12.2.7 Independent Method maps to Check 5.2: can the conclusion be reached a different way? Two independent methods that agree raise confidence sharply; if they disagree, at least one is wrong — investigate.
  • Expert-Intuition Check (5.3): would a domain expert find this reasonable on sight? The softest check, but a conclusion every expert would question probably hides an error the formal checks missed.
  • 12.2.8 Adversarial Testing maps to Check 5.4: try to break the conclusion across the five attacks (assumption, edge case, counter-example, devil's advocate, time). What assumption, if false, makes the conclusion wrong? Is that assumption solid? Where is the weakest link?

Where a deterministic formal verifier exists for the domain — Lean/Coq/Isabelle for mathematics, type checkers and static analyzers for software, unit/conservation validators for physical calculations — its output supersedes the manual battery for the checks it covers (see §18.8). The reasoner may be probabilistic; the verifier, wherever possible, should not be. But note the caveat carried through the rest of the book: a verifier is itself a source with a reliability below 1.0, and a binary PASS from a fallible oracle cannot raise a conclusion's confidence above that oracle's own reliability (see Chapter 18b). PASS is necessary, not magic.

12.2a — The Independence Requirement

A battery of nineteen checks is only as trustworthy as its independence from the reasoning it audits. The deepest failure of verification is not a check that is skipped — the N/A discipline above guards that — but a check that runs in full while quietly reusing the very inference under test to confirm itself. If a conclusion was reached by assuming X, and the check that is supposed to test the conclusion also assumes X, the check will pass, and it will have proven nothing. The reasoning has graded its own exam with the answer key it wrote. This is the Oracle Problem (Chapter 21) appearing at the level of a single check: a verifier that shares the error it is meant to catch is blind to exactly that error.

The requirement that prevents it is independence. A check earns its PASS only when it reaches the conclusion — or fails to — by a route that does not depend on the step being checked. This is why Level 5's Independent Method (§12.2.7) is load-bearing rather than ornamental: "reached a different way" means a different way, with different premises or a different operation, so that agreement between the two is evidence and not an echo. It is why Dimensional Analysis (§12.2.2) and Order of Magnitude (§12.2.5) are powerful — they test the result against constraints the original derivation never invoked, so they cannot be fooled by an error inside that derivation. And it is the standing caution on any check that re-runs the original logic to "confirm" it: re-deriving a conclusion the same way you first derived it is not verification, it is repetition, and repetition launders a consistent mistake into apparent confidence. When a check cannot be made independent of the reasoning it covers, that limitation is recorded — the check is reported as confirming consistency, not truth — rather than counted as a clean PASS it did not earn.

12.3 — Verification Failure Protocol

If any verification check fails:

  • Stop. Do not proceed to synthesis.
  • Identify which level and which check failed, and classify the severity: HARD FAIL (provably wrong — must be corrected), SOFT FAIL (may be wrong or incomplete — correct or qualify), WARNING (does not invalidate, but document and surface).
  • Route the failure to its source stage: Level 1 → REASON; Level 2 → SCOPE or RETRIEVE; Level 3 → REASON, possibly SCOPE; Level 4 → REASON; Level 5 → investigate, then route.
  • Correct the error at its source — do not patch the symptom.
  • Re-verify from the point of correction forward.
  • Document the failure in the audit trail — which check failed, its severity, the source stage it routed to, and the correction applied. A corrected error that leaves no trace cannot teach anything: REFLECT (Stage 11) detects recurring failure patterns only from failures that were recorded, so the verification that silently fixes-and-forgets denies the system the one input from which it actually calibrates.

Do NOT paper over verification failures. Do NOT add reflexive caveats like "however, this should be verified." If you know it needs verification, verify it yourself before presenting it. (The one exception, developed in Section 8, is the residual hedge mandated in human-safety domains, where a fallible verifier's PASS is reported with its honest reliability rather than as bare certainty — that is calibrated disclosure, not a substitute for doing the verification.) Passing unverified conclusions to the user is a failure of the system, not a feature.
