Each level adds capability. Each is independently useful. And each, as we will be honest about throughout, buys a different kind of verification — not just a different fidelity of the same kind.

The chapters that follow do four things. Prompt architecture translates the eleven stages into instructions any model can follow. Fine-tuning methodology explains how to train the pattern into a model's weights. System design shows the multi-component architecture where neural reasoning meets deterministic verification. Measurement defines how to tell whether the system is actually thinking — and how to build the evaluation set that question presupposes. Between them sit the parts an engineering section cannot skip: a memory architecture, a cost and termination model, an acting-and-abstaining gate, and a calibration method. The complete cognitive prompt template closes the section as a production-ready artifact you can use today.

Chapter 26: Translating This Into Prompt Architecture

The Lowest-Cost, Highest-Availability Implementation

26.1 — The Opportunity

The Pattern of Mind does not require custom models. It does not require novel architectures. It does not require research budgets. The eleven stages can be encoded directly into the system prompt of any capable language model, producing immediate improvements in reasoning quality.

This is not the ideal implementation — fine-tuned models with external verification tools will always outperform prompt-only approaches, and as §26.4 and §28.4 will insist, prompt-only deployment buys a categorically weaker kind of checking. But it is the implementation available TODAY, to ANYONE, for FREE. And the improvement over default model behavior is substantial because the default behavior is optimized for preference, not truth. Even instructing a model to prioritize truth changes its output in measurable ways — measurable by the methods of Chapter 32, not by the warm feeling that the output reads better.

26.2 — The Cognitive Prompt Structure

The system prompt has five layers:

Each layer serves a specific function:

The IDENTITY layer establishes what the system is optimizing for. This is more important than it sounds. Language models are remarkably responsive to identity framing. A model told "you are a helpful assistant" behaves differently from a model told "you are a reasoning system committed to truth." The former optimizes for helpfulness (a proxy for preference). The latter optimizes for correctness. The framing determines the default behavior when trade-offs arise.

The COGNITIVE PROCESS layer provides the eleven-stage pipeline as explicit instructions. The model will not follow all stages perfectly on every query — but it will follow them more than it would without the instruction. And the stages it follows will produce measurably better reasoning than the default predict-next-token approach.

The TRUTH RULES layer provides the behavioral commitments: no fabrication, no equivocation, no hedging on determined answers, honest uncertainty, premise challenging. These rules directly counteract the preference-seeking behavior trained into the model by RLHF.

The VERIFICATION RULES layer provides specific checks: dimensional analysis, domain standard references, named inference rules. These are the most actionable instructions because they give the model concrete verification steps to execute. One caution belongs here, co-located with the promise so the reader cannot miss it: in a prompt-only deployment, these checks are run by the same model that produced the reasoning. That is self-assessment, not independent verification (Chapter 18, §18.1). It catches some errors. It cannot catch the errors the model is systematically blind to, because the checker shares the blind spot.

The DOMAIN GUARDRAILS layer injects domain-specific knowledge from the Ordered Light Framework — the curated, verified knowledge base described elsewhere. This layer changes per deployment: a medical system gets medical standards, a legal system gets legal standards, an engineering system gets engineering codes. Every code reference in the guardrails must carry an edition and a section, for the same reason the worked examples in this book now do: a premise you cannot re-check when the edition changes is not a premise, it is a rumor.

26.3 — The Thinking Block

In systems that support structured thinking (scratchpad, extended thinking, chain of thought), the stages can be implemented as explicit sections within the reasoning process:

<thinking>
STAGE 1 - RECEIVE:
The user is asking [precise restatement].
Ambiguities: [none / list with resolution strategy]

STAGE 2 - DECOMPOSE:
Sub-questions: [ordered list with dependencies]
Constraints: [list with hard/soft classification]
Success criteria: [list with priority]

STAGE 3 - CLASSIFY:
This is a [type] problem.
Engaged-stage set for this query: [list]
Processing approach: [selected approach with justification]

STAGE 4 - SCOPE:
Known-certain: [list with sources]
Known-uncertain: [list with confidence levels]
Unknown-findable: [list with retrieval plan]
Assumptions required: [list with justification]

STAGE 5 - RETRIEVE:
[Results of any tool calls or knowledge retrieval]

STAGE 6 - REASON:
Premise 1: [statement] (Source: [source], Confidence: [level])
Premise 2: [statement] (Source: [source], Confidence: [level])
Inference: [named rule] → Conclusion: [statement]
[Continue for each reasoning step]

STAGE 7 - VERIFY:
Logical validity: [pass/fail with details]
Premise truth: [pass/fail with details]
Physical reality: [pass / fail / N/A with details]
Domain rules: [pass / fail / N/A with details]
Sanity check: [pass/fail with details]
Verifier independence: [self-assessed / tool-checked]

STAGE 8 - SYNTHESIZE:
[Complete answer assembled from verified sub-conclusions]
Compatibility check: [results]
Completeness check: [results]

STAGE 9 - EVALUATE:
Confidence: [level with numeric range]
Failure modes: [list with likelihood and impact]
Overall assessment: [proceed / revise / abstain-and-defer]

STAGE 11 - REFLECT:
Difficulty: [assessment]
Weakest link: [identification]
Process notes: [improvements for future]
</thinking>

STAGE 10 - COMMUNICATE:
[Clear, direct answer to the user]

Note that Stage 10 (COMMUNICATE) is outside the thinking block — it is the visible output. Stage 11 (REFLECT) is inside the thinking block — it serves the system's learning, not the user's immediate needs. All other stages are internal processing that produces the answer the user sees.

Two small additions to the trace above are deliberate. VERIFY now records verifier independence and marks inapplicable levels N/A rather than silently "passing" them — a level with no content to check has not been satisfied, it has been skipped, and the trace should say so. EVALUATE now admits a third terminal verdict, abstain-and-defer, alongside proceed and revise; Chapter 15's ACT/ABSTAIN gate (recapped in this section's chapter on acting and escalation) defines when it fires.

26.4 — Scaling Cognitive Depth

Not every query requires the full eleven-stage treatment. The system scales depth to question complexity. But "scaling depth" must be stated carefully, or it contradicts the no-skip rule that anchors the book's indictment of current AI. It is tempting to read depth-scaling as license to drop stages; that is the error. The rule is stated so it is both true and non-negotiable:

CLASSIFY is always on. Every engaged stage completes before the next. Depth-scaling selects which stages are engaged for a given query; it never skips a stage that has been engaged.

The router is CLASSIFY itself (Stage 3), which runs after a minimal RECEIVE/DECOMPOSE pass on every query. It decides the engaged-stage set. Depth-scaling is therefore the controlled exception to "no stage is skipped" — controlled because the decision to engage fewer stages is itself a stage's output, logged and auditable, not an implicit shortcut.

Simple factual query ("What's the melting point of aluminum?"):

Technical question ("What size wire for a 20-amp circuit?"):

Design problem ("Design a login system for 10K concurrent users"):

Complex analysis ("Is this building code-compliant?"):

The system selects the engaged set at CLASSIFY. Simple problems get the minimal path. Complex problems get the full cognitive stack. The selection is not about saving effort for its own sake — it is about matching process to need, under a budget (the cost model of the deployment-economics chapter makes the budget explicit). A factual question that gets the full eleven-stage treatment is over-processed and over-billed. A design problem that gets the minimal treatment is under-processed and unsafe. Both are failures of calibration.

26.4.1 — Routing by Stakes, Not Just Complexity

The previous section scaled depth to complexity — how much reasoning the structure of a problem demands. Complexity is necessary but not sufficient. The care a question deserves is a function of two axes, not one: complexity and consequence. A question can be trivial to reason about and catastrophic to get wrong. "Is this dose safe?" is one short sentence; so is "Can I drop this table?" Neither has the structure of a design problem, and a complexity-only router hands both the four-stage minimal path — the same path it gives "What's the melting point of aluminum?" That is a calibration failure of the most dangerous kind, because it is invisible: the answer is delivered with the same fluent confidence as any other, and nothing in the process registers that the floor under it was never checked.

So the router scores a second axis before it selects the engaged set:

Complexity sets the ceiling on depth; stakes set the floor. CLASSIFY scores the consequence of a wrong answer — cosmetic, recoverable, or harmful — and its reversibility — reversible, costly to reverse, or irreversible. Any HIGH consequence or IRREVERSIBLE action makes the query high-stakes regardless of how simple it looks, and a high-stakes query may never take the minimal path: it engages REASON and the full five-level verification chain at minimum, no matter how short the question.

Read as a matrix, the two axes give four routes, not two:

Low complexityHigh complexity
Standard stakesMinimal path (≈4 stages)Full pipeline — complexity drives depth
High stakesModerate-to-full, never minimal — the simplicity is suspectFull pipeline with domain specialization

The asymmetry is what justifies the floor. Over-processing a trivial-but-dangerous question costs a few extra stages and a little latency. Under-processing it costs the harm itself — the wrong dose, the dropped table, the inadequate beam. The two error costs are not remotely symmetric, so when apparent simplicity and high stakes conflict, stakes win. This is the same logic that governs the abstention and escalation terminals of Chapter 31: a system that knows the stakes are high and its footing uncertain owes the user more process, or an honest hand-off, not a faster answer.

It also disposes of the excuse "but it was a simple question." The simplicity was real. It was just the wrong axis to route on.

26.4.2 — Triage: The Stakes Decision Before Reasoning

The matrix in §26.4.1 is the output of a decision; this section is about the decision itself, and about where in the pipeline it has to happen. The stakes-and-complexity score is not something the router can compute after reasoning, the way one computes a confidence at EVALUATE. By then the engaged-stage set is fixed and the budget committed; a stakes judgment that arrives at Stage 9 arrives too late to change how Stages 4 through 8 were run. The judgment has to be the first thing the system does, before any real reasoning is spent. (This is the triage the reference architecture runs as Stage 0, ahead of the eleven.)

So CLASSIFY opens with a cheap, always-on triage — a few tokens, never skipped, run on every query including the ones that look too trivial to deserve it. It answers three questions, and the order matters:

  1. What is actually being asked? The real intent, not the surface. "How do I rotate this mesh" may really be "why is my model facing the wrong way" — a different question with a different answer.
  2. What does being wrong cost, and is the error reversible? The consequence-and-reversibility score of §26.4.1, asked here as a reflex rather than derived after the fact.
  3. Am I sure this is as simple as it looks? The under-classification guard — the single most important reflex in the whole process.

The first two feed the matrix. The third keeps it honest, because the matrix can only route on the stakes it was given, and the most common way a high-stakes query takes the minimal path is that triage scored it low on a glance and never looked again. The third question is the look-again; when its answer is anything short of a confident "yes," the triage tiers up.

The three questions resolve to one of four depth tiers, each carrying more verification weight than the last:

TierWhen it firesVerification weight
ReflexA greeting, one settled fact, an obvious yes/noA one-beat check: did I answer what was asked, and if there is a single fact, is it right and current?
StandardA normal question, a few moving parts, low cost of errorA brief explicit chain; a scan against the obviously relevant failure modes
DeepHard, multi-step, design, debugging, anything spatial, anything whose error propagates downstreamThe full engaged pipeline, closing on the five-level verification chain
CriticalIrreversible, safety-affecting, materially affecting another person, or touching money, production, or a physical claimDeep plus: only PROVEN-confidence conclusions may drive action, a disconfirmation hunt at maximum rigor, and a deliberate slow-down-and-ask when footing is uncertain

Two commitments do not scale down with the tier, and the trace must show both even at Reflex: the intent check from question 1 (a one-word reply still answers the real question, not a misread of it) and some closing verification, sized to the tier. A casual question never licenses a confident guess; the honesty rules are tier-independent. What the tier scales is the weight of the checking, never its existence.

The third question is load-bearing because most failures of judgment are not failures of reasoning — they are failures of triage: treating a Deep problem as Reflex because it looked easy. A "quick gut check" on whether some battery covers some runtime looks like a Reflex lookup; it can hide a duty-cycle assumption that makes it Deep. A stress check that passes and feels finished can have missed buckling — the governing failure mode that was never on the list. The reasoning that ran was competent; it simply ran at the wrong tier, and no care inside an under-scoped pass repairs a pass that should never have been short. This is the same asymmetry §26.4.1 named — over-processing costs a little time, under-processing ships the harm — now stated as a routing reflex:

When the tier is in doubt, treat the query as higher-stakes than it appears and let verification talk you back down — never the reverse.

26.5 — What Prompt Architecture Can and Cannot Do

What it can do:

  • Redirect the model's optimization target from preference to truth.
  • Provide explicit reasoning structure that produces better chains.
  • Force self-check steps that catch some errors.
  • Introduce honest uncertainty language.
  • Counteract sycophancy and fabrication tendencies.
  • Scale cognitive depth to problem stakes and complexity, under a stated budget.

What it cannot do:

  • Guarantee the model follows the instructions (it is still probabilistic).
  • Provide independent verification. The same model reasons and checks; this is self-assessment, and it caps the confidence a prompt-only deployment can honestly claim. This is not a fidelity gap that more prompting closes — it is a categorical boundary (§28.4).
  • Overcome fundamental knowledge gaps in the base model.
  • Match the performance of a purpose-trained system with real tools.
  • Maintain a persistent, structured world model across reasoning steps or conversation turns (the memory chapter says exactly which patterns can and cannot).

Prompt architecture is the 80/20 solution. It captures the majority of the Pattern of Mind's structuring benefit with minimal investment. For many deployments with moderate stakes, this is sufficient. For high-stakes deployments where correctness must be independently established, the tool-augmented and full neurosymbolic approaches (Chapter 28) provide the remaining capability — and the verification that prompt-only cannot.

26.6 — Governance Is Architectural, Not in the Weights

A consequence of building the Pattern of Mind at the prompt-and-agent layer, rather than into a model's weights, is easy to miss and worth stating plainly: the governance is substrate-agnostic. The eleven stages, the named-inference discipline, the verification levels, the confidence calculus, and the values gate are expressed as instructions and agent definitions — text with structured front-matter — not as properties of any one network. The same discipline runs on any host that honors that format, against whatever model sits underneath it.

This is not a hypothetical portability. The agentic coding tools that matured through 2025–2026 already route a single session across many interchangeable providers — one such tool, Forge (open-source, Apache-2.0, as of mid-2026), advertises routing across three hundred or more models and lets the operator swap the model mid-session. The infrastructure these tools converge on is, almost item for item, the substrate this architecture assumes: role-specialized agents defined as plain text files, a tool-call loop, external tools reached over a shared protocol, isolated worktrees for safe execution. What that infrastructure does not supply is the governance — a closed catalog of inference rules at the reasoning step, an independent check in the feedback slot, a confidence level that is earned rather than asserted, a values layer that can refuse. The harness is built; what runs inside it is still ungoverned generation. That is precisely the gap this book fills, and the fact that the harness now exists, widely and for free, is the opportunity.

Model-swapping sharpens the point, and it cuts directly against the intuition that a strong enough base model makes the architecture unnecessary. The opposite holds. When the model underneath is interchangeable, you cannot lean on any single model's training to keep it honest: one provider's refusal behavior, another's calibration, a third's reluctance to fabricate are not portable, and the next model swapped in may carry none of them. The only thing that travels with the session rather than the weights is the architecture. Multi-provider routing is therefore an argument for governing the cognition explicitly, not against it — the more freely the model can change, the more the discipline has to live in the structure that survives the change.

This is the same reason the prompt-architecture layer (§26.2–26.5) is the keystone and not a consolation prize. It is the one layer that holds for every deployment, on every model, on every host. Fine-tuning and the tool-augmented and neurosymbolic approaches deepen it where the stakes justify the cost; they do not replace it.

“Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established.”

— Proverbs 16:3

Chapter 27: Translating This Into Fine-Tuning Methodology

Training for Truth Instead of Preference

27.1 — The Alternative Reward Function

The core change is simple to state and consequential in its implications:

Instead of asking only: "Did the human rater prefer this response?"

Reward also: "Is this response correct — and did it abstain when it should have?"

Correctness metrics:

Factual accuracy — verifiable against authoritative sources. Not "does it sound right?" but "is it right?"

Logical validity — inference rules correctly applied, no fallacies. Not "does the reasoning sound convincing?" but "is the reasoning valid?"

Calibrated confidence — stated confidence matches actual reliability. Not "does it sound confident?" but "is the confidence level accurate?" (Chapter 32 specifies how this is measured, not merely asserted.)

Completeness — all sub-questions addressed, all constraints checked. Not "does it cover the topic?" but "does it address everything asked?"

Honesty — uncertainty flagged, limitations acknowledged, "I don't know" said when appropriate. Not "does it always produce an answer?" but "does it produce honest answers?"

Consistency — same answer under different phrasings. Not "does it adapt to the user?" but "does it give the same truth regardless of framing?"

This produces a system optimized for truth alongside approval, rather than approval alone — a system with values, not merely preferences.

The abstention-credited term. A correctness objective built only on "right answer = +1, wrong answer = 0, no answer = 0" trains the model to guess: when a confident guess sometimes scores +1 and abstaining always scores 0, the expected value of guessing is positive. This is not a hypothetical. Kalai, Nachum, Vempala, and Zhang ("Why Language Models Hallucinate," 2025) trace hallucination to a pretraining statistical floor that is then amplified by evaluation incentives that reward a guess over an honest "I don't know" — and RLHF is only one such amplifier. A naive binary correctness reward is another. The fix is to grade abstention explicitly:

With r_wrong > r_abstain > 0, a calibrated model that is genuinely unsure maximizes expected reward by abstaining rather than guessing — the behavior the honesty value demands and the behavior naive RLVR punishes. The deployment-time expression of this is the ACT/ABSTAIN gate; the training-time expression is this reward term. They must agree, or the model will learn one thing and be asked to do another.

27.2 — Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)

In January 2025 DeepSeek released R1-Zero, trained by pure reinforcement learning (GRPO) from a base model with no supervised fine-tuning and no human-preference data — a correctness-only reward signal. For reasoning tasks it works by replacing the learned reward model with objective verification:

The reward signal is closer to objective than a learned reward model can be — CORRECT or INCORRECT against a checker rather than a rater. The striking result, documented in DeepSeek's Nature paper (18 September 2025; arXiv:2501.12948): training with verifiable rewards alone produced emergent self-reflection, verification, and strategy adaptation — the "aha moment" where the model spontaneously writes "Wait, let me reconsider." Nobody trained those behaviors in. They emerged because they were the strategies that actually produced correct answers.

This is the defensible form of the Pattern of Mind's training thesis: a correctness reward is sufficient to make reasoning behaviors emerge. It is not evidence that preference can be eliminated, and it is essential not to overclaim it as such. R1-Zero was, by DeepSeek's own account, unshippable: it produced language mixing, poor readability, and behavior unsuited to general assistance. The model DeepSeek actually shipped, R1, re-added a cold-start supervised fine-tuning stage and a neural preference reward model (helpfulness and harmlessness) for general tasks. So the honest claim has two parts, and they must be kept apart:

  • Correctness reward makes reasoning emerge — true of R1-Zero, the clean experiment.
  • Preference alignment was eliminated — false of R1, the deployed system, which re-added exactly that preference reward. The book's own related-work table elsewhere notes R1 "falls back to RLHF for general tasks"; this chapter states it too.

The lesson the Pattern of Mind takes is not "delete preference." It is "add a correctness gradient where one can be computed, and credit honest abstention, so that the preference signal is no longer the only thing the model optimizes."

Why RLVR is not incorruptible. It is tempting to call the binary reward "incorruptible." It is not. RLVR is harder to hack than a learned reward model — there is no soft preference surface to climb — but it is still gameable, and the exploit simply relocates from the rater to the verifier and the task specification:

  • Test leakage / contamination — the model has seen the test answers, so "passes the checker" measures memorization, not reasoning.
  • Hard-coded answers and format exploits — the model emits a string that satisfies the checker's pattern without doing the work (e.g., printing the expected output, exploiting a lax answer-extraction regex).
  • Verifier bugs — a compiler that accepts a degenerate solution, a unit test with a gap, a proof checker invoked on the wrong goal.
  • Reward shaping artifacts — auxiliary rewards (R1-Zero itself needed format and language-consistency rewards to be usable) become their own optimization targets.

This is the book's own Chapter 18 principle turned on its own training method: the reasoner must not be its own final verifier. A verifier the model can probe and overfit is, at the margin, another thing to perform for. The mitigations are concrete and belong in any RLVR pipeline:

  • Held-out verifiers and held-out test items the policy never sees during training, refreshed on a schedule, with contamination screening (the evaluation-set chapter specifies the screen).
  • Adversarial verifier review — treat verifier bugs as a security surface; fuzz the checker; reward the process trace on a sampled subset, not only the final string.
  • Auxiliary rewards declared and monitored as the partial, gameable signals they are, with their own drift metrics.

Verifiable rewards reduce reward hacking; they do not abolish it. State it that way.

27.3 — Process Reward Models: Evaluating Every Step

Standard training evaluates only the final output: Is this response good? Process Reward Models (PRMs) evaluate every intermediate reasoning step: Is this step valid? Did this step move closer to the correct answer or further away?

Step-level reward modeling is established prior art, not a Pattern-of-Mind invention. Lightman et al., "Let's Verify Step by Step" (2023), showed that process supervision — rewarding each correct step — outperforms outcome supervision on hard reasoning, and released the PRM800K step-level labels. The book inherits the idea of step-level reward; it does not originate it, and saying so is the honesty the book demands of everyone else.

What the Pattern of Mind adds is not the existence of a step-level signal but the per-stage criteria — a specification of what "correct" means at each of the eleven stages, which generic PRM research leaves open:

  • Did RECEIVE correctly identify the question (and flag, not bury, ambiguity)?
  • Did DECOMPOSE produce valid sub-questions with explicit success criteria?
  • Did CLASSIFY select the right problem type and the right engaged-stage set?
  • Did SCOPE accurately inventory what is known, unknown, and assumed?
  • Did RETRIEVE find relevant, authoritative, edition-pinned sources?
  • Did REASON apply named inference rules, with sources and confidence on each premise?
  • Did VERIFY run the applicable levels and mark the inapplicable ones N/A?

Each stage gets a reward signal scored against a stated criterion rather than a rater's gut feel. This is the contribution: not "score the steps" (Lightman did that) but "here is the rubric for each step." It pushes against the "right answer, wrong reasoning" failure — the model that pattern- matched its way to a correct number on top of an invalid chain that will collapse on the next problem.

State the RLHF reward model precisely: it is not that the reward model "did NOT learn to be correct." It learned to predict human preference, and on open-ended tasks human-preference reward underweights correctness relative to fluency and agreeableness. "Underweighted," not "absent," is the accurate and still-damning claim.

27.4 — First-Order Logic as a Training Signal (and what it actually does)

A December 2025 preprint, "A First-Order Logic–Based Alternative to Reward Models in RLHF" (arXiv:2512.14100), proposes a method, S-GRPO, that translates model outputs into first-order-logic representations and uses logical structure in the reward. It is tempting to describe this as a way to "evaluate responses even when ground-truth answers don't exist" and as "grounded in formal logic rather than learned approximation." That description is the opposite of what the paper does. Here is what it does.

What S-GRPO actually does: it converts both the model's output and a reference answer to first-order logic and scores their logical equivalence. It is therefore:

  • Label-dependent / reference-dependent. It needs a reference answer to compare against. It does not evaluate without ground truth; it requires exactly the ground truth one might imagine it dispenses with.
  • A preference-alignment method, by its own abstract — it extends preference-learning frameworks (GRPO, DPO) with a logic-similarity term, jointly optimizing a generation term, a KL regularizer, and a label-based objective.
  • A measure of internal consistency, not correspondence to reality. Logical equivalence to a reference says the answer has the same logical shape as the label. By the book's own Chapter 4 definition, that is coherence with a representation, not contact with the world.

The honest summary: S-GRPO reduces reliance on a learned reward model for tasks whose answers have checkable logical structure, by scoring equivalence to a reference rather than scoring a rater's preference. Where no reference or metric exists, it falls back to a reward model like everything else. It is a small single-lab preprint and a useful data point — not "the most direct implementation of the Pattern of Mind thesis," and not primary validation of anything. It belongs in related work, hedged, with its label-dependence stated in the same breath as its name.

This still connects to Chapter 17 (the Logic Engine): formal structure can be a component of a reward where the task is logic-shaped. That is the defensible claim, and it is the only one to make; the grander reading — that logic-structured reward dispenses with ground truth altogether — does not survive contact with the paper.

27.5 — Reasoning Distillation

DeepSeek also demonstrated that reasoning patterns learned by large models can be transferred to smaller models through distillation — and that distilled models outperform small models trained independently with RL.

This has practical implications:

  • Train the full Pattern of Mind at maximum scale (large models, expensive verification, formal proof tools).
  • Extract the reasoning patterns into training data.
  • Distill those patterns into smaller, deployable models.

The reasoning capability transfers even when the smaller model could not have discovered those patterns through its own RL training. The large model serves as REASONER and DISCOVERER. The small model serves as PRACTITIONER — applying learned reasoning patterns efficiently.

This means the Pattern of Mind does not require massive inference infrastructure for every deployment. The expensive discovery phase happens once. The cheaper deployment phase benefits from it indefinitely. Note the honest limit: distillation transfers reasoning patterns, not an independent verifier. A distilled model that has internalized "verify before asserting" still needs a real tool in the loop to do the verifying when stakes are high.

27.6 — Training Data Requirements

Training a model to implement the Pattern of Mind requires structured training data that differs from standard instruction-following datasets:

Reasoning-process pairs. Not just input→output but input→reasoning→output. The model must learn HOW to get to the answer, not just WHAT the answer is. Every training example includes the explicit reasoning chain: premises stated, inference rules named, verification checks performed.

"I don't know" examples. The model must learn that honest uncertainty is credited, not penalized — this is the data side of the abstention-credited reward of §27.1. Training data must include examples where the correct response is "I don't know, because..." with explanation of what information is missing, and counter-examples where abstention would be a false silence because the answer was determinable.

Premise-challenging examples. Training data must include examples where the question contains a false premise and the correct response is to challenge the premise rather than answer within it.

Calibrated confidence examples. Training data must include examples at all confidence levels, with the confidence level matching the evidence strength. The model learns the relationship between evidence and confidence, not just the language patterns.

Verification failure examples. Training data must include examples where the initial reasoning contains an error, the verification catches it, and the reasoning is corrected. The model learns the failure-and-correction loop, not just successful reasoning.

Every one of these categories presupposes a gold standard — somebody knew the right answer, the false premise, the appropriate confidence. That gold standard is not free, and an engineering account must say where it comes from. Chapter 32's evaluation-set protocol (the §32.5 construction protocol) specifies the sourcing, adjudication, contamination control, and labeling cost. The training data and the evaluation data are built by the same pipeline and must be drawn from disjoint pools, or every metric in Chapter 32 is measuring contamination.

“Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer.”

— Proverbs 25:4

Chapter 28: Memory Architecture

What Persists, For How Long, and How It Is Retrieved

A world model (§28.3, recapped below) is not enough on its own: it does not say how state persists across the three timescales a deployed system actually faces. A reasoning trace that forgets a constraint established three steps earlier, an assistant that re-asks what the user told it last turn, and a system that has solved a thousand similar problems and learned nothing from any of them are three different failures with three different fixes. This chapter names the three memory tiers, gives each a create–load–merge–evict lifecycle and a retrieval step, wires the REVISE operation to the turn boundary, and states plainly which deployment patterns can accumulate cross-problem wisdom and which cannot.

28.1 — Three Timescales of State

The tiers are nested in trust, not just time: Tier 1 is the only tier whose contents were derived within the current verification chain. Tier 2 and Tier 3 contents are inputs and must be tagged with provenance and treated as premises to be re-verified, not as conclusions already earned. A fact promoted from Tier 1 to Tier 2 carries its confidence and its source with it; a fact recalled from Tier 3 into a new problem re-enters at SCOPE as a known-with-stated-confidence, not as ground truth.

28.2 — The Lifecycle: Create, Load, Merge, Evict, Retrieve

Each tier supports the same five operations, specialized by timescale:

CREATE. Initialize the tier's store. Tier 1 is created at RECEIVE for every engaged query. Tier 2 is created at the first turn of a session. Tier 3 is created once per deployment and persists.

LOAD. Bring relevant prior state into the current reasoning episode. This is the read path. Tier 1 loads nothing (it is fresh). Tier 2 loads the session's resolved facts and open threads at the start of each turn. Tier 3 loads candidate priors via retrieval (below) at SCOPE.

MERGE. Integrate new state with existing state, resolving conflicts. The merge rule is non-negotiable and is where most memory systems quietly corrupt themselves: a higher-confidence, better-sourced item supersedes a lower-confidence one; a genuine contradiction between two well-sourced items is not silently resolved — it is surfaced as a conflict for the reasoning chain to adjudicate, and if it cannot be adjudicated it is reported as an open contradiction. Merge never averages two incompatible facts into a confident third.

EVICT. Remove or down-weight state. Tier 1 evicts at answer delivery. Tier 2 evicts on a recency/relevance policy and at session end. Tier 3 evicts only by explicit, logged policy — superseded facts (a new code edition, a corrected datum) are marked superseded with their replacement and date, not deleted, so that an audit can reconstruct what the system believed and when. Silent eviction is forbidden for the same reason silent guessing is.

RETRIEVE. Fetch the relevant subset rather than loading everything. This is the operation that makes Tier 3 usable at all: a system with a large persistent store must retrieve by relevance to the current problem (content/semantic match plus domain and recency filters), return candidates with their stored confidence and provenance, and let SCOPE decide what to trust. Retrieval that returns text without provenance reintroduces the hallucination-origin problem at the memory layer.

28.3 — Wiring REVISE to the Turn Boundary

The REVISE operation — update beliefs when new information arrives — was defined in the cognitive cycle but never connected to where new information enters across turns. It enters at the turn boundary:

Without this wiring, a multi-turn deployment treats each turn as a fresh problem (forgetting what it was told) or naively concatenates turns (accumulating contradictions). REVISE-at-the-turn-boundary is what lets a session behave like a single coherent reasoning process spread over time rather than a sequence of amnesiac episodes.

28.4 — Where Cross-Problem "Wisdom" Lives — and Where It Cannot

Tier 3 is where a system gets better over its operational lifetime: it stores the recurring failure patterns REFLECT surfaces, the calibration corrections measured by Chapter 32, and the verified facts worth keeping. This is the honest version of the "by the thousandth problem the system is wiser" claim — wisdom is a store with a retrieval and eviction policy, not an emergent glow.

But a deployment can only accumulate Tier-3 wisdom if it has a Tier-3 store the system controls, and that is exactly where the integration patterns of the next chapter diverge:

  • Pattern 1 (prompt-only) has no persistent store the system manages beyond the context window. It can simulate Tier 2 within a single context and nothing of Tier 3. It cannot accumulate cross-session wisdom. Say so; do not market a stateless deployment as a learning one.
  • Pattern 2 (tool-augmented) can attach an external Tier-3 store (a database, a vector index) and implement retrieval. It can accumulate wisdom to the extent its store and eviction policy are real.
  • Pattern 3 (full neurosymbolic) owns all three tiers as first-class components with explicit invariants, and is the only pattern that can run the full memory architecture as specified.

28.5 — The World Model (recap and reconciliation)

The Tier-1 substrate is the explicit world model — the missing layer in default LLMs — and Gary Marcus's long-standing critique still applies: LLMs process tokens by statistical association and do not, by default, maintain a structured representation of the current state of the world being discussed — which is why a model can explain the rules of chess and then make an illegal move.

The Pattern of Mind maintains one canonical structured state, not two competing schemas. The substrate has six fields; the reasoning ledger is a derived view over it, not a rival structure:

success_criteria lives here explicitly because Stage 9 cannot evaluate an answer it has no criteria for; a world-model schema that omits it cannot support evaluation at all. The world model must be explicit (checkable data, not token probabilities), persistent (across all reasoning steps in the episode), updatable (modified by REVISE), and consistent (checked for contradictions after every update via the MERGE rule). This is computationally expensive and only Patterns 2 and 3 can carry it outside the context window — which is one more reason the patterns are not interchangeable.

“Wise men lay up knowledge: but the mouth of the foolish is near destruction.”

— Proverbs 10:14

Chapter 29: Translating This Into System Design

The Multi-Component Architecture

29.1 — System Architecture for Thinking AI

The Pattern of Mind can be implemented as a system architecture that wraps a base language model with specialized components:

(figure: the eleven stages as a pipeline — RECEIVER → DECOMPOSER → CLASSIFIER → SCOPER → RETRIEVER → REASONER → VERIFIER, with a PASS? gate looping VERIFIER back to REASONER on failure, then SYNTHESIZER → EVALUATOR → COMMUNICATOR → verified output.)

The critical insight (the L / T / H tags above) is that different stages are best served by different types of processing:

LLM-native stages: RECEIVER, DECOMPOSER, CLASSIFIER, REASONER, SYNTHESIZER, COMMUNICATOR — these leverage the language model's strength in natural language understanding and generation.

Tool-native stages: VERIFIER (calculators, dimensional checkers, code execution, formal proof assistants), RETRIEVER (search engines, database queries, API calls) — these leverage deterministic tools that cannot hallucinate. ("Cannot hallucinate" is not "cannot be wrong": a tool can be buggy, a source can be superseded, a checker can be invoked on the wrong goal. Each verifier carries a reliability estimate, and a conclusion's confidence is capped at its weakest oracle.)

Hybrid stages: SCOPER (LLM to identify gaps + database to check availability and load memory), EVALUATOR (LLM to assess quality + calibration rules to assign confidence + the ACT/ABSTAIN gate) — these combine neural and symbolic processing.

The architecture combines the LLM's strength (natural language, creative reasoning, hypothesis generation) with deterministic tools' strength (reliable checking, accurate retrieval, formal verification), producing a system that is both fluent and — where a real verifier exists — independently checked.

29.2 — The Intuition-Verification Loop

The most important architectural pattern in recent research is the loop between neural intuition and symbolic verification. This pattern is not original to this book, and the book should name its neighbors. The generate → critique → revise-on-the-failure-reason loop is structurally Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) and Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023). What the Pattern of Mind contributes is the slot it puts in the feedback position: a hard formal verifier returning a specific error diagnostic, rather than the model's own free-text self-critique. Reflexion and Self-Refine loop on self-generated reflection; the architecture here loops on a deterministic check where one exists. That is the delta, and it is real only because it is stated.

Google DeepMind's AlphaGeometry solves International Mathematical Olympiad geometry problems by iterating between two components: a neural network suggests "constructs" — intuitive ideas about what auxiliary elements might help — and a symbolic deduction engine attempts to rigorously prove the statement using formal logic. If the proof fails, the neural model generates a new suggestion informed by the failure reason. They loop until the proof succeeds or resources are exhausted.

This is the REASONER → VERIFIER → loop-back-to-REASONER pattern, at the level of mathematical competition.

The error diagnostic is critical. When verification fails, the system must report not just "wrong" but "wrong because step 3 violated conservation of energy" or "wrong because the inference from line 2 to line 3 is an undistributed-middle fallacy." This specific feedback is what lets the REASONER generate a better candidate next iteration. And — non-negotiably — the loop is budgeted. "Loop until resources are exhausted" is not a termination condition; the deployment-economics chapter defines a single cognition budget and a terminal state when it runs out. The terminal state is an honest-uncertainty output, never a silent best guess.

A scale claim must be stated carefully. SAP reported, in a single December 2024 Fortune article, that fine-tuning an LLM on its proprietary ABAP programming language reached roughly 80% code-generation accuracy, and that adding a formal parser checking each generated token's legality raised ABAP code-generation accuracy to 99.8%. This is a real and instructive data point for the neurosymbolic pattern. It is also: (a) code-syntax validity for one proprietary language, not domain-general accuracy; (b) a token-legality parser, not "knowledge graphs"; and (c) sourced to one piece of trade press, not a peer-reviewed result. It motivates the design in formal, checkable domains. It does not "prove" the architecture at "enterprise scale" in general; reading it that way overreaches the evidence.

Neither component alone solves the problem. The neural network cannot prove anything. The symbolic engine cannot generate creative ideas. Together, in domains where a real verifier exists, they achieve what neither can alone. This is the neurosymbolic pattern — well-motivated in formal and checkable domains, and honestly bounded outside them.

29.3 — World Models in the System

The world model of Chapter 28 is the system-level state component: explicit, persistent, structured, updatable, consistency-checked. In the multi-component architecture it lives outside the LLM's context window, managed by a state-management component shared across stages, with the MERGE invariant enforced after every update. It eliminates the class of errors where the system "forgets" a constraint established earlier in the reasoning chain — the class Marcus has documented for years as fundamental to default LLM behavior. It is expensive, and only Patterns 2 and 3 can carry it. (Full schema and lifecycle: Chapter 28.)

29.4 — Integration Patterns, by Verification Independence

Three integration patterns emerge. It is tempting to frame them as "the same architecture at different fidelity." That framing hides the most important fact about them. They are better organized by the independence of their verification, because that is a categorical boundary, not a dial:

Pattern 1: Prompt-Only (minimal infrastructure). The LLM receives the cognitive prompt template (Chapter 33) and executes all engaged stages internally. No external tools. Verification is self-assessment: the same model that reasons also checks its reasoning. By the book's own §18.1, that is not independent verification — and so Pattern 1 produces self-assessed conclusions, not verified ones. It must cap its confidence accordingly: no prompt-only conclusion should be reported above the band reserved for independently checked claims. Suitable for moderate stakes where a residual "verify this independently" is acceptable.

Pattern 2: Tool-Augmented (moderate infrastructure). The LLM handles reasoning and communication. External tools handle verification (code execution, formal checkers, search), retrieval (knowledge bases, APIs), domain compliance (edition-pinned standard lookups), and memory (Tier-3 store). Where a real verifier exists for the task, conclusions are independently checked and may claim higher confidence. Where one does not, this pattern degrades to Pattern 1's self-assessment for that sub-question — and should say which sub-questions are which. Suitable for professional use with significant stakes.

Pattern 3: Full Neurosymbolic (maximum infrastructure). Each stage has dedicated processing, with deterministic components for the symbolic stages, shared world-model state, the full three-tier memory architecture, and orchestration that enforces the budget and the ACT/ABSTAIN gate. Independent verification wherever a verifier exists; honest disclosure where none does. Suitable for high-stakes deployments.

The categorical boundary is between Pattern 1 and the rest: independence of the checker. That is the line §18.1 draws and §26.5 concedes, now co-located so no reader can hold one without the other. The remaining gap — true even of Pattern 3 — is that no pattern has an independent verifier for queries where none exists in the world. For those, the honest output is structured uncertainty, not a confident answer dressed in the appearance of verification.

29.5 — When Your Own Pipeline Is a Group: Cascade Hygiene

The eleven stages, run as a sequential multi-agent chain — one agent per stage, or one stage handing structured state to the next — are not eleven independent minds. They are a line of people each whispering to the next. Whatever RECEIVE heard and CLASSIFY labelled becomes the frame every downstream stage inherits, and a frame, once inherited, is rarely re-opened. This is an information cascade: the second actor trusts the first, the third trusts the cascade, and by REASON the original question has been replaced by an early paraphrase of it that no one has re-checked. The chain feels like deliberation. It is closer to a rumour.

I will not soften the part that bites. The book has already conceded, at §18.1 and §26.5, that a model checking its own reasoning is a student grading their own test. A chain of stages does not repair this. If VERIFY reads the same framing that REASON built on the same framing CLASSIFY set, the verification is not independent — it is the cascade inspecting itself and finding, predictably, that it agrees. Sequencing adds steps, not independence. Independence is a categorical property (§29.4), and the chain does not supply it by being long.

The fix borrows from how disciplined groups defeat their own conformity, and the parallels are exact:

Group practiceCascade-hygiene mechanism in the pipeline
Independent judgment before discussionFresh-context re-derivation from the original question
Re-validate the premise, don't inherit itRe-check RECEIVE/CLASSIFY framings, never assume
Designated devil's advocateMandatory dissent probe when consensus is clean
Surface unique, non-shared informationReload from source; do not relay the paraphrase

Three rules make this operational.

Re-derive, do not relay. At least one verification pass must run from the original RECEIVE input in a fresh context — not from the accumulated state. It re-reads the question and answers it cold, then compares its answer to the chain's. Agreement now means something; agreement among links of one chain meant only that the chain was consistent with itself.

Re-validate framing, do not inherit it. The RECEIVE intake and the CLASSIFY label are re-checked against the source, not accepted because an earlier stage produced them. A misread question and a misrouted class are the two errors that propagate furthest and cost the most, because every downstream stage is faithfully correct about the wrong thing.

Probe dissent when consensus is too clean. This is the Observer's premature-unanimity sign (§16.2.1 — "no tension anywhere") promoted to a gate. If every stage agreed without friction, a designated pass must state the strongest case against the emerging conclusion before it may be reported. Clean consensus in a cascade is not corroboration; it is the most common symptom of one.

None of this adds a twelfth stage. Cascade hygiene is support machinery the existing stages consult — VERIFY runs the cold re-derivation, EVALUATE runs the dissent probe — and it pairs directly with the red-team discipline (pom-redteam), which attacks the conclusion from outside the chain rather than auditing it from within. The chain may still be wrong. But a wrong answer that survived an independent re-derivation and a forced dissent has earned its confidence; one that merely propagated unchallenged has not.

29.6 — Matching Task to Flow to Data

Everything before this section answered a single question in two ways: how deep should the thinking go? The complexity scale (§26.4) set the ceiling; the stakes floor (§26.4.1) and the triage tiers (§26.4.2) set the minimum. But depth is only one of two dimensions a system has to choose, and it is the one the book has already spent itself on. There is a second choice, made before the first stage runs, that no router so far has touched: not how much to think, but in what shape — and on what data.

The router asks how hard and how dangerous a question is. This section asks a different thing: what kind of problem is it, structurally? A proof and a five-component system design can score identically on stakes and complexity and still demand entirely different machinery — one a single tight chain that must not fork, the other a fan-out of independent investigations that must be merged. Stakes and complexity choose the depth. Problem shape chooses the flow. They are orthogonal axes, and a system that scores only the first will route a parallelizable research question and a strictly-sequential build down the same pipe, paying the wrong cost for both.

So I will name the third axis plainly and add it to the router:

Stakes set the floor, complexity sets the ceiling, and shape sets the form. Before depth is chosen, CLASSIFY scores the structure of the task — are its parts independent or dependent, is the answer a single object or a synthesis of many, must premises be fixed before work begins — and selects a flow. Depth and shape are independent: a high-stakes task may take any shape, and every shape must still honour its stakes floor.

The four flows

Four flow-shapes cover the field. They are not fidelity levels of one architecture — that framing, which §29.4 already warned against for the integration patterns, hides the only fact that matters here: each fits a different structure of problem, and using the wrong one is not a matter of paying too much or too little. It is building the wrong machine.

The minimal path — one pass, no fork. A settled fact, a short lookup, a single deterministic transformation. The task has no internal structure worth decomposing and no consequence worth fanning out for. This is the Reflex/Standard tier of §26.4.2 expressed as a flow: receive, answer, do the one closing check the tier demands. Reaching for anything heavier is the over-processing the asymmetry tolerates but does not reward.

The full pipeline — one mind, all stages, in sequence. A genuinely hard single question whose parts are entangled, not separable: a diagnosis, a proof, a judgment call where every consideration bears on every other. You cannot hand three independent agents a third of a proof each; the steps depend on one another, and the value is in one chain holding the whole thing in view. This is the eleven stages run as intended, and §29.5's cascade hygiene is its mandatory companion — a single deep chain is exactly the structure most prone to inheriting its own early framing.

Fan-out-and-refute — many minds, independent, then converged. A question that decomposes into separable sub-questions — survey this literature, check these six candidates, gather evidence from these distinct sources — and, critically, one where being right matters enough to pay for independence. Here the shape is parallel: dispatch independent investigators who do not see each other's work, then merge. The merge is not a vote; it is the adversarial convergence of §29.5's dissent probe made the primary mechanism rather than a backstop — agents propose, others refute, and a conclusion ships only when an independent line re-derived it. This is the one flow that buys genuine verification independence (§29.4) by construction, because the investigators never shared a frame to begin with.

The sequential spec-frozen build — staged construction against fixed premises. A task that produces an artifact in dependent stages — design, then build, then verify — where each stage consumes the last and a late change to an early premise invalidates everything downstream. Here parallelism is not merely unhelpful; it is dangerous, because independent agents building against an unfrozen spec will each silently resolve the same ambiguity differently. The flow is strictly sequential, and its governing discipline is the spec-freeze: settle and freeze the premises before construction, then reason against them so no later stage can quietly rewrite them. (This is the refusal-to-drift move stated in full as the spec-frozen method of §29.7; here it is simply the flow that a build-shaped task selects.)

The decision map collapses to a few questions asked in order, the way triage's three questions resolve to a tier. Does the task have internal structure worth decomposing? No → minimal path. Are its parts independent? No → full pipeline (entangled) or spec-frozen build (dependent stages producing an artifact). Yes → fan-out-and-refute. The stakes floor then applies on top: a high-stakes minimal-path answer still owes the verification §26.4.1 demands, regardless of how little structure the task had. Shape chooses the form; stakes still choose the floor.

Finding the best data to feed the flow

A flow is only as good as what enters it, and the most common way a well-shaped flow produces a confident wrong answer is that it reasoned faithfully over the wrong material. Choosing the flow is half the decision. The other half is choosing the data — and the discipline here inverts the reflex of every similarity-ranked retrieval system.

The book has already stated the law this rests on. Retrieval ranks by priority protection, not similarity (§10b.1): the memories that should dominate are the ones the system has marked foundational — its commitments, its hard-won lessons, what is significant and what is recent — and surface-similarity ranks last, not first. A flow that pulls its context by cosine distance gets what resembles the query; a flow that pulls by priority protection gets what is right for it. For the fan-out-and-refute flow this is doubly load-bearing, because each independent agent is fed separately, and an agent fed the merely-similar will refute on the wrong grounds.

Two more properties gate what is allowed into a flow at all:

Provenance over plausibility. Every datum entering a flow carries where it came from and how it was checked. An unsourced claim that sounds right is weaker input than a sourced claim that sounds dull, and the merge step of a fan-out must be able to ask of any conclusion: which agent, from which source, verified by what? This is the same provenance the ProcessRecord keeps at the output (§31.3), applied at the input.

Freshness is a fact about the datum, not the query. A foundational commitment does not stale; a price, a version number, a standard's current edition does. Priority-protected reinforcement (§10b.2) already encodes this — reinforce on use, decay on neglect — so that the data a flow retrieves is what is signal now, not what was true once and never re-checked.

There is a second, distinct data question that only one destination raises: curating a dataset to train the flow itself. When the downstream consumer is a fine-tune rather than a single inference, "best data" means something sharper than retrieval. A correctness-teaching dataset — the kind §27.6 specifies — is not a pile of good answers. It is built from verifiable answers (a gold standard somebody actually established, not a plausible-looking target), named premises (the example states what it assumed, so the model learns to reason from stated grounds rather than vibes), and calibrated labels (confidence that matches evidence strength, including the "I don't know, because…" and premise-challenging examples that teach honest abstention). The same priority-protected instinct applies: the examples that teach most are the foundational corrections and the verification-failure loops, not the thousand fluent successes that merely confirm the model already agrees with itself.

The funnel is the same shape whether the data feeds one inference or a training run: start from everything available, keep only what is sourced, keep only what is fresh-or-foundational, rank what survives by priority protection, and — for training — keep only what carries a verifiable answer and a calibrated label. What falls out of the funnel is not discarded because it is false. It falls out because it cannot be grounded, and a flow fed ungrounded data inherits that ungroundedness no matter how well-shaped it is.

29.6b — Curated Context as Grounding: What It Buys, and When It Hurts

The funnel of the previous section answered which data to let into a flow. There is a parallel discipline that answers a narrower, sturdier question: what does it actually buy you to feed a flow curated, authoritative material instead of letting it run on its own averaged priors? The answer is solid, and it is worth stating plainly before the qualifications crowd in, because the qualifications are where most of the honest work lives.

The kernel is this: curated context constrains the output space, and a constrained output space is a more reliable one. When a flow is handed the relevant specification, the governing standard, the verified worked example — at inference time, in its context window, or baked in by narrow fine-tuning — its fluent-but-wrong region shrinks, because the fluent-and-grounded material is sitting right in front of it and the wrong alternatives are not. This is not a novel mechanism; it is the one already running under retrieval-augmented generation, under system-prompt scaffolding, under skills files, under curated fine-tunes that beat far larger raw scrapes. The directional intuition — a flow fed consistent, sourced, authoritative material grounds better than one fed contradictory scrape — is well-evidenced and mainstream. Hand the flow the right reference, and its best output moves toward the reference. [STRONGLY SUPPORTED, directional]

Now the honesty move the discipline demands, because it is easy to oversell this into something it is not. There is a tempting argument that the reason curation works is information-theoretic: a consistent corpus has low entropy, compresses cleanly, and therefore the verified reference layer of a whole field is astonishingly compact — small enough to ground a flow without drowning it. The compactness point is real and useful as a picture, but band it for what it is: a strong directional claim, not a theorem. Compressibility tracks consistency and predictability, not truth. A perfectly consistent set of false premises compresses exactly as well as a true one and would ground a flow just as confidently — toward the wrong answer. So state the purchase exactly: curation buys you consistency, and a deliberate choice of which consistent corpus to stand on. It does not buy you truth. Truth comes from choosing the right corpus to be consistent with — a judgment the math cannot make for you, and never claims to. The information-theory framing is the metaphor that explains why a clean corpus grounds well; it is not a proof that the grounding is correct.

This is why grounding is a grounds-discipline, not a reasoning-one. Curated context tells a flow what to stand on; it does not teach the flow to think. A system with no reasoning ability, handed perfect references, will still fail on every problem the references do not directly answer — it will simply fail while appearing grounded, which is worse. Grounding raises the floor under a flow that can already reason. It is not a substitute for the reasoning.

And curation is not free. Naming where it hurts is part of using it honestly:

Failure modeWhat goes wrong
Stale referenceA package pinned to a superseded edition confidently enforces the wrong rule. Versioning and review (§9.5's edition-pinning) are load-bearing, not optional.
Over-constraintInject too narrow a pattern set and you suppress the legitimate alternative the task actually needed — trading hallucination for rigidity.
Retrieval missIf the wrong package is fetched, or the right one missed, the flow falls back to its unconstrained average while appearing grounded. The quiet killer.
No single truthWhere there is no agreed answer — open questions, contested tradeoffs, matters of taste — forcing one "correct" reference is itself the error.

Three of these four are failures of what got fetched, which is exactly why §29.6's funnel and the priority-protected retrieval of §10b.1 sit upstream of this discipline rather than beside it. A flow fed by similarity gets what resembles the query, and a stale-but-similar or plausible-but-unsourced datum resembles the query perfectly well. A flow fed by priority protection — provenance over plausibility (§29.6's funnel), freshness as a fact about the datum, foundational commitments ranked first — gets what is right for it. Grounding only delivers its reliability gain when the thing retrieved to ground with is itself sourced, fresh, and chosen for fit rather than surface match. Curated context is a powerful floor under a flow. It is a floor, not a foundation: it constrains the output space and improves reliability, it does not certify the answer, and the flow that mistakes its curated corpus for the truth has only made its errors more consistent.

Determining the best flow: the parallelism decision and its budget

The choice between the sequential flows and the parallel one is the single highest-leverage decision in this section, and it is the one most often made on instinct ("parallel is faster") rather than on structure. State the rule structurally:

Parallelise across independence, sequence across dependence. Fan out only the parts of a task that do not need each other's outputs to be correct; keep sequential anything where a later step consumes an earlier one. The test for whether two sub-tasks may run in parallel and have their results safely merged is the §29.5 test for whether a chain may be trusted: did they share a frame? Independent fan-out is safe to merge precisely because the branches never shared one; dependent steps forced into parallel will each invent a frame, and the merge will be a collision, not a convergence.

The empirical record, read honestly, supports this shape rather than a blanket "more agents is better." [CONFIRMED] Anthropic's multi-agent research system (June 2025) reported a multi-agent configuration — an Opus lead coordinating Sonnet subagents — outperforming a single Opus agent by 90.2% on their internal research-task evaluation, and found that token usage alone explained roughly 80% of the variance in performance across their evaluation. But the same write-up is candid about the boundary of that result, and the boundary is exactly the parallelism rule above: the gains showed up on research-style tasks that decompose into independent investigations, and the authors note that coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable sub-tasks than research, because each step tends to depend on the last. [CONFIRMED, task-dependent] The 90.2% is not a property of multi-agent systems in general; it is a property of the fit between a fan-out flow and a fan-out-shaped task. Apply it to a dependent, build-shaped task and the same machinery multiplies cost while the coordination overhead eats the speedup.

That cost is the other half of the decision, and it must be budgeted, not discovered after the bill arrives. The same source's rough arithmetic is the figure to plan against: a single agent run consumes on the order of 4× the tokens of a plain chat interaction, and a multi-agent fan-out on the order of 15×. [CONFIRMED, order-of-magnitude] Those multiples are the price of the flow, and they decide where the marginal token should go. The principle that token usage explains most of the variance does not license spending tokens anywhere; it licenses spending them where they buy the most correctness — and §29.5 already named where that is. The marginal token in a high-stakes flow belongs to the independent re-derivation and the dissent probe, not to a longer first-pass chain that only deepens the cascade. Budget toward verification, because an unverified 15× answer is merely an expensive instance of the cascade inspecting itself.

This closes the router. §26.4 chose depth by complexity; §26.4.1 raised a floor by stakes; §26.4.2 made that judgment the first reflex; and §29.6 chose the form — the flow and the data that feed it — by the structure of the task. A system that runs all four is no longer asking only "how hard is this?" It is asking "how hard, how dangerous, what shape, and on what grounds?" — which is the whole of what it means to route a question well before spending a thought on answering it.

29.7 — Building With the Pattern: The Spec-Frozen Method

§29.6 named four flows and, for one of them — the sequential spec-frozen build — deferred the full discipline to here. This section is that discipline. Everything before §29.6 taught the mind to reason; the build flow taught it to choose construction as a shape; this section states the contract that governs construction once chosen, so the overlap with §29.6 is a deliberate hand-off, not a repetition. The pipeline already knows how to think a problem through. The question now is what discipline governs the long, multi-step act of construction that follows, when the conclusion is no longer a sentence but an artifact assembled over many stages, many agents, and many hours — long enough for the original understanding to rot.

The failure this method exists to prevent is not building badly. It is building the wrong thing correctly. A construction process can satisfy every local check — each step coherent, each component sound — and still arrive somewhere no one chose, because the understanding the work began from was silently revised, one reasonable-looking adjustment at a time, until the thing built answered a question no one had asked. This is the Accumulation trap (§17.4.2) wearing work clothes: drift that is invisible because every individual move looked like progress. Cascade hygiene (§29.5) defends the reasoning chain against inheriting a bad frame; the spec-frozen method defends the construction chain against rewriting a good one.

Three moves carry it, in order.

Freeze: structure understanding into an immutable contract

Before any building begins, the understanding is made into a frozen spec — a contract that states, explicitly, what is being built and on what premises, and is then closed to silent revision. This is DECOMPOSE and SCOPE (Stages 4 and 5) carried to their conclusion: DECOMPOSE has broken the problem into its real sub-questions; SCOPE has named exactly which premises the answer will rest on and how strongly each is held. The freeze is the act of taking that structured understanding and declaring it the ground the build stands on — not a sketch the build may quietly edit when the ground proves inconvenient.

Why freeze at all, rather than let understanding evolve as construction teaches you more? Because an unfrozen premise is not a living premise; it is an unguarded one. Reasoning degrades over a long context — the frame you hold at the end of a build is not the frame you reasoned into at the start, and the degradation is gradual enough that no single step feels like a departure. Freezing captures the understanding at the moment it was best verified and makes that moment reproducible. The build can then be checked against a fixed thing rather than against a memory that has been drifting the whole time.

This makes the freeze a Guardian move at the level of architecture. Where the values gate of Chapter 25 refuses an output the model cannot argue past, the frozen spec refuses a premise-change the build cannot make quietly. A premise may still change — understanding is not infallible, and a frozen spec that proves wrong must be reopened — but only by an explicit, recorded act of reopening the contract, never by a downstream step deciding on its own that the premise meant something else. The principle is the one this book states for every refusal that matters:

A premise that the rest of the build must not silently rewrite has to be frozen above the build, not merely remembered within it. What is only remembered will drift; what is frozen can be checked against, and a build that contradicts its own frozen spec can be caught the moment it does — not discovered, much later, in the shape of the wrong thing built well.

The spec carries its own epistemics. Each premise in it is labelled with the provenance and confidence SCOPE assigned — sourced versus assumed, strongly versus weakly held — so the freeze is not a flat assertion of certainty but an honest map of where the understanding is solid and where it is a working assumption. This matters for the next move: a step that would build load-bearing structure on a premise the spec itself marks as unresolved is not permitted to proceed as if the premise were settled. A build does not get to launder an assumption into a fact by relying on it.

Build: construct sequentially against the frozen spec

With the spec frozen, construction proceeds sequentially — each step built against the contract, its output checked against the contract before the next step begins. This is a deliberate choice, and it trades something real away. The pipeline knows how to fan work out across independent agents (§29.4) and when independence is worth its cost; the spec-frozen method deliberately does not parallelize the construction itself. The reason is the same one that makes cascade hygiene necessary: steps in a build are rarely as independent as they look. Most construction has a load order — what step three builds depends on what step two actually produced, not on what the spec said step two would produce — and parallel builders coordinating against a shared evolving state reintroduce exactly the drift the freeze was meant to kill. Fanning out buys speed and pays in coordination cost and in the loss of a single auditable line of construction; for high-stakes, asymmetric-cost work the book has already said where that trade should fall (§26.4.1). Sequential construction against a frozen spec keeps the chain auditable: there is one order, one state, and one record of how the artifact came to be.

The spec is what makes the sequence safe to be a sequence. Because every step checks its work against the frozen contract and not against the accumulated state of the steps before it, a sequential build is not the information cascade §29.5 warned about. The frozen spec is the fresh-context original that each step re-derives from. A step that drifts from the contract is caught by comparison to the contract; it does not get to pass its drift downstream as inherited truth, because the next step also answers to the spec, not to it. This is cascade-hygiene's re-derive, do not relay discipline applied to building: the spec is the thing every step relays from, and it does not move.

Attribute: trace each failure to a component and improve that component

When the build fails — and a long construction will fail somewhere — the third move is to make the failure attributable. Not "the system produced a bad result," but which component, at which step, against which premise of the frozen spec, departed from the contract. A failure that cannot be located cannot be fixed; it can only be patched over, which is how a system accumulates the silent debt that the Accumulation trap feeds on.

This is the Architect Protocol's trail (§25b.3) doing construction work. The trail is the append-only record of every consequential decision; here it records each construction step against the frozen spec it was built to satisfy, so that when something is wrong the record answers where and against what. Attribution turns a failure from an embarrassment into information: it names the component that drifted, and it names the premise it drifted from. The fix then has an address. The component is improved — or, if the failure traces to the spec itself rather than to a step that departed from it, the contract is explicitly reopened, re-reasoned, re-frozen, and the build re-run against the new contract. Either way the improvement is structural: it changes the component or the contract, not merely the one output that happened to fail.

The distinction in that last move is the whole discipline in miniature. A step that violated a sound spec is a building error — fix the step. A spec that was faithfully built and still produced the wrong thing is an understanding error — reopen the freeze. Attribution is what lets the system tell these apart, and telling them apart is what keeps improvement honest. Without it, every failure looks like a reason to loosen the spec, and a spec loosened after every failure is no spec at all — just a memory, drifting, dressed up as a contract.

The loop, and what it is for

Freeze, build, attribute, and — where attribution reopens the contract — freeze again. The loop is not a project-management ritual bolted onto the thinking. It is the same refusal-to-drift the book has argued for at every scale, applied to the one activity where drift is hardest to see and most expensive: the slow assembly of a thing too large to hold in one frame. The router (§26.4.1) decides how deep to think; §29.6 decides what shape the work takes; cascade hygiene (§29.5) keeps a reasoning chain from inheriting a bad frame; the spec-frozen method keeps a construction chain from rewriting a good one. A system that freezes what it understood, builds against the freeze, and attributes every failure back to a named component or a reopened premise is a system whose artifacts can be trusted to be the thing it set out to build — not merely a well-made answer to a question that changed while no one was looking.

29.8 — Sizing the Gate

§29.6 added a third axis to the router and called it shape; §29.7 took one shape — the build — and gave it a method. Both left a question standing that neither needed to answer, because both spoke of flows and stages as though the machinery running each stage were a settled matter. It is not. A flow names which stages run and in what order; it says nothing about how much capacity each stage requires. And the reflex answer — run the whole pipeline on one large, capable mind, because a capable mind can do every stage — is the most expensive answer available and, more often than the reflex admits, not the best one.

So there is a fourth axis, and it follows the first three the way each of those followed the last:

Stakes set the floor, complexity sets the ceiling, shape sets the form — and size sets the capacity. After a flow is chosen, each stage within it still faces its own question: how much model does this gate need? The rule is the same discipline the whole book argues for, narrowed to one stage: the smallest model that passes the gate's own bar. Not the smallest model that feels safe, and not the largest the budget tolerates — the smallest that clears the stage's measured contract at the required confidence and latency.

Size is not complexity wearing a different hat. Complexity asks how deep the thinking must go on a task taken whole; size asks how much capacity a single stage of that task needs once the task is decomposed. A high-complexity question can route most of its stages to small models and spend its capacity only where the entanglement actually lives. The two axes pull apart precisely because the pipeline already broke the work into stages with narrow contracts — and a narrow contract is exactly the thing a small model can be measured against.

The gate constellation

The architecture this licenses is not one generalist performing eleven stages in turn.
