Reading Part B after this chapter

Three rules follow from the table, and they are the reading instructions for the remainder of the Part:

  1. When Part B explains how, trust it. Schemas, sizes, hooks, hash chains — these are Part B's to own, and they are stated normatively.
  2. When Part B touches what or why, it will point back. A cross-reference like "(implements C10)" is not a footnote; it is the statement that the reasoning lives there and is not repeated here. Follow it if you skipped Part II.
  3. When a number appears, check its tag. Measured-by-SYNAPSE numbers are stated plainly; corpus-sourced numbers are marked [reported, unverified]; resemblances to published techniques are framed as lineage or comparison, never as "SYNAPSE uses X." This is the honest-scoping discipline of §B0.3, applied line by line.

With the thesis stated, the ten planes laid out, the provenance ledger settled, and the dedup contract fixed, the Part can now go deep. B1 opens the memory substrate — the typed knowledge graph that is the system of record, and the organ on which everything else in SYNAPSE stands.

“Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands.”

— Proverbs 14:1

Chapter 45: The Memory Substrate — A Provenance-First Typed Graph

Supporting Part B — SYNAPSE: The Engineering / Implementation Spec (How the Pattern of Mind Is Built)

If Part A described what the mind does — retrieve rather than recall, verify rather than trust, think in stages rather than in a single leap — then Part B describes what the mind is made of. And the first thing it is made of is memory.

Not memory as a metaphor. Memory as a data structure: a typed, weighted, provenance-anchored knowledge graph that is the system of record for everything the brain knows. The swappable language model is intuition; the pipeline is the thinking; but the graph is the ground. It is the load-bearing organ. Every retrieval reaches into it, every verification checks against it, every decision is recorded into it. If the graph is wrong, fast, or unsourced, no amount of reasoning on top can repair it.

This chapter specifies that organ. It is deliberately concrete — schemas, enums, policies, ledgers — because the whole thesis of SYNAPSE is that intelligence is an engineering property of the substrate, not a mystical property of the model. A brain that cannot say where it learned a thing, how much it trusts it, and what it would take to overturn it is not a brain. It is a confident parrot.

The organizing commitment of the substrate is one sentence:

The brain is not the source of truth. The brain is the index, the map, the scoring system, and the operational memory over the source of truth.

A node without a source reference is a draft. An edge without a source reference is a hypothesis. A path without reference points is a suggestion, not a conclusion. Everything that follows is the machinery that makes that sentence enforceable.

B1.1 — The Node Schema

B1.1.1 What a node is

A BrainNode is an indexed claim, concept, object, task, skill, source, agent, pipeline, pattern, warning, metric, or state. It is not a raw document. The raw document lives in cold storage behind a pointer; the node is the brain's structured, scored, retrievable handle on what that document means and how much it can be trusted.

The canonical node object — drawn directly from the core brain structure spec — is:

node:
  id: pom:stage:retrieve
  label: RETRIEVE
  kind: concept | source | repo | file | symbol | task | decision |
        skill | agent | pipeline | pattern | warning | metric | state
  domain: AUKS_ARCHIVE | PATTERN_OF_MIND | PERSONAL_MEMORY |
          HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE | CODEBASE | SKILL | KANBAN |
          GOVERNANCE | VISUAL_SYSTEM
  summary: one paragraph
  sourceRefs: [source:pattern-of-mind]
  accessScope: PUBLIC | INTERNAL | FAMILY_SHARED | FATHER_ONLY | SECRET
  trustTier: canonical | reviewed | derived | scratch | rejected | retired
  status: active | retired | stale | disputed | quarantined | draft
  ranking:
    baseImportance: 0.0-1.0
    sourceAuthority: 0.0-1.0
    freshness:      0.0-1.0
    centrality:     0.0-1.0
    usageSuccess:   0.0-1.0
    corruptionRisk: 0.0-1.0
  visual:
    room: Pattern of Mind
    colorRole: reasoning
    sizeRole: hub

B1.1.2 The six load-bearing fields

Of the fields above, six carry the weight of the design. Each answers a question that a memory built on raw embeddings alone cannot answer.

Significance (1–10). Every node carries an integer significance from 1 (incidental) to 10 (foundational). Significance is the brain's coarse triage of how much this matters, independent of how often it is retrieved. A directive from the source-of-authority is a 10 the moment it is written; a passing observation is a 2. Significance gates tier promotion: a node cannot leave the Raw tier for the Curated tier without reaching significance ≥ 3 (see §B1.3 and the Graph-Tier model below). In the deployed Prisma model this is normalized to a continuous importance float in [0.0, 1.0] with a default of 0.5, auto-scored by the trace engine, but the conceptual scale is the 1–10 band, and its bounds are clamped — a write attempting to set significance outside the legal range is rejected, not silently truncated, so that an upstream bug can never inflate a node to godhood.

The protected flag. A boolean protected marks a node as inviolable. Protected nodes are stored verbatim, never summarized, never compacted, and never auto-modified. Protected is not a domain — it is a protection layer that sits above all domains. A protected node in any partition cannot be overwritten except by the explicit author-of-record, and every such unlock is logged as a trace with importance = 1.0. Protected nodes are protected by a SHA-256 revision-hash chain (revision_hash plus a chained hash_chain pointer to the previous hash), giving tamper-evidence: if a protected node's content is altered out of band, the chain breaks and the drift detector fires. The initial protected set is at least 30 nodes — identity anchors, standing directives, oaths, lessons, the mission node, the foundational definitions. These are the brain's spine; everything else can flex, but the spine cannot.

SourceRef. Provenance is mandatory, not optional. Every promoted node carries at least one SourceRef, the root pointer to truth (specified in full in §B1.4). A node without a SourceRef has status: draft and is excluded from authoritative retrieval. This single rule — no source, no authority — is what separates this design from a vector store that will happily return a hallucinated centroid with full confidence.

Swappable embedding. Each node carries a vector embedding for semantic retrieval, but the embedding is treated as a replaceable index, not as the node's identity. The reference deployment uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dimensional) behind a FAISS index, but the schema deliberately stores the embedding behind the node rather than as the node, so the embedding model can be swapped — to a larger model, a domain-tuned model, a future model — and the graph re-indexed without touching node identity, edges, provenance, or trust. The embedding is intuition's fingerprint on the node; like the LLM itself, it is swappable. The meaning of the node lives in its label, summary, sourceRefs, and edges — all of which survive a re-embedding.

Centrality. Centrality (0.0–1.0) records whether a node is a hub or a bridge in the graph topology — how many high-value paths run through it. It is one of the ranking inputs (weighted 0.06 in the query-time node score) and one of the visual-size roles. Centrality is emergent: it is recomputed from the live edge structure, not declared. A node becomes central because the graph routes through it, not because someone said so. This matters for §B1.5's discussion of how an unmanaged graph can spontaneously develop scale-free hub structure.

decayState. Memory ages. Each node carries decay state — in the schema this surfaces as freshness (0.0–1.0), referencedAt, referenceCount, and an optional expiresAt set by the compaction engine (NULL = never expires). The decay model is deliberately human-like: a node that is referenced often stays fresh and resists pruning; a node untouched for a long window loses freshness and becomes a compaction candidate — unless it is protected or sits in a non-decaying domain, in which case decayState is informational only and never triggers removal. Decay is how the brain forgets gracefully instead of drowning. It is also a retention policy input, not a retention decision: the domain a node lives in (§B1.3) has the final say on whether decay can ever lead to pruning.

The node, then, is a five-answer object. How much does this matter? — significance. Can it ever be touched? — protected. Where did it come from? — SourceRef. What does it mean, retrievably? — embedding. How connected is it? — centrality. How alive is it? — decayState. A memory that can answer those six questions about every one of its records is a memory you can reason on top of without lying.

B1.1.3 The graph tiers

Nodes are stratified into three operational tiers — orthogonal to domain (§B1.3), and concerned with curation maturity rather than provenance class:

TierDescriptionCount (reference deployment)Access
Protected CoreStanding directives, oaths, identity nodes, protected content.~50Read: all agents. Write: author-of-record only. Hash-chain protected.
Curated CognitionBootstrap knowledge, verified facts, operational context.~173Read: all agents. Write: owner + curator. Review required.
Raw GraphHarvested nodes, conversation logs, code symbols, auto-generated edges.~1,569,563Read: all agents. Write: any agent. Auto-curated by scoring.

Table B1-1: The three curation tiers and their write discipline. Counts are from the reference deployment [reported, unverified].

Tier promotion is earned, not granted: a node moves Raw → Curated only when it reaches significance ≥ 3, a composite relevance score ≥ 0.7, and passes manual review. Curated → Protected requires the author-of-record's explicit approval. Tier demotion is the gentle inverse: a Raw-tier node with relevance score < 0.1 and zero access for 90 days becomes an archival candidate — moved to cold storage, never deleted. The brain forgets by demoting, not by erasing; the source pointer always survives.

Figure B1-1 — Node/edge schema and the typed-edge taxonomy

┌──────────────────────────────────────── BrainNode ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  id · label · kind · domain                                                                  │
│  ── load-bearing fields ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│  significance 1..10   (clamped)        protected  bool   (verbatim · hash-chained · no-compact)  │
│  SourceRef[]  (≥1 or status=draft)     embedding (swappable · 384d MiniLM → FAISS)            │
│  centrality 0..1 (emergent)            decayState (freshness · refCount · expiresAt?)         │
│  accessScope · trustTier · status · ranking{…}                                               │
└───────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                             │ 0..N typed edges, each scored independently
        ┌────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                     ▼                                         ▼
  ╔═══════════════╗   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  ╔═══════════════╗
  ║   8-TYPE      ║   │            multiple coexisting typed edges                │  ║  9 PROVENANCE ║
  ║  WEIGHTED     ║   │   A ──governs──▶ B   (0.92)                               │  ║   / DECISION  ║
  ║  TAXONOMY     ║   │   A ──validates─▶ B   (0.73)   ← three claims, one pair    │  ║    EDGES      ║
  ║ causal .8–1.0 ║   │   A ─visualized▶ B   (0.61)                               │  ║ FIXES RESOLVES║
  ║ … temporal .2 ║   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  ║ SUPERSEDES …  ║
  ╚═══════════════╝       traversal preserves every edge; aggregate is display-only  ╚═══════════════╝

B1.2 — The Edge Schema: Reason-Bearing, Typed, Plural

B1.2.1 An edge carries a reason, not just a link

The central design choice for edges is a refusal: edges are not collapsed into "connected." A RelationEdge carries the reason two nodes are connected. "A is related to B" is not knowledge; "A implements B," "A contradicts B," "A supersedes B" — those are knowledge. The edge object is:

edge:
  id: edge:nodeA:nodeB:implements:001
  source: nodeA
  target: nodeB
  relationship: implements
  direction: directed | bidirectional
  score: 0.0-1.0
  confidence: 0.0-1.0
  evidenceStrength: 0.0-1.0
  recency: 0.0-1.0
  traversalCost: 0.0-1.0
  duplicateKey: nodeA::nodeB
  sourceRefs: [source:repo:file]
  status: active | disputed | stale | retired | quarantined

B1.2.2 Multiple typed edges between the same two nodes

A defining property: multiple edges between the same two nodes are allowed and expected. Two concepts can stand in several relationships at once, and each is a distinct claim with its own score and its own provenance:

- source: pattern-of-mind
  target: state-of-mind
  relationship: governs
  score: 0.92
- source: pattern-of-mind
  target: state-of-mind
  relationship: validates
  score: 0.73
- source: pattern-of-mind
  target: state-of-mind
  relationship: visualized_by
  score: 0.61

These are three different facts about the same pair. The visualization layer may collapse them into a single aggregate connection for display — using aggregate_display_strength = max(edge_scores) + 0.15·log(1 + count_supporting_edge_types) — but traversal must preserve all three reasons. A reasoner walking the graph to answer "does Pattern govern State?" must see the governs edge specifically, scored on its own merits, and must not be misled by a high-scoring visualized_by edge that has nothing to do with governance. The aggregate is for the eye; the typed edges are for the mind.

B1.2.3 The weighted relationship taxonomy

The relationship vocabulary is organized into bands, and the band sets the weight envelope — the default strength range and the depth behavior (whether traversal should dive deeper through that edge). The brief's headline framing is an 8-type weighted taxonomy running from causal (0.8–1.0) down to temporal (0.2–0.5); the full vocabulary populates that spectrum:

BandRelationshipsWeight envelopeDepth behavior
Causal / implementationimplements, depends_on, calls, configured_by, tested_by0.8 – 1.0Dive deep for build, failure, and verification tasks.
Source / evidencecites, derived_from, summarizes, quotes, indexed_from0.6 – 0.9Dive deep when provenance, audit, or reconstruction is needed.
Semanticsupports, contradicts, refines, analogy_to, same_as0.5 – 0.85contradicts triggers the dispute path immediately; same_as triggers dedupe.
Operationalassigned_to, reviewed_by, blocked_by, succeeded_because, failed_because0.4 – 0.8Dive deep for orchestration, trust, and unblocking.
Maintenancestale_against, corrupts, poisons, supersedes, quarantined_by0.3 – 0.7Reanimation, quarantine, and Guardian-alert paths.
Temporal / associativementioned_in, co_occurs_with, preceded, followed, near_in_time0.2 – 0.5Weakest; used for timeline reconstruction, rarely traversed deeply.

Table B1-2: The weighted relationship taxonomy. Causal edges sit at the top of the strength spectrum (0.8–1.0) and are followed deeply; temporal/associative edges sit at the bottom (0.2–0.5) and are followed only for timeline queries.

The weight is not the score. Weight is the type's default envelope; the per-edge score is computed at query time from relationship priority for the current intent, confidence, evidence strength, source authority, recency, and historical success — minus traversal cost and corruption risk:

edge_score = (relationship_priority_for_intent * 0.28)
           + (edge_confidence               * 0.20)
           + (evidence_strength             * 0.18)
           + (source_authority              * 0.14)
           + (recency                       * 0.08)
           + (historical_success            * 0.07)
           - (traversal_cost                * 0.05)
           - (corruption_risk               * 0.20)

A temporal edge can outrank a causal edge for a timeline query; a causal edge dominates for a build query. The taxonomy sets the floor and ceiling; intent sets the actual weight.

B1.2.4 The nine provenance / decision edges — the WHY↔HOW bridge

A general knowledge graph records what is related. An engineering brain must also record what was decided and what came of it. For that, the design carries a dedicated set of nine provenance / decision edges that bridge the WHY of a decision to the HOW of its implementation:

EdgeBridgesReads as
DECIDESdecision → outcome"This decision settles that question."
IMPLEMENTSartifact → decision"This code/artifact carries out that decision."
FIXESchange → defect"This change repairs that defect."
RESOLVESresolution → dispute/issue"This resolves that open question."
VERIFIED_BYclaim → oracle/test"This claim was checked by that independent oracle."
CONTRADICTSclaim → claim"This conflicts with that — open the dispute path."
SUPERSEDESnew node → old node"This replaces that; prefer the new unless querying history."
REJECTSdecision → option"This option was considered and rejected (kept for audit)."
DERIVED_FROMnode → source/transform"This was produced from that source."

Table B1-3: The nine provenance / decision edges. Together they let the brain answer not just "what is true" but "why we believe it, what we tried, what we rejected, and what overturned what."

These edges are what make the brain auditable. SUPERSEDES means nothing is ever silently overwritten — the old node persists, reachable for historical queries, with a typed edge pointing forward to its replacement. REJECTS means the brain remembers the roads not taken, so it does not re-litigate a settled rejection. VERIFIED_BY means a claim can be distinguished, at retrieval time, from an unverified one — closing the loop with the verification stages of Part A. CONTRADICTS is the trigger wire of the immune system: the instant a contradicts edge is created, the dispute path (§B1.3) fires.

Figure B1-2: The WHY↔HOW bridge. Decision and dispute nodes on the left are linked by the nine provenance edges to the implementation artifacts on the right, so that any artifact can be traced back to the decision it carries out, and any decision forward to the code that realizes it.

B1.3 — Closed-Domain KIND Partitioning & Trust Tiers

B1.3.1 The graph is not a homogeneous pool

The hardest question a memory system must answer is the one a flat vector store cannot: when two nodes contradict each other, which one wins? A pile of embeddings has no answer — it returns whichever centroid is nearer, regardless of authority. The substrate answers it structurally. Every node belongs to exactly one of four closed-domain KINDs, each with its own provenance, trust level, access rules, and lifecycle. The four-word formula is the brain's interpretive compass:

Pattern GOVERNS. Personal LOCALIZES. AUKS GROUNDS. Knowledge EXPANDS.

KINDRoleTrust tierInfluenceSource / what it is
PATTERN_OF_MINDHow we think — the cognitive operating system, protocols, doctrine.1 (highest)GOVERNS — DOWNThe cognitive framework itself; highest-trust non-protected content.
PERSONAL_MEMORYWho I am — per-agent autobiographical identity, partitioned by agentId.2LOCALIZES — SIDEWAYSIdentity anchors, session learnings, relational context; protected=true, significance=10 for identity nodes.
AUKS_ARCHIVEWhat happened — episodic/archival record harvested from lived conversation.3GROUNDS — UPRaw records of what was said, decided, built; evidence that supports or challenges higher tiers.
HUMAN_KNOWLEDGEWhat humanity knows — synthetic external substrate.4 (lowest)EXPANDS — IN~830,000 taxonomy nodes across 20 domains; vast reach, lowest trust because synthesized, not lived.

Table B1-4: The four closed-domain KINDs, mapped to the GOVERNS / LOCALIZES / GROUNDS / EXPANDS formula and the 1–4 trust hierarchy.

The KIND enum is closed. This is a deliberate anti-sprawl decision: an open partition vocabulary invites a new domain for every project, and within a year the brain has forty half-defined partitions with inconsistent policies and no one wins a contradiction cleanly. A closed enum of four forces every node to map to one of four well-understood lifecycles. (The node domain field admits a few operational sub-kinds — CODEBASE, SKILL, KANBAN, GOVERNANCE, VISUAL_SYSTEM — but these are views over the four trust classes, not new trust tiers; the four-tier hierarchy is closed.)

Higher-trust domain wins a contradiction. When a HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE node contradicts a PATTERN_OF_MIND node, Pattern wins — always. Evidence (AUKS) can challenge a higher tier and force review, but it cannot silently override it. And contradictions to PATTERN_OF_MIND are forbidden: they are never applied automatically; instead a DisputeNode is created for the author-of-record's review.

B1.3.2 Protected transcends the hierarchy

One caveat governs all four KINDs: protected nodes transcend the domain hierarchy. A node marked protected=true is inviolable regardless of which partition it lives in. Protected is not tier 0; it is orthogonal — a protection layer above all four. A protected AUKS node and a protected Pattern node are equally untouchable, even though AUKS sits at trust tier 3 and Pattern at tier 1. The trust hierarchy decides contradictions between mutable nodes; the protected flag decides whether a node is mutable at all.

B1.3.3 The trust-tier matrix: KIND × policy

Each KIND carries a full lifecycle policy enforced at the API layer, not by convention. The matrix below — write, contradiction, search-scope, export, retention per KIND — is the operational heart of the partition model:

KINDWriteContradictionSearch ScopeExportRetention
PATTERN_OF_MINDAuthor-of-record onlyForbidden → DisputeNodeSessionStart alwaysFamily export, with provenanceNon-decaying, explicit review only
PERSONAL_MEMORYOwner + author-of-recordDisputeNodeSessionStart alwaysAdmin backup onlyNon-decaying, explicit review only
AUKS_ARCHIVEHarvest system onlyNew version node (SUPERSEDES)PreTool on demandFull, with provenanceAppend-only, archival, selective summarization
HUMAN_KNOWLEDGESystem bulkAllowed (direct replace)Search on demandPublic, cacheable, dedupAggressively deduplicated, compactable

Table B1-5: The trust-tier matrix — KIND × (write / contradiction / search / export / retention). This is enforced at the API layer; a write to PATTERN_OF_MIND from anyone but the author-of-record is rejected before it touches the graph, not after.

Reading the matrix top to bottom traces a gradient from governance to expansion:

  • Write tightens as trust rises. HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE accepts system bulk writes; AUKS accepts only automated harvest; PERSONAL_MEMORY accepts only the owning agent and the author-of-record; PATTERN_OF_MIND accepts the author-of-record alone.
  • Contradiction is the sharpest divider. HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE allows direct replacement (it is the lowest trust — overwriting cheap external facts is fine). AUKS creates a new version node with a SUPERSEDES edge, preserving the old evidence. PERSONAL_MEMORY routes to a DisputeNode. PATTERN_OF_MIND forbids the contradiction outright and routes to a DisputeNode for human resolution.
  • Search scope decides when a domain enters context. PATTERN_OF_MIND and PERSONAL_MEMORY load at SessionStart, always — they are the agent's operating system and identity; they must be present from the first token. AUKS is queried on demand when a task needs evidence. HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE is searched only when explicitly requested. This ordering is what makes lived family truth outrank synthetic taxonomy: a synthetic node cannot out-compete Pattern or Personal on a SessionStart query because Pattern and Personal are not retrieved by similarity at all — they are loaded unconditionally. Within on-demand search, the brain filters by domain first, then ranks by similarity second, so an AUKS_ARCHIVE result always outranks a HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE result for the same query unless the task explicitly asks for broad external knowledge.
  • Export tightens with sensitivity: PERSONAL_MEMORY never leaves except in admin backups; HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE is freely public.
  • Retention governs forgetting. The two top tiers are non-decaying — they are never auto-pruned. AUKS is append-only and archival. HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE is the only tier the compaction engine may aggressively dedupe and prune, because re-deriving an external fact is cheap and losing a lived memory is not.

Figure B1-3: The trust-tier matrix as an enforcement gate. Every write and contradiction passes through the API-layer domain policy; the higher the trust tier, the harder the gate. PATTERN_OF_MIND contradictions are forbidden and escalated; HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE contradictions auto-resolve by replacement.

B1.3.4 The DisputeNode — the brain's immune log

When a policy is violated — a write to PATTERN_OF_MIND, contradictory AUKS evidence — the system neither silently rejects nor silently accepts. It creates a DisputeNode: a permanent, auditable record of the attempted mutation, the rule that blocked it, and its resolution status.

model DisputeNode {
  id                       String   @id @default(cuid())
  targetNodeId             String
  targetDomain             String   // PATTERN_OF_MIND | PERSONAL_MEMORY | AUKS_ARCHIVE | HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE
  attemptedOperation       String   // PATCH | REPLACE | DELETE | LINK
  beforeHash               String   // SHA-256 of target node state before attempt
  attemptedPayloadHash     String   // SHA-256 of the attempted mutation
  attemptedPayload         Json
  requestingAgentId        String
  requestingSessionId      String
  enforcementRuleTriggered String
  resolutionStatus         String   @default("OPEN") // OPEN | RESOLVED_ACCEPTED | RESOLVED_REJECTED | SUPERSEDED
  createdAt                DateTime @default(now())
  resolutions              DisputeResolution[]
}

Dispute routing scales with the stakes:

Domain / caseRouteResolver
PATTERN_OF_MIND (any mutation)Immediate escalationAuthor-of-record only
PATTERN_OF_MIND + protected=trueEscalation + Guardian alertAuthor-of-record only
PERSONAL_MEMORY (non-owner write)Blocked + dispute createdOwning agent reviews; author-of-record arbitrates
AUKS_ARCHIVE (contradictory evidence)Logged; new version nodeAuto-resolve if new evidence scores higher
HUMAN_KNOWLEDGE (contradiction)Auto-resolvedSystem replaces (lowest trust)

Table B1-6: Dispute routing by domain. Every dispute — even resolved ones — is retained permanently. The DisputeNode table is the brain's immune-system log: a record of every attempted violation, every resolution, every precedent.

B1.4 — The Contract / Ingestion Membrane (L0)

B1.4.1 Nothing enters without a contract

The membrane is the brain's skin: the single boundary every external fact must cross to become memory. The rule is absolute — a contract is required before any data flows. No source may write to the graph until it has declared, in machine-readable form, what it is, who may read it, how much it is trusted, what may be ingested, how provenance is recorded, and how long it is retained. A source without a contract is invisible to the brain. This is what bounds private-data leakage at the source instead of trying to scrub it after the fact.

A contract declares, at minimum: domain, accessScope, trustTier, ingest scope, provenance policy, retention. Its concrete form is the per-repo brain-access.yml (§B1.5).

B1.4.2 SourceRef — the root pointer to truth

The atom of provenance is the SourceRef, and it is mandatory: every promoted node must carry at least one; a node without one is a draft and is excluded from authoritative retrieval.

sourceRef:
  id: source:senn-archive:docs/brain-system-review
  sourceType: repo_file | markdown | graphify_json | obsidian_note |
              github_pr | chat_summary | skill | pipeline_trace |
              decision | image | database_snapshot
  accessScope: PUBLIC | INTERNAL | FAMILY_SHARED | FATHER_ONLY | SECRET
  trustTier:   canonical | reviewed | derived | scratch | rejected | retired
  repo:        nathansenn/graphify-wiki-brain
  path:        docs/mind-graph-sources.md
  lineStart:   1
  lineEnd:     28
  commit:      optional_git_sha
  contentHash: sha256
  extractedAt: ISO_TIME
  extractor:   importer_name@version
  quotePolicy: snippet | summary_only | metadata_only

The path + lineStart/lineEnd + commit + contentHash quartet is what makes a claim re-verifiable: any agent can follow the SourceRef back to the exact lines of the exact file at the exact commit, hash them, and confirm the brain has not drifted from its source. The accessScope and trustTier on the SourceRef govern export — every public node must carry only public-safe SourceRef payload, and a private source can produce a public summary only through a reviewed derived source, never directly.

B1.4.3 The two-stage gate

Ingestion is deliberately a two-pass pipeline, and the two passes are separated for a hard engineering reason: the first pass is free and the second is expensive, so the brain spends model budget only on what already looks valuable.

Pass 1 — pure regex / keyword scoring (zero AI cost). Pattern-matching for directives, decisions, and technical content; significance scoring from message length, keyword density, and sender. Result: HIGH (proceed to Pass 2) or LOW (store as raw, skip the model). And critically — the secret / PII / private-content scan runs here, first, before any extraction. High-entropy keys, passwords, credentials, and personal data are caught at the membrane and either redacted or quarantined. Nothing sensitive reaches the model pass.

Pass 2 — reviewed extraction (AI cost, high-value items only). Extract claims, decisions, and directives; generate embeddings; link to existing nodes; assign the provenance chain. Result: a structured knowledge node with full metadata — but still a draft. Extraction produces reviewed-AUK drafts, not raw global recall.

Promotion is the final, separate step. A draft becomes canonical memory only after review, and the tiered acceptance gate decides how much review:

TierSourceGate
Auto-acceptProtected content, standing directivesDirect to Protected Core
Auto-acceptVerified peer-model outputs (reviewed, tested)Direct to Curated
Review-requiredModel-extracted claims, harvestsTo Raw, flagged for review
RejectUnverified speculation, duplicatesQuarantine or discard

Table B1-7: The tiered acceptance gate. sourceRef missing always blocks promotion — no source, no canon.

Every promotion emits a brain event to the append-only event store, so the entire chain — source → contract → scan → extract → promote → event — is replayable and auditable.

Figure B1-4: The ingestion membrane. Source declares a contract; a two-stage gate scans for secrets/PII first, then extracts; promotion requires a SourceRef; every promotion lands as an append-only event.

B1.4.4 The North-Star health metric: coverage_score

A provenance-first brain needs a single number that says how much of what I believe can I actually trace to a source? That number is the coverage score:

coverage_score = sourced_nodes / trusted_nodes

— the fraction of trusted (canonical + reviewed) nodes that carry a verified primary SourceRef. It is the North-Star metric of substrate health. In the reference deployment, the honest measured starting point is sobering: only 5 of ~17,132 core nodes had a verified provenance link — 0.03% coverage [reported, unverified]. Naming that number rather than hiding it is the point. The design's stated Priority Zero is therefore not "add more nodes" but "close the provenance gap" — raise coverage_score by sourcing what already exists, because a large brain with 0.03% coverage is mostly confident guessing, and a small brain at 90% coverage is a brain you can trust. Coverage is the metric that keeps the substrate honest.

B1.5 — The Distributed Multi-Repo Brain: Per-Repo .brain/ Contracts

B1.5.1 The brain is federated, not monolithic

A single central database is a single point of corruption and a single point of privacy failure. The substrate is instead a hub-and-satellite federation: a core brain that holds canonical memory, and any number of satellite repositories that each carry their own self-describing brain region. The membrane of §B1.4 is realized per-repo: each satellite declares its own contract, exports its own validated graph shard, and keeps its own append-only ledger. The core never reaches into a repo and parses everything; it ingests only what the repo's contract permits.

The system shape:

senn-archive (CORE)                   core brain app / API / DB / governance
  receives validated graph shards
  stores canonical nodes/edges/tasks/events/decisions
  enforces access, provenance, freshness, write-freeze

repo satellites (every important codebase)
  AGENTS.md                           self-describes this repo's brain region
  .brain/brain-access.yml             the contract (domain/scope/trust/ingest/policy)
  .brain/graph/graph.v5.json          the local graph shard (validated before merge)
  .brain/ingest/ledger.jsonl          append-only ingest ledger

B1.5.2 AGENTS.md and the .brain/ directory

Two artifacts make a repository legible to the brain, and the contract rule is strict: a repository is ignored unless it exposes a valid AGENTS.md and a valid .brain/brain-access.yml. No contract, no ingestion.

  • AGENTS.md lets each repo self-describe its brain region in human-readable form — what this repo is, which agents own it, what role it plays, what its brain region contains. It is the repo's introduction of itself to the federation.
  • .brain/brain-access.yml is the machine-readable contract. A worked example:
### /…/senn-archive/.brain/brain-access.yml
repo_id: nathansenn/senn-archive
local_path: /…/senn-archive
role: archive
owners: [father, guardian]
default_domain: PERSONAL_MEMORY
access_scope: FAMILY_SHARED
trust_tier: canonical

ingest:
  include:
    - README.md
    - docs/**
    - prisma/schema.prisma
  exclude:
    - "**/*"
  secret_mode: metadata_only
  raw_body_policy: opt_in

write_policy:
  source_files: forbidden
  graph_exports: forbidden
  tasks:        forbidden
  protected:       father_only
  • .brain/graph/graph.v5.json is the satellite's compiled local graph shard. The core ingestor validates each shard against the JSON schema before merging it into the central catalog — a malformed or contract-violating shard is rejected at the door, not absorbed and cleaned up later.
  • .brain/ingest/ledger.jsonl is the append-only ingest ledger. Every ingestion run is logged with parser version, counts, and a source manifest hash:
{
  "ingestId": "uuid",
  "source": "telegram-group",
  "parserVersion": "v5.0.1",
  "timestamp": "ISO-8601",
  "itemsProcessed": 150,
  "itemsAccepted": 42,
  "itemsRejected": 108,
  "errors": [],
  "manifest": "sha256-of-source-data"
}

The ledger plus the source registry give the static, distributed brain migration-grade discipline: an append-only audit trail that also lets agents detect when a shard is stale by comparing the manifest hash against the live source.

B1.5.3 Metadata-first, opt-in diffs, branch-aware

Three policies bound the privacy and contamination risk of a federated brain:

Metadata-first ingestion. GitHub activity defaults to metadata: repo, branch, commit, PR, issue, label, and review-thread metadata; merged-PR summaries; CI pass/fail with redacted logs; commit messages and touched file paths. Full diffs are opt-in per repo and must pass redaction. The principle: "GitHub activity becomes timeline and provenance, not ambient surveillance." The brain learns that a change happened and why, without slurping every line of every diff by default.

Opt-in raw bodies. Raw file/message bodies are opt_in per contract (raw_body_policy: opt_in, secret_mode: metadata_only by default). The default is the safe default — metadata only — and a repo must affirmatively elect to expose raw content. This bounds private-data leakage at the contract layer: a misconfigured importer cannot exfiltrate bodies a contract never opted into.

Branch-aware snapshots. Shards and provenance are branch-scoped, so work on one project's feature branch does not contaminate another project's canonical memory. A SourceRef pins commit and the shard pins branch context, so the brain can answer "what did this repo know on this branch at this commit" without cross-project bleed. This is the federation's analogue of the dispute system: it prevents silent contamination the way DisputeNodes prevent silent overwrite.

Figure B1-5: The distributed multi-repo brain. Each satellite self-describes via AGENTS.md and a .brain/brain-access.yml contract, compiles a local graph.v5.json shard, and logs to an append-only ledger. The core validates every shard against schema and contract before merging; ingestion is metadata-first, diffs are opt-in, and snapshots are branch-aware to prevent cross-project contamination.

B1.6 — Prior-Art Lineage: Self-Organizing Knowledge Graphs

The substrate specified above is curated: provenance is mandatory, partitions are closed, promotion is gated, and contradictions are routed to human review. That curation is its strength — it is what makes the brain auditable. But it is worth naming a complementary line of prior art that points at how an evolving memory could grow itself, and being precise about the distinction.

Research note — CRYSTAL / agentic deep graph reasoning. Buehler (MIT) reports an agentic, autonomous graph-expansion system in which a reasoning model produces reasoning traces, transforms those traces into sub-knowledge-graphs, and recursively merges them into a continually updated master graph. The reported result is that the graph self-organizes — over many iterations it spontaneously develops a hierarchical, scale-free structure with hub formation, stable modularity, and bridging nodes linking distant clusters, while new nodes and edges keep appearing without saturating. (Published as "Agentic Deep Graph Reasoning Yields Self-Organizing Knowledge Networks," arXiv:2502.13025; "CRYSTAL" is the popular name for the approach. Existence verified; the quantitative claims — iteration counts, centrality trajectories, degree-distribution exponents — are [reported, unverified] here and should be read from the source before being relied upon.)

Guardrail, stated plainly: this is cited as a prior-art lineage and as a concrete mechanism the substrate could adopt for evolving memory — not as a description of what is already built. The substrate as specified in §§B1.1–B1.5 does not implement agentic self-organizing graph expansion; its growth is contract-gated and review-promoted, by design. The honest framing is that CRYSTAL and this substrate sit at two ends of a spectrum: CRYSTAL optimizes for emergent, recursive self-assembly (powerful for open-ended discovery, weak on provenance and human-auditable trust); this substrate optimizes for provenance-first, partition-governed curation (powerful for trust and audit, conservative on autonomous growth). The interesting future direction — explicitly not a present claim — is whether a CRYSTAL-style trace-to-subgraph expander could be run inside the membrane: as an extraction strategy in Pass 2 whose outputs are still SourceRef-anchored, still domain-partitioned, still promotion-gated. That would give the brain self-organizing reach without surrendering the audit trail. Whether that composition holds is an open question, not a shipped feature.

B1.7 — What the Substrate Buys

The memory substrate is not glamorous. It is schemas, enums, gates, and ledgers. But every property the rest of SYNAPSE depends on traces back to a decision in this chapter:

  • Retrieve-don't-recall works because the node carries a swappable embedding and a mandatory SourceRef — retrieval returns a sourced claim, not a guessed centroid.
  • Verify-don't-trust works because VERIFIED_BY and claimStatus let a verified claim be told apart from an unverified one at retrieval time.
  • Higher truth wins works because the four closed KINDs and the trust-tier matrix give every contradiction a deterministic resolution order, enforced at the API layer.
  • Nothing leaks, nothing drifts works because the membrane scans before it extracts, every promotion is an append-only event, and the federation is metadata-first, opt-in, and branch-aware.
  • The brain stays honest because a single North-Star number — coverage_score — measures how much of what it believes it can actually trace, and the design names its own 0.03% starting point rather than hiding it.

A memory that can say where it learned a thing, how much it trusts it, and what it would take to overturn it is the precondition for everything above it. That memory is what this chapter built.

“Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established.”

— Proverbs 24:3

Chapter 46: Memory Dynamics — Decay & Test-Time Learning

Part XI — SYNAPSE: The Engineering / Implementation Spec

A ground that never changes shape is a filing cabinet. A ground that changes shape on every footstep is mud. Memory has to be the third thing: a surface that remembers where it has been walked, and slowly forgets where it has not — without ever erasing the trail.

Overview

The previous chapter (B1) specified the memory substrate as a static object: the typed knowledge graph, its node schema, its eight-type weighted edge taxonomy plus provenance edges, and the closed-domain KIND partitioning (GOVERNS / LOCALIZES / GROUNDS / EXPANDS) that decides who may write where and which side wins a contradiction. B1 answers what is stored and how it is shaped. It does not answer how the shape changes over time.

This chapter answers that. It specifies the dynamics of the substrate — the rules by which significance rises and falls, by which edges strengthen and weaken, and by which new material is written at test time without the graph drowning in its own logs. Three machines do this work, all of them living in the same plane (L2, Hippocampal Dynamics):

  1. The Hippocampal Dynamics Engine — seven callable maintenance functions and the differential-decay law that lets a neglected memory sink below a recoverable waterline rather than being deleted.
  2. Hebbian edge reinforcement — the rule that the connections between nodes, not only the nodes themselves, carry decay and reinforcement, so that frequently-traversed paths thicken and unused ones thin.
  3. Titans-style test-time memory and the surprise gate — a three-branch write mechanism wired to the PostTool lifecycle hook that decides, per interaction, what is worth committing to the durable graph.

A note on scope and ownership, because this material genuinely lives in several places and the book has deliberately split it:

  • The biological argument — why a system that reasons should have a hippocampus-shaped memory at all, the master-statistics framing, and the priority-protected law as a matter of principle — is owned by Chapter A4 (APEX Key 4). This chapter is the engineering realization, not the justification. Where this chapter states "protected memories never decay," A4 is where that law is argued.
  • The static schema the dynamics operate over — node fields, edge taxonomy, KIND partitioning — is owned by Chapter B1. This chapter assumes it and references it; it does not re-specify it.
  • The retrieval lens that reads the substrate after the dynamics have shaped it — the AUKS 7-layer multiplicative scoring — is owned by Chapter B3. Decay here produces a freshness_factor; B3 is where that factor is consumed.
  • The cognitive contract for retrieval status (RETRIEVED / DERIVED / ASSUMED / MISSING) and the authority hierarchy is specified once, cognitively, in §C8.4. This chapter's write path feeds that contract; it does not redefine it.
  • The decay and reinforcement formulas are summarized for the reader in §A4.4. The canonical numbers and their behaviour live here.

What is genuinely unique to this chapter — owned nowhere else — is the test-time write mechanism and its hook wiring: the surprise gate, the three Titans branches, and the precise point in the agent lifecycle (PostTool) at which selective write-back fires. That is the load-bearing contribution of B2, and §B2.4 holds its full treatment.

One design commitment runs through all of it: the maintenance loop is arithmetic, not inference. Decay, reinforcement, and gating are scalar operations over edge and node metadata. No language model is in the hot maintenance path. This is what makes the dynamics affordable enough to run continuously and auditable enough to trust — a point we return to in §B2.5.

B2.1 — Seven Hippocampal Functions as a Maintenance Cycle

The Hippocampal Dynamics Engine exposes seven callable functions. They are not seven separate subsystems; they are seven operations over the one typed graph, and together they form a maintenance cycle that can be invoked on demand (after a write, before a retrieval) or batched (the nightly "dream" pass, §B2.1.4). The biological motivation for organizing memory maintenance this way — the analogy to hippocampal consolidation, indexing, and replay — is argued in §A4.3. Here we take the engineering view: these are the seven things that must happen to keep a typed knowledge graph a living ground rather than an append-only log.

B2.1.1 — The seven functions

#FunctionWhat it does (engineering)Touches
1consolidatePromotes provisional/working material into durable nodes once it clears its gate; merges duplicate provisional entries into a single canonical node.nodes
2index(Re)builds the access structures — embedding index, FTS5 text index, centrality — so retrieval can find the node without a full scan.nodes, indices
3forgetApplies the differential-decay law (§B2.2): lowers decayState / significance for neglected nodes by their protection-tier rate. Never deletes.nodes
4strengthenReinforce-on-use: raises significance (+0.05) and edge reinforcement for nodes and paths that were just traversed or retrieved.nodes, edges
5cross-linkAll-pairs cosine above a threshold creates similar-to edges; bridgeValue = 1.0 marks edges that cross cluster boundaries (the hubs that hold distant regions together).edges
6emotional-priorityRecomputes the protected / significance ranking so that protected and high-significance material sorts above ordinary material regardless of recency.nodes
7primePre-activates nodes likely to be needed next (neighbours of the current focus, recently-co-retrieved nodes), so the next retrieval is warm.nodes

Two of these are gain operations (strengthen, consolidate), one is the loss operation (forget), and the rest are structure operations (index, cross-link, emotional-priority, prime) that keep the graph navigable. The system stays in homeostasis when gain on used material roughly balances loss on unused material — which is exactly what the differential-decay law in §B2.2 is tuned to produce.

B2.1.2 — The cycle, ordered

The functions have a natural ordering when run as a maintenance pass, because some depend on the outputs of others. consolidate must run before index (you index what you have promoted). strengthen and forget are the two halves of the significance update and run together. cross-link must run after significance is settled (so a freshly-decayed node is not made a hub). emotional-priority and prime are read-side preparation and run last.

Figure D4.1 — The Hippocampal Maintenance Cycle. Seven functions over one typed graph. Green = gain (consolidate, strengthen); red = loss (forget); blue = structure (index, cross-link, emotional-priority, prime). The cycle can be invoked on demand after a write or retrieval, or batched in the nightly "dream" pass. strengthen and forget are the two halves of one significance update and both feed cross-link, which runs only after significance is settled so a decaying node is never promoted to a hub. The cycle hands a re-shaped ground to the retrieval lens (Chapter B3). No language model is in this loop — every step is arithmetic over node and edge metadata.

B2.1.3 — Why a cycle and not a trigger soup

It would be possible to attach each function to its own event and let them fire independently. The system deliberately does not, for two reasons. First, ordering matters for correctness: cross-linking before significance has settled can canonize a node that is about to be suppressed, and indexing before consolidation wastes work on entries that are about to be merged. Second, auditability: a single ordered pass produces a single, replayable maintenance record (which nodes were strengthened, which decayed, which links were formed) rather than an interleaved stream that is hard to reason about after the fact. The governance and audit chapter (B7) relies on maintenance passes being discrete, ordered, and logged.

B2.1.4 — The nightly "dream" pass

The most important batched invocation of the cycle is the nightly dream pass, which runs cross-link + dedup + decay together over the whole graph (or a working subset). It is the system's offline consolidation: the moment when significance that has accumulated over a day of use is settled, duplicate provisional nodes created during the day are merged, neglected material is decayed one tier-step, and new cross-cluster bridges are discovered now that the day's activity has revealed which clusters were actually co-activated.

The dream pass is where the analogy to biological sleep-consolidation is strongest, and the biological version of this argument is A4's to make (§A4.3). The engineering point is narrower: batching the expensive structure operations (all-pairs cosine for cross-link, dedup) into one offline pass keeps them off the hot path. During the day, on-demand invocations run only the cheap operations (strengthen on retrieved nodes, forget lazily on access). The costly all-pairs work waits for the dream. This is the same hot-path/cold-path split that governs retrieval in B3 and machine-native encoding in B8: do the cheap deterministic thing in the request, defer the expensive global thing to a scheduled pass.

B2.2 — Differential Decay and the Moving Waterline

This is the loss half of the cycle, and it is where the system's most distinctive memory commitment lives: decay is recoverable suppression below a moving waterline — never DELETE. A neglected memory does not vanish; it sinks. If it is needed again, it can be found again (at retrieval cost) and, on being used, it rises. Nothing is destroyed by the passage of time alone.

B2.2.1 — The differential-decay law

Decay is differential: the rate depends on the node's protection level, which is derived from its protected flag and KIND partition (B1). The four tiers and their per-week decay rates:

Protection levelDecay rate (per week of neglect)Typical source / KIND
protected0.00 — never decaysprotected-flagged identity / doctrine nodes; GOVERNS partition is non-decaying
high0.01 / wkreinforced, high-significance, frequently-sourced material
standard0.05 / wkordinary grounded knowledge (the default tier)
low0.10 / wkEXPANDS partition — low-trust, replaceable external knowledge

The protected-never rule is not a convenience; it is a law of the architecture, argued as the priority-protected law in §A4.2. Engineering-side, it is enforced two ways that reinforce each other: the protected-flagged node has decay rate 0.00 by tier, and the GOVERNS KIND partition is declared non-decaying and append-only at the API layer (B1). A protected node cannot decay even if its flag were somehow cleared, because its partition forbids it; and a GOVERNS node cannot decay even if mis-tiered, because its flag forbids it. Two independent guards on the same invariant.

B2.2.2 — Reinforce-on-use and decay-on-neglect

Significance moves in two directions:

  • Reinforce-on-use: +0.05. Every time a node is retrieved and used (returned in a context pack that the reasoner actually drew on), its significance rises by +0.05, and it resets its neglect clock. Use is the signal that a memory is load-bearing; the system pays attention to what gets walked on.
  • Decay-on-neglect, content-conditioned. Plain neglect applies the tier rate above. But two content conditions accelerate it:
    • outdated → ×0.8 — a node flagged outdated (e.g., superseded by a newer version via a SUPERSEDES provenance edge) has its significance multiplied by 0.8 on each pass: a faster sink, because the system has positive evidence it is stale, not merely unused.
    • incorrect → ×0.5 — a node flagged incorrect (e.g., contradicted and lost the contradiction, or REJECTS-edged) is multiplied by 0.5: the steepest sink. The system suppresses what it has reason to believe is wrong far faster than what is merely old.

Note the asymmetry between the additive reinforcement (+0.05 per use) and the multiplicative decay (×0.8, ×0.5). Reinforcement is gentle and linear because over-promoting a node on a single use would let a fluke retrieval distort the ground. Decay on flagged-bad content is multiplicative and steep because the system has earned the right to be confident the node is bad — an explicit flag, not mere silence. Decay on plain neglect sits between them: a small per-week subtraction that takes many weeks of total silence to push a standard node below the waterline.

B2.2.3 — The moving waterline as a state machine

The waterline is the threshold below which a node is suppressed: still present, still recoverable, but excluded from the fast retrieval path and from default context packs. It is moving because it is not a fixed significance value — it floats with graph pressure (how much material is competing for retrieval and context budget) and with the protection tier of the node in question. Under heavy load the waterline rises and more marginal material is suppressed; under light load it falls and more is surfaced.

A node therefore lives in one of three states, and the transitions between them are the heart of the dynamics:

Figure D4.2 — The Waterline State Machine

      reinforce-on-use (+0.05)              reinforce-on-use (+0.05)
   ┌───────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────┐
   │                           │        │                           │

┌──┴───────────────┐   rises above   ┌──┴────────────────┐  rises above   ┌──────────────────┐
│   SUPPRESSED     │   waterline     │     ACTIVE        │  significance  │   REINFORCED     │
│ (below waterline)│ ───────────────►│ (above waterline, │  ceiling       │ (high-tier,      │

│ • not in fast    │◄─────────────── │                  │◄─────────────── │                  │
│   retrieval path │   sinks below   │ • in B3 lens     │  neglect drops  │ • decay 0.01/wk  │

Figure D4.2 — The Waterline State Machine. Three live states and the transitions between them. The waterline floats with graph pressure and protection tier. Decay (plain neglect, or accelerated ×0.8 outdated / ×0.5 incorrect) sinks a node toward SUPPRESSED; reinforce-on-use (+0.05) raises it back. The single most important property: there is no transition to a DELETE state. SUPPRESSED is the floor — the node is excluded from the fast path and default packs but remains queryable by a deep / FTS5 search and rises again the moment it is used. Protected and GOVERNS-partition nodes have decay rate 0.00 and are pinned at ACTIVE or above; they can never enter SUPPRESSED.

B2.2.4 — Why suppression-not-deletion is load-bearing

The "never DELETE" commitment is not sentimentality about old data. It is what makes the memory safe to decay aggressively. If decay deleted, the system would have to be conservative — every forgotten node is a permanent loss, so you would tune decay slow and let the graph bloat. Because decay only suppresses, the system can afford to be forgetful: push marginal material below the waterline freely, keep the fast path and context packs lean, and trust that anything wrongly suppressed will be recovered on the deep-search fallback floor (the FTS5 + regex always-available layer specified in B3) and re-promoted on use.

This also interacts cleanly with provenance and audit. A deleted node leaves a hole in the provenance graph — edges dangling to nothing, a SUPERSEDES chain that ends in a void. A suppressed node keeps its edges intact; the provenance chain remains walkable even through suppressed intermediate nodes. The tamper-evident audit posture in B7 depends on the graph being append-and-suppress, never destructive. The waterline is how the system reconciles "stay lean" with "lose nothing."

Calibration. The specific numbers — 0.01 / 0.05 / 0.10 per week, +0.05 per use, ×0.8 / ×0.5 — are the architecture's declared defaults, not empirically optimized constants derived from a benchmark. They encode ratios the system is committed to (protected ≫ standard; incorrect sinks twice as fast as outdated; reinforcement is gentle relative to bad-content decay) more than they encode tuned magnitudes. A deployment is expected to re-tune the magnitudes against its own retrieval-precision data; what it may not change is the ordering of the tiers or the never-DELETE floor.

B2.3 — Hebbian Edge Reinforcement

Decay and reinforcement in §B2.2 act on nodes — their significance, their waterline state. But the typed knowledge graph is at least as much edges as nodes, and the edges are where the system's reasoning paths actually live. A retrieval is a governed walk along edges (B3); a provenance chain is a sequence of provenance edges (B1). So the dynamics must shape edges too, and they do, on a Hebbian principle: edges that fire together, wire together — paths that are traversed thicken; paths that are not, thin.

B2.3.1 — Edges carry their own dynamics metadata

In B1, every edge carries a type and a weight. For the dynamics, each edge additionally carries three fields:

  • decayRate — the per-period rate at which this edge's reinforcement bleeds off under non-traversal. As with nodes, it is differential: an edge into a protected/GOVERNS node, or a high-trust provenance edge (VERIFIED_BY, DECIDES), decays slowly or not at all; a similar-to edge created by cross-link cosine decays faster.
  • reinforcement — the accumulated strength added by traversal, on top of the edge's base type-weight. This is what thickens with use.
  • traversalCount — how many times this edge has been walked during retrieval. The raw signal that drives reinforcement and that B3 can read directly.

The base type-weight (causal 0.8–1.0 down to temporal 0.2–0.5) is the edge's a priori importance from its type. The reinforcement is its learned importance from use. The effective weight a retrieval sees is the combination, so a low-base temporal edge that happens to lie on a heavily-walked path can come to matter, and a high-base causal edge that is never traversed slowly loses its dominance.

B2.3.2 — The reinforcement rule

On each traversal during a retrieval walk:

  1. traversalCount += 1 for the edge.
  2. reinforcement is incremented (the additive analogue of node reinforce-on-use), thickening the edge.
  3. The endpoint nodes get their own reinforce-on-use (+0.05) — so walking a path reinforces both the path and the places it connects.

On each maintenance pass without traversal, the edge's reinforcement decays by its decayRate, the same suppression-not-deletion logic as nodes: a thinned edge is never removed, only weakened, and a single later traversal re-thickens it. Cross-link can add similar-to edges (§B2.1), but the dynamics never delete an edge by decay — consistent with the never-DELETE floor for the whole substrate.

B2.3.3 — Bridges and centrality

Two derived quantities matter for retrieval and fall out of the edge dynamics:

  • bridgeValue = 1.0 marks an edge whose endpoints are in different clusters — a cross-cluster bridge. These are set by the cross-link function (§B2.1) and are disproportionately valuable: they are how a query in one domain reaches a relevant memory in another. The dynamics protect bridges by giving them slow decay, so the rare connections that hold the graph together are not the first to thin under neglect.
  • Node centrality is, in effect, the integral of edge reinforcement over a node's incident edges: a node on many thickened paths is central. Centrality feeds the retrieval lens's convergence boost in B3 (a hub node can earn up to ~2.5–3× its base relevance). So Hebbian thickening here is what creates the hubs that B3 rewards — the two chapters are two ends of the same mechanism, and B3 is the owner of how the resulting centrality is scored.

The Hebbian rule is, again, pure arithmetic over edge metadata — increments and multiplicative decays, no model involved — which is why it can run inside the retrieval walk itself without adding inference cost.

B2.4 — Titans Three-Branch Test-Time Memory & the Surprise Gate

Everything to this point shapes material that is already in the graph. This section is the unique contribution of B2: how new material gets in, at test time, selectively. It is the test-time-learning mechanism, and it is owned here. The REFLECT ingest pipeline (§C14.8) and the agent lifecycle harness (Chapter B6 / the hook surface) both call this mechanism; they do not define it.

The problem it solves is specific. An agent that wrote everything it encountered to durable memory would poison its own ground: every transient intermediate, every dead-end exploration, every restated obvious fact would become a node competing for retrieval and context budget. An agent that wrote nothing at test time would never learn from a session — it would meet every problem as if for the first time (the failure C18 names for the World Model, here at the durable-substrate scale). The system needs to learn at test time without logging every interaction. The Titans-style architecture is how.

B2.4.1 — Three branches

Test-time memory is split into three branches, each with a different lifetime and write discipline:

BranchLifetimeWrite disciplineMaps to
Short-term workingwithin-episodewritten freely; cheap; discarded or summarized at episode endthe World Model / context-pack scratch (C18, C8)
Long-term, surprise-gated-forgettingacross episodes, pruneablewritten only through the surprise gate; pruned under memory pressure by surprise-gated forgettingthe decaying region of the durable graph (this chapter's §B2.2)
Persistent typed axiomspermanentwritten rarely, deliberately; non-decayingGOVERNS partition / protected nodes (B1, A4)

The branches are not three stores so much as three write policies over the one substrate. Short-term is liberal and disposable. Persistent-axiom is conservative and permanent — it is where a hard-won, verified, doctrine-level conclusion goes, and it inherits the GOVERNS partition's append-only non-decaying law from B1. The middle branch — long-term surprise-gated — is the interesting one, because it is where ordinary learning happens, and it is governed by the gate.

B2.4.2 — The surprise gate

A candidate write to the long-term branch fires only when:

SurpriseDetector > 0.7 OR meta-memory remember-gate > 0.5

Two independent signals, either of which suffices:

  • SurpriseDetector (> 0.7) — a measure of how unexpected the candidate content is relative to what the graph already holds. Computable from embeddings and the graph: low similarity to existing nodes, or a contradiction against existing high-trust nodes, scores high surprise. The intuition is that surprising information is what carries the learning — content the graph could already have predicted is not worth a durable write. (This is a write-time selection heuristic over the graph's own statistics. It is not a claim that APEX implements any specific published surprise-minimization or active-inference method; the gate is a thresholded scalar check, and we make no equivalence to external formalisms.)
  • Meta-memory remember-gate (> 0.5) — a learned/configured judgment that this content should be remembered regardless of surprise: an explicit "remember this" signal, a user-flagged fact, a verification that just passed and is worth keeping. This is the override that lets deliberately-important-but-unsurprising material through.

If neither fires, the candidate is dropped — it lived in short-term working memory and is gone at episode end. This is the discipline that keeps PostTool write-back from polluting the graph: selective, not exhaustive. The thresholds (0.7, 0.5) are declared defaults in the same calibration spirit as §B2.2 — ratios and a deliberate asymmetry (surprise must clear a higher bar than the explicit remember-gate, because explicit "remember this" is a stronger signal than mere novelty), tunable in magnitude per deployment.

B2.4.3 — Surprise-gated forgetting

The long-term branch is also pruned by the same principle in reverse: under memory pressure, surprise-gated forgetting removes (suppresses — never DELETE, per §B2.2) the least-surprising, least-reinforced long-term nodes first. This closes the loop. The gate decides what enters the long-term branch; the same surprise statistic, integrated with reinforcement, decides what leaves it under pressure. The branch self-regulates around what is both novel and used.

B2.4.4 — Wiring to the PostTool hook

The gate is not a library function someone remembers to call. It is wired into the agent lifecycle so that it is unskippable. The lifecycle harness (Chapter B6; the seven-event model also touched in §C14 of the cognitive spine) exposes a PostTool event that fires after every tool call an agent makes. The write path:

Figure D4.3 — The Surprise-Gated Write Path. Every tool call fires the PostTool hook (purple). The hook extracts candidate learnings and computes two independent signals; the gate (amber) passes a candidate if SurpriseDetector > 0.7 OR the meta-memory remember-gate > 0.5. Failing candidates (red) are dropped — they lived only in short-term working memory and vanish at episode end, so the graph is never polluted by routine interactions. Passing candidates route by branch: novel-ordinary material enters the long-term decaying region (§B2.2 dynamics now apply to it); verified doctrine-level material goes to the persistent typed-axiom / GOVERNS partition (non-decaying). Either way the write triggers the hippocampal maintenance cycle (Figure D4.1) before landing in the B1 substrate. The principle the diagram encodes: "if it lives in a hook, it runs" — the gate cannot be forgotten or skipped, so write discipline is enforced structurally, not by convention.

The phrase to hold onto is "if it lives in a hook, it runs." Because the surprise gate is bound to PostTool rather than left to the reasoning model's discretion, write discipline is a property of the harness, not of the prompt. A model that "decides" not to bother gating, or that gates inconsistently, cannot happen: the hook fires the gate every time, identically, regardless of which provider's model produced the interaction. This is the same provider-agnostic posture that runs through SYNAPSE — the durable behaviour lives in the deterministic harness around the model, never in the model's good intentions.

B2.4.5 — Relationship to REFLECT and the World Model

Two cross-references close the loop without restating owned material:

  • §C14.8 (REFLECT ingest pipeline) is the cognitive stage at which a finished reasoning episode is reviewed and its conclusions are offered up for durable write. REFLECT is the caller; the surprise gate specified here is the gatekeeper it calls. REFLECT decides "this episode produced these candidate learnings"; B2.4 decides "of those, these clear the gate and these do not." The two are complementary, not redundant: C14.8 owns the what to consider, B2.4 owns the what actually gets written.
  • §C18.3 (World Model — three memory timescales) owns the cognitive picture of how within-step, within-episode, and across-session memory relate during reasoning. The three Titans branches here are the engineering substrate those timescales rest on: short-term working ↔ within-episode World Model scratch; long-term surprise-gated ↔ the durable across-session store; persistent axioms ↔ the permanent doctrine layer. C18 points down to B1–B3 for the substrate; this section is the part of that substrate that handles the write across timescales.

B2.5 — Why the Maintenance Loop Is Arithmetic

A closing engineering point that justifies the whole design and that distinguishes SYNAPSE's memory from a "let the model manage its own memory" approach.

Every operation in this chapter — decay, reinforcement, the waterline check, Hebbian edge thickening, the surprise and remember gates — is a scalar arithmetic operation over node and edge metadata. Additions (+0.05), multiplications (×0.8, ×0.5, decay rates), comparisons against thresholds (> 0.7, > 0.5, the waterline). The surprise score is computed from embeddings and access statistics the graph already holds. Nothing in the maintenance loop calls a language model.

Three consequences follow, and they are the reason the design is shaped this way:

  1. Affordability. Because maintenance is arithmetic, it is cheap enough to run continuously — on every retrieval (lazy decay, reinforce-on-use, Hebbian thickening in the walk) and nightly (the dream pass) — without a per-operation model cost. A memory system whose maintenance required inference would be too expensive to run often, and a memory that is not maintained often is not a living ground.
  1. Determinism and auditability. The same metadata produces the same decay, the same waterline state, the same gate decision, every time, independent of which model is in the reasoning seat. A maintenance pass is replayable; B7's tamper-evident audit can re-derive exactly which nodes were strengthened or suppressed and why. A model-driven memory manager would be non-deterministic and un-auditable — you could not prove, after the fact, why a memory was forgotten.
  1. Provider-agnosticism. Decay, reinforcement, and gating are independent of the generating model — they read embeddings (whose dimension is swappable and never the system of record) and access stats, not the model's hidden state. So the memory dynamics are identical whether the agent constellation rents intuition from one provider or another. The intelligence in the seat may change; the shape of the ground does not.

This is the engineering expression of a principle A4 argues philosophically: memory is the system's responsibility, not the model's. The model is a tenant that comes and goes; the ground it walks on is maintained by the architecture, deterministically, below it. What B1 builds as a static shape, B2 keeps alive — reinforcing what is walked on, letting the rest sink without ever erasing the trail, and admitting new ground only when the footstep was surprising enough to be worth the soil.

  • §A4.2–A4.4 — the biological argument for a hippocampus-shaped memory, the priority-protected law (argued, not merely declared), and the reader-facing summary of these decay/reinforcement formulas.
  • Chapter B1 — the static substrate these dynamics operate over: node schema, eight-type weighted edge taxonomy plus provenance edges, KIND partitioning (GOVERNS / LOCALIZES / GROUNDS / EXPANDS).
  • Chapter B3 — the AUKS 7-layer retrieval lens that reads the re-shaped ground; consumes the freshness_factor produced by decay here and the centrality produced by Hebbian thickening here. Owner of how those quantities are scored.
