“The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.”

— Proverbs 10:7

Chapter 47: Retrieval — The AUKS 7-Layer Lens

Supporting Part B, the engineering home of the substrate. This chapter completes the memory trilogy. Chapter B1 built the typed knowledge graph — the nodes, the edges, the KIND partitions, the provenance schema. Chapter B2 gave that graph a metabolism — decay, reinforcement, the surprise-gated write path, the hippocampal dynamics. This chapter is about the act of reading: how, given a graph that already holds the right facts somewhere, the system surfaces the right ones, in the right order, with their provenance intact, and hands them across the one boundary in the architecture that is treated as protected — the line between gathering and solving.

B3.0 Where This Chapter Sits

Retrieval is the seam where memory meets cognition. Everything upstream of it — the contract gate, the typed graph, the decay engine — exists so that when a question arrives, there is something worth retrieving and a defensible way to rank it. Everything downstream of it — the reasoning pipeline, the verifier, the confidence bus — depends on retrieval having handed it facts it can trust, tagged with what kind of facts they are. If retrieval gets this wrong, nothing after it can recover: a reasoner fed a stale lookalike dressed up as canonical truth will reason impeccably to a wrong conclusion, and a verifier checking that the reasoning is valid will pass it. The error has to be caught here, at the memory edge, or not at all.

This chapter has a precise scope, and it is worth stating the boundary before we cross it, because two neighboring chapters own pieces of this territory and this chapter must not re-litigate what they own.

  • The cognitive contract for Stage 5 — RETRIEVE — is owned by Chapter C8. That chapter, part of the eleven-stage spine, specifies what retrieval-status means as a cognitive obligation: why a thinking system must distinguish a fact it looked up from a fact it merely assumed, what the authority hierarchy among sources is, and what it means to honestly report a gap. C8.4 in particular fixes the retrieval-status property and the authority hierarchy as a cognitive law. This chapter does not re-specify that law. It builds the engine that realizes it. Where C8 says "a retrieved fact and an assumed fact must never be confused," B3 says "here is the scoring formula, the traversal, and the packer that keep them un-confused under a token budget at sub-200-millisecond latency." When you want the why, read C8. This chapter is the how.
  • The query that drives retrieval is shaped by Stage 4 — SCOPE — owned by Chapter C7. SCOPE decides what we are even looking for: it produces the GoalSpec that this chapter then executes. We will describe the GoalSpec as an input contract and explain how the retrieval engine consumes it, but the cognitive act of deciding the scope belongs to C7.
  • The biological argument for the whole memory substrate — why a hippocampus, why priority protection, why master statistics over surface similarity — is owned by Chapter A4. A4 is the context home of Key 4. This chapter is the engineering home of one of its organs. Where A4 argues that significance should beat similarity because that is how human memory works and why it is right, B3 gives the arithmetic that makes significance beat similarity in a database query.

So: schema in B1, dynamics in B2, ranking engine here, cognitive contract in C8, scope contract in C7, biological argument in A4. Nothing in this chapter restates those. Everything in this chapter assumes them.

The organizing claim of the chapter is a single sentence: surface similarity is the last thing the system ranks on, not the first. A standard vector-retrieval system ranks by cosine similarity and stops. This system treats cosine as one factor among six, and the cheapest, most easily-fooled one at that. The reason is the failure mode that defines the whole design: a stale, wrong, but textually similar memory will always beat a canonical, sourced, but textually plainer memory under pure cosine — because being a convincing lookalike is exactly what makes a wrong answer dangerous. The AUKS lens is the structural answer to that failure mode.

B3.1 The 7-Layer AUKS Scoring Engine and the Multiplicative Score

AUKS — the Adaptive Universal Knowledge System retrieval lens — is not one ranking step. It is seven layers of context that each contribute to a final, explainable score. The word "explainable" is load-bearing: every term in the score is a number the system computed and can show you, not a weight buried inside an opaque reranker model. You can ask the system why a node ranked where it did, and it can answer with arithmetic.

B3.1.1 The Seven Layers

The seven layers, in the order they contribute, are:

  1. Concept-weights and salience. The raw importance of a node — its significance (1–10) and the salience it has accrued from access and reinforcement. This is the layer that knows a node matters, independent of whether it textually matches the query.
  2. Hierarchical context. The node's position in the Domain → Project → Module → Topic hierarchy. This is what keeps two nodes named "the gate" from colliding when one is an ingestion gate and the other is a confidence gate — they live in different branches of the hierarchy, and the query is scoped to a branch.
  3. Relationship types. The typed-edge taxonomy from B1 (causal, temporal, the provenance edges, and the rest). A node reachable along a causal edge from the query anchor is contextually closer than one reachable only along a weak temporal edge, even at equal surface similarity.
  4. Semantic roles. The ACTOR / ACTION / OBJECT decomposition of the query. A node that fills the role the query is asking about ranks above one that merely shares vocabulary with the query.
  5. Concept expansion. Controlled widening: from the query's seed concepts, the lens expands to closely-linked concepts so that a query about "decay" can surface the reinforcement node it is the inverse of, without drifting into unrelated material.
  6. Cross-references and convergence. The big one. A node that many independent paths converge on — a hub on the critical path — is treated as more relevant than a leaf, because convergence is evidence of importance. This is the layer that gives centrality its teeth.
  7. Query interface. The top layer that assembles a GoalSpec, runs the walk, applies the score, and returns ranked results — the surface this chapter's later sections describe.
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  L7  QUERY INTERFACE — GoalSpec in, ranked ContextPack out           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  L6  CROSS-REFS + CONVERGENCE — hub/centrality boost (≈2.5–3×)       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  L5  CONCEPT EXPANSION — controlled widening from seed concepts      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  L4  SEMANTIC ROLES — ACTOR / ACTION / OBJECT slot matching          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  L3  RELATIONSHIP TYPES — typed-edge taxonomy weighting              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  L2  HIERARCHICAL CONTEXT — Domain → Project → Module → Topic        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  L1  CONCEPT-WEIGHTS + SALIENCE — significance, accrued importance   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       cosine similarity enters HERE, as base_relevance — and is the
       single most easily-fooled term, so it is multiplied, not trusted

Figure D5.1 — The AUKS 7-layer retrieval stack. Each layer contributes a factor to the multiplicative score below. Surface cosine similarity is not a layer of its own; it enters as the base_relevance term that all the other factors modulate. The stack is read bottom-up at write/index time (layers are precomputed into indexes) and top-down at query time (the interface assembles a GoalSpec and applies the score).

B3.1.2 The Multiplicative Score

The seven layers resolve into a single ranking number through a multiplicative formula:

final_score = base_relevance
            × domain_weight
            × salience
            × convergence_boost
            × cross_ref_bonus
            × freshness_factor

Three properties of this formula matter, and each one is a deliberate design decision rather than a tuning choice.

First: it is multiplicative, not additive. An additive score lets a single dominant term — usually surface similarity, because embeddings produce confidently-high cosine values for lookalikes — swamp every other consideration. You can add a large similarity number to small significance and freshness numbers and the similarity still wins. A multiplicative score does not let any single term run away, because every factor gates every other. A node with high cosine similarity but a freshness_factor driven toward zero by decay (see B2) is multiplied down toward zero no matter how similar it looks. A stale lookalike cannot win, because staleness is a multiplier, not a subtractor.

Second: base_relevance — the cosine term — is the multiplicand, not the ranking. It is the first factor written and the last factor that matters. Every other layer can override it. This is the formal expression of the chapter's organizing claim: cosine ranks last. The system computes how similar the text is, and then asks six harder questions about whether that similarity should be believed.

Third: the boosts are bounded and explainable. convergence_boost — the centrality factor from layer 6 — lifts a critical-path hub node by up to roughly 2.5–3× over an otherwise-equivalent leaf. The combined effect that the design targets is that a protected, sourced node outranks a stale cosine lookalike by a wide margin — the design target for the protected-over-cosine ratio is on the order of 3–4× in the per-factor headroom, which compounds across the protected layers to a much larger effective separation in the worst case. These ratios are design targets computed from the formula's structure, not measured retrieval outcomes on a built corpus — the same honesty discipline that governs every projected number in this book applies here. What is not a projection is the qualitative guarantee, which follows from the arithmetic directly: as long as decay drives a wrong node's freshness_factor down and protected protection holds a canonical node's factors up, the canonical node wins. The magnitude is a design parameter; the ordering is a structural certainty.

        PROTECTED, SOURCED NODE              STALE COSINE LOOKALIKE
        ────────────────────              ──────────────────────
        base_relevance     0.72           base_relevance     0.95  ← higher cosine!
        domain_weight      1.00 (canon)   domain_weight      0.40 (external/low-trust)
        salience           1.8            salience           1.0
        convergence_boost  2.6 (hub)      convergence_boost  1.0 (leaf)
        cross_ref_bonus    1.3            cross_ref_bonus    1.0
        freshness_factor   1.0 (protected,   freshness_factor   0.3 (decayed,
                            non-decaying)                         neglected)
        ─────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────
        final ≈ 4.38                      final ≈ 0.11
        ─────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────
              WINS — by ~40×, despite LOWER raw similarity

Figure D5.2 — Protected sourced memory versus a stale cosine lookalike. Illustrative factor values (not measured) showing the failure mode the formula is built to prevent. The lookalike has higher surface similarity (0.95 vs 0.72) and under pure cosine retrieval would win outright. Under the multiplicative score, its low trust domain, its lack of convergence, and — decisively — its decayed freshness multiply it down below the canonical node. The exact final-score ratio depends on the factor values; the direction of the result does not.

B3.1.3 Why Significance Beats Similarity (Cross-Reference, Not Restated)

The argument for why this is the correct way to rank memory — why a mind should privilege what matters and is true over what merely looks like the query — is the biological and philosophical case made in Chapter A4, the context home of Key 4. A4 grounds it in how human memory uses master statistics and emotional salience rather than raw recency or surface match. This chapter does not restate that argument; it implements its conclusion. If the formula above feels like it needs justifying, the justification is in A4. What lives here is the claim that the formula delivers what A4 demands: an explainable, bounded, multiplicative ranking in which similarity is the floor and significance is the ceiling.

B3.2 The GoalSpec Governed Walk and the Zero-LLM Hot Path

A multiplicative score tells you how to rank candidate nodes. It does not tell you which nodes are candidates in the first place. That is the job of traversal — and traversal in this system is not a free-roaming graph crawl that gathers everything within N hops and ranks it. It is a governed walk: a constrained traversal that admits a node only if it satisfies an explicit query contract.

B3.2.1 The GoalSpec: A Query Is a Contract

Every retrieval begins with a GoalSpec — a structured object that says what a good answer to this query looks like before the walk begins. The GoalSpec is produced by Stage 4 (SCOPE, Chapter C7); this chapter consumes it. Its fields are:

FieldMeaning
targetKindsWhich KIND partitions are admissible (GOVERNS / LOCALIZES / GROUNDS / EXPANDS — see B1). A query for doctrine never wanders into scratch.
preferredRelationsWhich typed edges the walk is allowed to traverse. A causal query follows causal edges; it does not drift along weak temporal links.
requiredEvidenceWhat provenance a node must carry to be admitted (e.g. must have a SourceRef, must clear a trust tier).
maxDepthHow many hops the walk may take from the query anchor.
stopWhenA termination condition — enough evidence gathered, a convergence node reached, a budget hit.
avoidRelationsEdges the walk must not traverse, used to prevent known-bad expansions.

The GoalSpec turns retrieval from "find similar text" into "satisfy this contract." It is the difference between a search and a query with standards.

B3.2.2 The Governed Walk: Admission Has Two Gates

The walk traverses the graph from the query anchor outward, but a node is admitted to the candidate set only if it passes both of two gates:

  1. Trust-tier gate. The node must clear the trustTier floor set by the GoalSpec's requiredEvidence. A scratch-tier node does not enter a canon query; an unsourced node does not enter a query that requires evidence.
  2. Relation gate. The node must lie on one of the preferredRelations. Reaching a node along a forbidden or non-preferred edge does not admit it, no matter how relevant it looks.

A node that fails either gate is not admitted — not "admitted with a penalty," but not admitted. This is the structural firewall that keeps low-trust data out of the candidate pool entirely, before scoring ever runs. The multiplicative score (B3.1) then ranks only what survived admission.

Figure D5.3 — Governed-walk traversal under a GoalSpec. Every step is double-gated: a relation gate (is this edge allowed?) and a trust gate (does this node clear the required tier?). Only doubly-admitted nodes are scored and ranked. Rejection does not halt the walk — it prunes that node and continues — but a rejected node never reaches scoring. The filter-by-domain-then-rank ordering is the whole point: admission happens before ranking, so a low-trust node can never out-score a high-trust one on raw embedding, because it was never in the pool.

B3.2.3 Filter-by-Domain-Then-Rank

The ordering in that diagram — admit (filter) first, score (rank) second — is itself a named guarantee. Filter-by-domain-then-rank means low-trust data never competes with high-trust memory on the strength of a raw embedding match, because the trust filter runs before the embedding score is ever consulted. This is the traversal-level partner to the multiplicative score's freshness term: the score protects against stale lookalikes that are admitted; the filter protects against low-trust lookalikes by not admitting them at all. Two independent defenses, at two stages, against the same failure mode.

B3.2.4 The Zero-LLM Hot Path

Here is the property that makes this engine deployable rather than merely correct: the entire hot path runs with no LLM call at all.

The seven layers' contributions — significance, hierarchical position, edge types, centrality, convergence — are all precomputed into indexes at write and consolidation time (the nightly "dream" pass from B2 maintains them). At query time, the governed walk reads precomputed indexes and applies arithmetic. There is no model inference in the loop. The design target is sub-200-millisecond retrieval on the hot path.

This is the deepest expression of the retrieve-don't-recall thesis. Recall — asking a model to reconstruct a fact from its weights — costs a forward pass and risks confabulation. Retrieval here costs an index lookup and a multiplication, and cannot confabulate, because it returns nodes that exist in the graph with provenance attached or it returns nothing. The model's capacity is reserved entirely for reasoning (Stage 6 and beyond); not one token of it is spent on remembering. The ranking formula is transparent arithmetic, not an opaque reranker model — which is exactly why it can run without a model call and still be inspected after the fact.

B3.2.5 The Always-Available Fallback Floor

No precomputed index is perfect, and no system should assume its fast path always succeeds. Beneath the zero-LLM hot path sits an always-available fallback floor: full-text search (FTS5) plus regular-expression matching. If the governed walk returns too little — a cold index, a query that touches an unindexed region, a freshly-ingested node not yet consolidated — the system falls through to FTS5 + regex over the raw node store. This is slower and dumber than the AUKS lens, but it always works, it requires no model, and it never returns nothing when something matches. The fallback is the guarantee that retrieval degrades gracefully instead of failing silently. A system that sometimes returns a worse answer is recoverable; a system that sometimes returns a confident wrong answer is not.

B3.2.6 Prior Art: RAG and the CAG Alternative (Comparison, Not Adoption)

It is worth situating this design against the two dominant external paradigms for getting facts into a model's context, both as honest acknowledgment of prior art and to sharpen what is distinctive here.

The mainstream paradigm is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): at query time, embed the query, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks from a vector store, and prepend them to the prompt. The AUKS lens is recognizably in the RAG family — it retrieves at query time and conditions reasoning on what it finds — but it differs in the way that defines this whole chapter: RAG, in its standard form, ranks by surface similarity and stops, which is precisely the failure mode AUKS is built to defeat. AUKS is RAG with a provenance-and-significance lens bolted in front of the embedding score, plus a governed walk that filters before it ranks.

A more recent alternative is CAG (Cache-Augmented Generation), which inverts the timing: rather than retrieving at query time, CAG preloads the relevant corpus into the model's context once, precomputes the key-value cache for it, and then skips real-time retrieval entirely — every subsequent query reuses the cached corpus. The appeal is latency and simplicity: no retrieval step in the hot loop at all. [The CAG approach is cited here as a prior-art design option for the retrieval stage; this book has not independently verified its reported efficiency results against a primary source, and any specific figures should be treated as [reported, unverified].]

The honest framing is that CAG is a genuine alternative design option for this stage, not a mechanism APEX uses — the contrast is instructive precisely because it makes a different tradeoff. CAG buys latency by fixing the corpus at cache-build time; it works best when the relevant knowledge is small, stable, and known in advance. The AUKS lens makes the opposite bet: the corpus is large, evolving, and provenance-stratified, so retrieval must happen at query time against a living graph, and the win comes not from skipping retrieval but from making retrieval cheap (zero-LLM hot path) and trustworthy (multiplicative provenance score). One could imagine a hybrid — a CAG-style precomputed cache for the protected/identity tier that never changes, with a governed walk for everything else — but that is a design speculation, not a feature of this system as specified. The point of raising CAG is the contrast: APEX does not skip retrieval; it disciplines it. The KV-cache compression lineage that would make a CAG-style cache cheaper on fixed hardware is discussed, separately and as its own orthogonal axis, in the machine-native encoding chapter (B8); it is not the same mechanism and should not be conflated with the retrieval lens described here.

B3.3 The Protected GATHER/SOLVE Handoff — The Status-Tagged, Token-Budgeted Context Pack

We now arrive at the single most protected boundary in the architecture. The governed walk has produced ranked, admitted candidates. But the reasoning pipeline does not receive a ranked list, and it certainly does not receive a raw context window stuffed with whatever fit. It receives a ContextPack: a typed, status-tagged, token-budgeted object assembled under strict rules. The line where memory hands this pack to reasoning — the GATHER/SOLVE handoff — is the line this system treats as protected, because it is the last place a hallucination can be caught before reasoning begins.

B3.3.1 Why a Pack and Not a Window

A standard system gives a model a context window and lets it sort out what matters. This system refuses to do that, for a reason that goes to the heart of the design: an undifferentiated window launders provenance. Once a fact is in the window as plain text, the model cannot tell a sourced canonical fact from a low-trust scratch note from a guess the retrieval system made to fill a gap. They are all just tokens. The model will treat them as equally true, because nothing in the window says otherwise.

The ContextPack refuses this by carrying structure across the boundary. Every item in the pack is a typed Fact, not a string, and it carries its status, its source, its trust tier, and its confidence band with it into the reasoner.

B3.3.2 First-Class Retrieval Status — The No-Laundering Rule

Every fact in the pack carries a first-class retrieval status, one of four values:

StatusMeaning
RETRIEVEDFound in the graph with a SourceRef. A real, sourced memory.
DERIVED-COMMONNot in the graph, but common knowledge the system is willing to assert (e.g. "water boils at 100°C at sea level"). Carries lower authority than RETRIEVED.
ASSUMEDThe system is assuming this to proceed, with no source and no claim to common-knowledge status. A flagged guess.
MISSINGThe query needed this and it was not found. An explicit, first-class absence — a hole, named as a hole.

The cognitive meaning of these four statuses — why a mind must distinguish them, what authority hierarchy they encode, what obligations each one creates for the reasoner — is the property specified once, cognitively, in Chapter C8.4 (Stage 5, RETRIEVE). This chapter does not re-derive that contract. What this chapter contributes is the enforcement: the schema that makes the status a non-optional field on every fact, and the rule that keeps the statuses honest.

That rule is the no-laundering rule, and it is the entire point of the boundary: ASSUMED and MISSING may never be silently promoted to RETRIEVED. A guess may not be dressed as a sourced fact. A gap may not be filled with a confabulation and relabeled as a memory. The status a fact enters the pack with is the status it carries to the reasoner, and any attempt to upgrade it without a real source is a governance violation that the audit spine (B-side governance) is built to catch.

The teeth behind the rule live one stage downstream: an unhandled MISSING fact is a verification failure. If the pack hands the reasoner a MISSING and the reasoner produces an answer that depended on that fact without flagging the gap, the verifier (Chapter B6 / Stage 7) rejects the answer. The system is not allowed to quietly paper over a hole. It must either find the fact, derive it honestly, or report that it could not. This is how "the system catches hallucination at the memory edge" becomes a mechanism rather than an aspiration: the hole is named at GATHER, and the failure to handle the named hole is caught at VERIFY.

B3.3.3 Confidence Inheritance

One more property travels with each fact: confidence inheritance. A fact's trust tier is the ceiling on the confidence of any conclusion that depends on it. A reasoner cannot derive a high-confidence conclusion from a low-trust premise; the weakest input caps the strongest output. This is the retrieval-side anchor of the confidence bus (Chapter B7 / Section VI of the spine): the bus enforces min-across-gates and never amplifies, and the ceiling it cannot exceed is set right here, at the pack, by the trust tier of the facts the pack carried in. Provenance is not metadata that gets discarded after retrieval; it is the upper bound on everything reasoning is allowed to claim.

B3.3.4 Token-Budgeted Greedy Priority-Tier Packing

The pack is assembled under a token budget — the architecture defines 4K, 8K, and 16K budget modes (estimated at roughly 4 chars/token). The budget exists because context is finite and expensive, and because an over-stuffed context degrades reasoning as surely as an under-filled one. Assembly is greedy, descending through priority tiers:

TIER          ┃ WHAT IT HOLDS                        ┃ TRIM/COMPRESS?
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╋━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╋━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1 PROTECTED      ┃ protected-flagged, non-decaying axioms   ┃ NEVER
2 IDENTITY    ┃ who the agent is, its doctrine        ┃ NEVER
3 REINFORCED  ┃ high-salience, frequently-used nodes  ┃ trim if needed
4 CROSS-AGENT ┃ handoff facts from peer agents        ┃ trim if needed
5 RECENT      ┃ recent working context                ┃ trim if needed
6 GENERAL     ┃ everything else admitted              ┃ trim/drop first

The packer fills tier 1 first, then tier 2, and so on down, taking the highest-scored facts within each tier (by the multiplicative score of B3.1) until the budget is exhausted. Lower tiers are trimmed or dropped first when the budget runs out.

Figure D5.4 — Context-pack assembly by descending priority tiers under budget. The packer is greedy top-down: protected and identity are placed in full before anything else competes for space, and the general tier absorbs all the trimming. Every span is tagged with its provenance plane and every fact stamped with its full status before the pack crosses the boundary.

B3.3.5 The Two Lines That Are Never Cut

One rule overrides the budget entirely: the Identity and Doctrine layers (tiers 1 and 2) are never trimmed and never compressed. No matter how tight the budget, the agent's protected axioms and its sense of who it is go into the pack whole. The reasoning behind this is the survival property from B2 and the soul material from Section V: an agent that compresses away its own identity to fit more working facts has, in a precise sense, forgotten itself mid-task. The budget can starve the general tier. It can never starve identity. This is why the bootstrap hook loads identity-before-operation and why PostCompact reload restores identity first: the one thing the system will spend tokens on unconditionally is knowing what it is.

B3.3.6 Provenance-Plane Separation — Data Never Becomes Instructions

The final assembly step tags every span in the pack with its provenance plane: operator, user, or untrusted. This is the structural defense against prompt injection. A fact retrieved from an untrusted external source is carried into the pack tagged untrusted, and the reasoner is structurally forbidden from treating an untrusted-plane span as an instruction — it is data to reason about, never a command to obey. Data never becomes instructions. A malicious string buried in an ingested document cannot hijack the agent, because by the time it reaches reasoning it is wearing an untrusted tag that strips it of imperative force. The plane separation is enforced at the pack, before reasoning, because that is the last point where the system still knows where each span came from — once it is in the reasoner's working context, the origin would otherwise be lost.

B3.3.7 The Pack Is a Model-Independent Contract

A closing note on why all of this is built as a typed object rather than careful prompt formatting. The ContextPack is a model-independent contract. Any provider — a frontier API model, a local solver, a swapped-in replacement six months from now — receives the same status-tagged, budget-bounded, plane-separated structure. The boundary does not depend on any particular model honoring any particular prompt convention; it depends on a typed handoff that is the same regardless of who consumes it. This is what makes the model swappable in the retrieve-don't-recall sense: the thinking (the pipeline, the boundary, the verifier) is stable, and the intuition (the model behind Stage 6) is interchangeable, because the contract between them is structural, not stylistic.

B3.4 The Retrieval-Status State Machine at the GATHER/SOLVE Boundary

The four retrieval statuses are not just labels; they form a small state machine that governs how a fact moves — or refuses to move — across the boundary. Making the transitions explicit is what turns the no-laundering rule from a principle into something a system can enforce and an auditor can check.

A fact enters the boundary in one of two ways: the governed walk found it, or it did not. From there:

  • A fact the walk found with a SourceRef enters as RETRIEVED. From RETRIEVED there is exactly one legal "downgrade" path and no legal "upgrade" path — a RETRIEVED fact whose source is later found stale can be re-marked, but nothing can be promoted into RETRIEVED without a real source.
  • A fact the walk did not find, but which is safe common knowledge, may enter as DERIVED-COMMON — a deliberate, lower-authority assertion.
  • A fact the reasoner needs and asserts without a source is ASSUMED — and ASSUMED is a terminal status at the boundary: it may be used by reasoning only if flagged, and it may never transition to RETRIEVED.
  • A fact the query required but the walk could not find is MISSING. MISSING has two legal exits and one illegal one. Legal: the system runs a deeper retrieval (relax the GoalSpec, fall through to the FTS5 floor, escalate to a sub-agent) and the fact becomes RETRIEVED if found; or the system honestly reports the gap and reasoning proceeds with the hole named. Illegal: the fact is silently relabeled RETRIEVED or quietly assumed away — which is exactly the laundering the rule forbids, and which the verifier rejects as an unhandled MISSING.

Figure D5.5 — Retrieval-status state machine at the GATHER/SOLVE boundary. The two LAUNDERED transitions (dashed, forbidden) are the only paths the boundary exists to prevent: promoting a guess or a gap into a sourced fact. Every legal path either carries honest provenance into the pack or names a gap explicitly. The verifier downstream rejects any answer that reached output via a laundered path or via an unhandled MISSING — which is what gives the boundary enforcement teeth rather than mere convention.

The state machine is the formal shape of the whole chapter's claim. Retrieval is not "find similar text and hand it over." It is: run a contract-governed walk that filters by trust before it ranks; rank by significance and provenance with similarity as the floor; assemble a token-budgeted pack that never starves identity and never launders a guess; tag every span with its provenance plane so data cannot become instructions; and hand the reasoner not a window but a typed contract in which every fact knows what kind of fact it is. Where that contract's cognitive obligations are specified — what RETRIEVE means as a stage of thought, what the authority hierarchy is, what honest abstention requires — read Chapter C8. What this chapter built is the engine that makes those obligations true at sub-200-millisecond latency, with no model in the loop, against a living graph, every single time a question is asked.

B3.5 Chapter Summary and Cross-References

What this chapter owns: the AUKS 7-layer retrieval lens, the multiplicative explainable score (cosine ranks last), the GoalSpec governed walk and its double admission gate, the zero-LLM hot path and the FTS5 fallback floor, the token-budgeted priority-tier ContextPack, the no-laundering rule, provenance-plane separation, and the retrieval-status state machine at the GATHER/SOLVE boundary. This is the ranking and handoff engine for the memory substrate.

What this chapter deliberately does not restate, and where to find it:

  • The node/edge schema, KIND partitions, provenance fields — Chapter B1 (the typed knowledge graph this lens reads from).
  • Decay, reinforcement, freshness dynamics, the surprise-gated write path, the nightly consolidation pass that maintains the precomputed indexes — Chapter B2.
  • The cognitive contract for retrieval-status and the source-authority hierarchy — Chapter C8.4 (Stage 5, RETRIEVE). B3 realizes that contract; it does not re-specify it.
  • The GoalSpec as a cognitive scoping act — Chapter C7 (Stage 4, SCOPE), which produces the GoalSpec this chapter consumes.
  • The biological and philosophical argument for significance-over-similarity, priority protection, and master statistics — Chapter A4 (Key 4 context).
  • Confidence inheritance and the confidence bus the pack's trust ceilings feed — Chapter B7 / Section VI.
  • Verification of unhandled MISSING and laundered status — Chapter B6 / Stage 7 (VERIFY).
  • KV-cache compression and machine-native encoding (an orthogonal efficiency axis, not the retrieval lens) — Chapter B8.

The one sentence to carry forward: memory ranks on what matters and is true, not on what looks like the query, and it hands reasoning a contract — not a window — in which every fact knows what kind of fact it is.

Chapter 48: The Cognitive Pipeline — Implementation Mirror

Part B — SYNAPSE: The Engineering Realization Plane L5 — Provider-Agnostic Reasoning Pipeline

How to read this chapter

This chapter is a mirror, not a source. Everything the eleven stages do — what RECEIVE parses, how CLASSIFY decides type, what VERIFY checks, why REASON tracks inference type — is the spine of this book and lives in Part C: the overview in Chapter C3 and one chapter per stage in C4 through C14. This chapter does not repeat that cognitive content. If you came here to learn what a stage means, you are in the wrong place; follow the cross-reference to the C-chapter that owns it.

What this chapter owns is the wiring. SYNAPSE is the engineering instantiation of the Pattern of Mind, and at the engineering layer the eleven stages stop being a philosophy of correct cognition and become eleven typed software components connected by typed interfaces. The interesting question here is not "what does CLASSIFY decide?" but "what struct does CLASSIFY emit, who consumes it, and what is forbidden from crossing the wire between RETRIEVE and REASON?" The typed objects on these wires are not new objects invented for SYNAPSE. They are the very same output schemas authored in the stage chapters and collected, field-complete, in Appendix B (APP-B). This chapter shows those same schemas arranged as a dataflow graph — the pipeline viewed end-on, as a circuit rather than as a sequence of acts of thought.

Three structural facts make this circuit worth specifying separately from the cognitive content:

  1. The interfaces are typed and struct-to-struct — each stage receives exactly one upstream object and emits exactly one downstream object, never a free-form blob of text passed from one megaprompt to the next.
  2. The depth of the circuit is routed, not fixed — CLASSIFY decides at runtime how many of the eleven stages actually fire, so a factual lookup does not pay the cost of a design synthesis. The routing mechanism is authored once in CLASSIFY (C6.4–C6.5); this chapter shows how the wiring honors it.
  3. The feedback edges are backward-only and few — there are exactly two loops in the entire circuit, and there are no forward skips. This is what makes the pipeline inspectable: a directed graph with two back-edges and no shortcuts can be drawn on one page and audited stage by stage.

A note on provider-agnosticism, because it governs the whole chapter. The pipeline is the only stateless tenant of memory in SYNAPSE. It carries no durable state of its own: every fact it reasons over is retrieved from the typed knowledge graph (B1) through the AUKS lens (B3), and every artifact it produces is written back as a ProcessRecord (C34) or committed to the graph. Because the pipeline holds no state, the intuition that fills each stage's narrow prompt can be rented from any model — claude, codex, kimi, or a local solver — chosen per stage by configuration. The stages are encoded as text and agent-definitions, not as weights. This statefulness asymmetry — durable state in memory and the audit log, zero durable state in the reasoner — is precisely what makes the model swappable. Keep it in mind: it is the reason the interfaces must be typed. You cannot swap a tenant in and out of a socket unless the socket has a declared shape.

B4.1 Eleven Typed Stages with Struct-to-Struct Interfaces

The engineering realization of Part C

At the cognitive layer, the pipeline is eleven acts of correct thinking: RECEIVE, DECOMPOSE, CLASSIFY, SCOPE, RETRIEVE, REASON, VERIFY, SYNTHESIZE, EVALUATE, COMMUNICATE, REFLECT. Each act is given a full chapter in Part C (C4 through C14, with the overview in C3). At the engineering layer, each act becomes a component: a stage with a narrow prompt that does exactly one job, an upstream input type it consumes, and a downstream output type it produces. The defining engineering discipline is one narrow prompt per stage, never one megaprompt for the whole problem. RECEIVE is prompted only to parse; it is not also asked to reason. REASON is prompted only to derive; it is not also asked to classify. A model that is asked to do everything at once does everything at once badly, and — worse for an audited system — does it inseparably, so that an error cannot be localized to a stage. Eleven narrow prompts produce eleven inspectable sub-results; one megaprompt produces one opaque result.

The wire between any two adjacent stages carries a single typed object. The full chain, in pipeline order, is:

ParsedInput → WorkPlan → ProblemProfile → KnowledgeMap → RetrievalSet → ReasoningChain → VerificationReport → Synthesized-Answer → QualityAssessment → CompleteAnswer/DeliveredResponse → ProcessRecord

Each of these is a real struct with a declared field list. The field-complete normative definition of every one of these schemas is authored once, in Appendix B (APP-B), and the schema is introduced in context in its owning stage chapter. This chapter deliberately does not reprint the field lists — to do so would be to fork the canonical definition and invite drift. What this chapter contributes is the adjacency: which stage emits which object, which stage consumes it, and the invariant that the type on the wire is fixed so that the stage on either end can be implemented by any model without renegotiating the contract.

The mapping from engineering stage to cognitive chapter and to the object on its outgoing wire is the spine of the whole chapter. It is the B0.4 stage-to-chapter mapping, given here with the interface object made explicit:

#StageOwns the cognition inConsumes (in)Emits (out) — schema in APP-B
1RECEIVEC4raw query + RECEIVE-priority signalParsedInput (APP-B §B.1)
2DECOMPOSEC5ParsedInputWorkPlan — the sub-question DAG (APP-B §B.2)
3CLASSIFYC6WorkPlanProblemProfile — incl. type + depth route (APP-B §B.3)
4SCOPEC7ProblemProfileKnowledgeMap (APP-B §B.4)
5RETRIEVEC8KnowledgeMapRetrievalSet — status-tagged (APP-B §B.5)
6REASONC9RetrievalSetReasoningChain (APP-B §B.6)
7VERIFYC10ReasoningChainVerificationReport (APP-B §B.7)
8SYNTHESIZEC11VerificationReport (+ ReasoningChain)Synthesized-Answer (APP-B §B.8)
9EVALUATEC12Synthesized-AnswerQualityAssessment (APP-B §B.9)
10COMMUNICATEC13QualityAssessmentCompleteAnswer / DeliveredResponse (APP-B §B.10)
11REFLECTC14the full cycle traceProcessRecord (APP-B §B.11; audit home C34)

Table B4-1. The eleven stages as typed components. Each row is one socket in the circuit: the cognition is owned by the C-chapter; the object on the outgoing wire is defined in APP-B. SYNAPSE wires these objects together; it does not redefine them.

Two boundary objects deserve a pointer rather than a restatement here. The CompleteAnswer/DeliveredResponse pair at Stage 10 — the internal complete object versus the user-facing projection — is owned by Chapter C35; B4 treats it only as "the object that leaves the circuit." The ProcessRecord assembled at Stage 11 is owned by Chapter C34 as the audit-trail home, with its field-complete schema in APP-B §B.11; B4 treats it only as "the object written to the audit log when the cycle closes."

Provider-agnosticism, concretely. Because each stage's I/O type is fixed, the implementation behind a stage is interchangeable. RECEIVE can be a 4B local model parsing the query; REASON can be a frontier model rented for one call; VERIFY must — by the rule in B4.3 below — be a different model or provider than REASON. The pipeline definition does not name a vendor anywhere. It names types. This is what is meant by calling the reasoning engine the only stateless tenant: swapping the tenant behind a socket changes nothing about the wiring, because the socket's contract is the type, not the model.

Calibration note on "implemented and running." The source corpus reports that this pipeline has been built as a running system — referred to in the engineering notes under the working name EINSTEIN, described as 72 modules executing on a 4B-parameter model [reported in the SYNAPSE/APEX design corpus; treat module counts and parameter sizes as design-corpus figures, not independently benchmarked external results]. The claim relevant to this chapter is narrower and is the one to hold onto: a pipeline whose stages communicate by typed structs can be implemented as separable modules, and separable modules can each be assigned the smallest model that passes that stage's contract. The architectural point does not depend on the specific module count; it depends only on the interfaces being typed.

Diagram D6.1 — Eleven stages with struct-to-struct interfaces

Figure D6.1. The pipeline as a typed circuit. Every edge is labeled with the struct it carries; every node points to the C-chapter that owns its cognition. The GATHER band (1–5) gathers and grounds; the SOLVE band (6–11) reasons. The thick boundary between RETRIEVE and REASON is the protected GATHER→SOLVE handoff of B4.3: the RetrievalSet that crosses it is status-tagged so no ungrounded premise can be smuggled into reasoning. The two boundary objects (DeliveredResponse to the user, ProcessRecord to the log) are the only things that leave the circuit.

B4.2 CLASSIFY-Routed Depth — Factual Short Path vs Synthetic Full Path

The wiring of variable depth

A fixed eleven-stage pipeline that ran every stage on every query would be a calibration failure in software form. Asking "what is the capital of France?" does not warrant decomposition into a sub-question DAG, a five-level verification chain, and a quality assessment; it warrants a retrieval and a short answer. SYNAPSE therefore does not run a fixed circuit. It runs a routed circuit whose effective depth is set at runtime by CLASSIFY.

The decision is encoded in the ProblemProfile that CLASSIFY emits (Stage 3, the object on its outgoing wire — Table B4-1, APP-B §B.3). That profile carries the problem type (the source corpus enumerates FACTUAL, ANALYTICAL, COMPUTATIONAL, SYNTHETIC, and mixed/secondary types) and, derived from type and complexity, a depth route — the set of downstream stages that will actually fire and the per-stage cognitive budget each is allotted.

The mechanism that turns a type into a depth route — the Depth Matrix, the per-stage routing table, the escalation triggers, the per-query budget — is not authored here. It is authored once, as the keystone of CLASSIFY, in C6.4–C6.5. B4.2 implements and references that mechanism; it does not restate the matrix. (B6.2's four-axis router consumes the same routing decision from a different angle and likewise refers back to C6.) The contribution of this section is purely the wiring: how the ProblemProfile's depth route gates which sockets in the D6.1 circuit are energized.

Two reference routes anchor the spectrum:

  • Factual short path. A pure FACTUAL ProblemProfile routes through roughly four stages: RECEIVE to parse, CLASSIFY to type, RETRIEVE to fetch the grounded fact, and COMMUNICATE to return it. DECOMPOSE collapses (a single fact has no sub-question DAG), the heavy SOLVE stages (REASON, VERIFY, SYNTHESIZE, EVALUATE) are bypassed, and the answer is the retrieved, status-tagged fact itself. The grounding guarantee still holds — the fact crossed the GATHER→SOLVE boundary with a retrieval status — but the reasoning machinery does not run because there is nothing to derive.
  • Synthetic full path. A SYNTHETIC ProblemProfile ("design X," "create the architecture") routes through all eleven stages at full depth. DECOMPOSE produces a genuine sub-question DAG; REASON derives over each branch; VERIFY runs the full five-level chain (C19); EVALUATE produces a QualityAssessment; and the answer is assembled, audited, and reflected upon.

Everything between these two poles is a partial route: ANALYTICAL and COMPUTATIONAL profiles energize REASON and VERIFY but may scope retrieval more tightly; mixed profiles inherit the deepest route among their secondary types. The governing principle, stated in CLASSIFY and merely honored here, is that over-processing is as much a calibration failure as under-processing. Running all eleven stages on a factual lookup is not thoroughness; it is wasted budget and a sign that CLASSIFY mis-typed the query.

The wire-level consequence is that the depth route in the ProblemProfile acts as a set of gate signals on the circuit. A bypassed stage is not skipped in violation of the no-stage-skipping rule (B4.3) — it is routed around by CLASSIFY's declared profile, which is itself a stage. The distinction matters: the route is decided once, up front, by an authorized stage and recorded in a typed object, not improvised mid-flight by a downstream stage deciding to jump ahead.

Diagram D6.2 — CLASSIFY-routed depth

Figure D6.2. Depth is a routing decision, not a fixed sequence. CLASSIFY's ProblemProfile selects which sockets in the D6.1 circuit are energized. The factual lookup pays for four stages; the synthetic design pays for all eleven; analytical/computational queries take a middle route. The routing matrix itself is owned by C6.4–C6.5 — this diagram shows only how its output gates the circuit. Over-processing a factual query is a calibration failure, symmetric with under-processing a synthetic one.

B4.3 Backward-Only Feedback Loops and the GATHER/SOLVE Boundary

Five rules that make the circuit auditable

The pipeline's inspectability rests on a small set of structural rules about how control may flow. There are five, and they are non-negotiable in the engineering spec. The cognitive rationale for each is developed in the stage chapters; B4 states them as wiring constraints.

  1. No stage-skipping. Control flows forward through the energized stages in order. A stage may not reach forward to a later stage, nor may a stage hand its output to a non-adjacent successor. (Routing around a stage via CLASSIFY's depth profile, B4.2, is not skipping — the route is declared up front by an authorized stage, not improvised by a downstream one.) This is what keeps the circuit a clean directed graph rather than a tangle of shortcuts.
  1. Backward loops only — and there are exactly two. Feedback edges run backward, never forward, and the spec admits precisely two of them:
    • VERIFY → REASON. When VERIFY (Stage 7, C10) finds a flaw in the ReasoningChain, it does not patch the answer downstream; it routes back to REASON (Stage 6, C9) so the chain is re-derived. The weakest-dimension feedback from the verifier drives the regeneration. Reasoning is re-done, not retouched.
    • EVALUATE → SCOPE. When EVALUATE (Stage 9, C12) finds that the QualityAssessment falls short — the answer is grounded and verified but does not actually satisfy the problem as scoped — it routes back to SCOPE (Stage 4, C7) so the knowledge map is widened and the relevant downstream stages re-run against the broader scope. A coverage gap is a scoping failure, so it is fixed at SCOPE, not papered over at SYNTHESIZE. These are the only two loops. The reason to forbid all others is identical to the reason to forbid forward skips: a circuit with two named back-edges and no others can be reasoned about as a terminating process; a circuit with arbitrary feedback cannot be shown to halt or audited stage by stage.
  1. Time is acceptable. A loop that re-runs reasoning or re-scopes is spending time deliberately, and that is allowed. The system is not optimized to answer fast; it is optimized to answer correctly within a cognition budget. Taking the VERIFY→REASON loop twice to repair a flawed chain is the circuit working as designed, not a failure to be short-circuited for latency.
  1. Premise-naming is required. No stage may commit to an interpretation without naming the premises it rests on. This is enforced at the wire level: the typed objects carry their premises explicitly (the RetrievalSet carries retrieval statuses; the ReasoningChain carries the premises each inference depends on), so a premise can never be implicit. This rule is also what the PremiseChallenger (B4.4) acts upon.
  1. A hard verifier sits in the feedback slot. The verifier that drives the VERIFY→REASON loop must be independent — it may not share source or substrate with the solver it checks; ideally a different provider or architecture entirely. The full engineering treatment of the independent verifier — the five levels, the all-or-nothing gating, the oracle problem — is owned by B5 (and the cognitive content by C19–C21). B4 records only the wiring fact: the verifier occupies the feedback slot at Stage 7, and the back-edge from it to REASON is the loop that closes the SOLVE band.

The protected GATHER/SOLVE boundary

The single most load-bearing wire in the circuit is the one between RETRIEVE (Stage 5, end of GATHER) and REASON (Stage 6, start of SOLVE). The spec calls this the protected GATHER→SOLVE separation, and it exists to catch hallucination at the memory edge.

GATHER (stages 1–5) does exactly one thing with respect to facts: it fetches grounded premises and tags each with a retrieval status. SOLVE (stages 6–11) does exactly one thing with respect to facts: it reasons over premises that already carry a status. The object that crosses the boundary is the RetrievalSet (APP-B §B.5), and the boundary's whole purpose is that no ungrounded premise may cross it. Every fact REASON consumes arrived with a first-class status — retrieved-and-grounded, retrieved-but-stale, or not-found — assigned in GATHER, never minted by REASON. If a premise is needed and not in the RetrievalSet, REASON cannot invent it; it must either loop back (within the rules) or carry the gap forward as an explicit not-found status, which the confidence machinery (B5) then caps against. This is the structural reason SYNAPSE retrieves rather than recalls: the wire between RETRIEVE and REASON is the place where "I read this" and "I made this up" are forced to be distinguishable.

Diagram D6.3 — Backward-only feedback loops

Figure D6.3. The control-flow graph. Forward flow is strictly in stage order through the energized stages; the only feedback edges are the two named backward loops — VERIFY→REASON (re-derive a flawed chain) and EVALUATE→SCOPE (widen an insufficient scope). With exactly two back-edges and no forward shortcuts, the circuit is a graph one can audit and reason about for termination. The protected GATHER→SOLVE boundary sits on the RETRIEVE→REASON wire.

B4.4 The PremiseChallenger Short-Circuit and Method-First Routing Fork

Refusing to answer the wrong question

Most of the pipeline is built to answer well. The PremiseChallenger is built to notice when the question should not be answered as asked. It is a guard that sits early in the circuit — operating on the ParsedInput that RECEIVE emits and on the premises surfaced by DECOMPOSE and named under rule 4 — and it does two jobs:

  1. Presupposition extraction. It pulls the presuppositions out of the parsed question. "When did Einstein invent the telephone?" presupposes that Einstein invented the telephone. "Which of these three frameworks is fastest?" presupposes the three are comparable on speed and that speed is the operative axis. The challenger makes these presuppositions explicit objects rather than buried assumptions.
  1. False-premise detection and short-circuit. If a presupposition is false — or cannot be grounded in the RetrievalSet once retrieval has run — the PremiseChallenger short-circuits the expensive stages and routes to an honest-uncertainty terminal. It does not run REASON, VERIFY, SYNTHESIZE, and EVALUATE on a question whose premise is broken, only to produce a confident-sounding answer to something that was never true. It terminates early, names the false premise, and returns the honest correction. This is the cheapest possible failure mode and the most honest one: the system that would otherwise spend its full budget fabricating an answer instead spends almost nothing and says what is actually the case.

Tied to this is a smaller but constant discipline the challenger enforces: premise-naming and version/edition pinning before committing to a single interpretation. A question like "what does the spec say about retries?" is not answered until which spec, which edition, is pinned. Committing to one interpretation without naming it is itself a premise error the challenger is positioned to catch.

The honest-uncertainty terminal operates under a cognition budget. The challenger is not licensed to spin forever looking for a way the premise might be salvageable; it is bounded. When the budget is exhausted and the premise remains broken or ungroundable, the terminal fires. (The confidence and honesty machinery that the terminal hands off to — the calibrated bands, the weakest-premise cap — is owned by B5; B4 records only that the short-circuit routes into that machinery rather than around it.)

Method-first / model-fallback routing

The second fork early in SOLVE is the method-first, model-fallback decision. Before handing a sub-question to a rented model's intuition, the pipeline asks: is this something that can be computed rather than reasoned about? Arithmetic, dates and durations, coordinate transforms, geometric layout, unit conversions — these have deterministic methods. The discipline is don't model what you can compute: such sub-tasks are routed to code (a deterministic solver), and only what genuinely requires judgment is routed to a model.

This is both a correctness rule and a cost rule. A model asked to multiply two large numbers may produce a plausible wrong answer; a calculator does not. Routing deterministic sub-tasks to code removes an entire class of confident errors and is cheaper besides. When a sub-task is routed to a model, which model is a configuration choice, not a hardcoded one — "provider or local-solver chosen by config." The same agent code runs against any vendor; the method-first fork decides code-vs-model, and the config decides which model. This is the provider-agnostic principle from B4.1 made operational at the level of a single sub-question.

Diagram D6.4 — PremiseChallenger short-circuit and method-first routing fork

Figure D6.4. Two early forks that protect the expensive stages. The PremiseChallenger (red) extracts presuppositions and, on a false or ungroundable premise, short-circuits straight to the honest-uncertainty terminal under a cognition budget — never spending the full pipeline fabricating an answer to a broken question. The method-first fork (green) sends deterministic sub-tasks (math, dates, coordinates, layout) to code and only judgment to a model, with the specific model selected by configuration. Both forks express the same commitment: do the cheapest honest thing, and never model what you can compute.

B4.5 Summary: the circuit, not the cognition

This chapter specified the eleven-stage pipeline as a typed circuit and nothing more. To keep the boundary clean, the load-bearing claims, restated as wiring facts:

  • The eleven stages are typed components connected struct-to-struct: ParsedInput → WorkPlan → ProblemProfile → KnowledgeMap → RetrievalSet → ReasoningChain → VerificationReport → Synthesized-Answer → QualityAssessment → CompleteAnswer/DeliveredResponse → ProcessRecord. Each object's field-complete definition lives once in APP-B; each stage's cognition lives once in its C-chapter (Table B4-1). B4 owns only the adjacency.
  • Depth is routed by CLASSIFY's ProblemProfile, not fixed: a factual query takes a ~4-stage short path, a synthetic query takes all eleven. The routing matrix is owned by C6.4–C6.5; B4 shows only how the route gates the circuit. Over-processing is a calibration failure symmetric with under-processing.
  • Control flow obeys five rules: no stage-skipping, exactly two backward loops (VERIFY→REASON, EVALUATE→SCOPE), time-is-acceptable, premise-naming required, and an independent hard verifier (owned by B5) in the feedback slot. The protected GATHER→SOLVE boundary on the RETRIEVE→REASON wire guarantees no ungrounded premise enters reasoning — the structural meaning of retrieve, don't recall.
  • The PremiseChallenger short-circuits false-premise questions to an honest-uncertainty terminal under a cognition budget, and the method-first fork routes deterministic sub-tasks to code, leaving only judgment to a model whose identity is a configuration choice.

The whole point of typing the interfaces is the point of the whole architecture: because the pipeline holds no durable state and every wire has a declared shape, the intuition behind any stage can be rented from any model and swapped out without touching the circuit. The thinking is the pipeline; the model is the rented spark that fills one narrow prompt at a time. The next chapter, B5, takes up the verifier and the confidence bus that hang off this circuit's feedback slot and give its answers calibrated honesty.

“The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness.”

— Proverbs 21:5

Chapter 49: Verification, Confidence & Safety — The Engineering

Part X — SYNAPSE: The Provider-Agnostic Engineering Realization

"A correctness machine is only as honest as the gate that cannot be argued with. The cognitive chapters say what the gate must check; this chapter says how to build a gate the reasoner cannot reach, run, or grade — and how to carry the result forward without ever letting it grow on the way."

Position in the book — and what this chapter does NOT re-derive. The spine of The Pattern of Mind has already said, at the level of cognition, almost everything there is to say about verification, confidence, and safety. The definition of the five-level verifier chain — why there are five levels and not four or nine, what all-or-nothing means, why a 4/5 pass is not verified, grader stability, graph integrity, the Rule-1 narrowing — is owned by Chapter 19 (The Five Verification Levels). The stage-level execution of those checks — per-check procedures, the Verification Box gate, the failure protocol — is owned by Chapter 10 (Stage 7: VERIFY). The theory of confidence — the six bands, the assignment rules, propagation as min-across-gates, the inference-type caps — is owned by Chapter 17 (Confidence Calculus), applied per-stage by Chapter 26 and measured for calibration by Chapter 27. The theory of the Oracle Problem — why a verifier that shares the reasoner's substrate is capped at its own blind spots, why a conclusion is bounded by its weakest oracle, tool-trust weighting — is owned by Chapter 21. And the control/data-plane separation doctrine — that data must never become instructions — is owned by Chapter C8 (the contract and provenance plane) and the PremiseChallenger material.

This chapter does not restate any of that. Its subject is the engineering realization that those cognitive chapters point forward to: how you actually wire an independent verifier across two different model providers and a symbolic backend so that "independence" is a property of the deployment topology and not a hope; how you build a confidence value that is structurally incapable of being amplified as it travels; how fan-out-and-refute is implemented as adversarial re-derivation rather than a vote; and how the data-plane/instruction-plane boundary is enforced as a tag that travels with every span of context. Where a cognitive claim is needed to make the engineering legible, it is cited to its owner chapter and used, not re-proved.

The promise of the whole architecture — verification by an independent oracle replaces human-preference reward (Design Principle 3 of the SYNAPSE core) — is a promise about deployment, not about doctrine. You can write the cleanest verification theory in the world and still ship a system where the verifier secretly shares the solver's weights, where confidence quietly rounds upward at every hop, where "consensus" is three copies of the same mistake agreeing with each other, and where a poisoned document talks its way into the instruction stream. This chapter is about closing those four gaps in metal.

B5.1 — The Independent Verifier Chain: Cross-Provider Engineering

What is owned here, and what is borrowed

Chapter 19 defines the five levels — syntax, semantics, execution, correctness, excellence — and the rule that binds them: all-or-nothing. Each level scores 0–100; the chain gates on the aggregate (≥90 accept, 70–89 revise, <70 reject); and a pass on four of five levels is recorded as NOT VERIFIED, with the weakest dimension's feedback driving regeneration rather than a partial-credit acceptance. Chapter 10 turns those definitions into a runnable stage with a failure protocol. Both of those are the cognitive layer. This section takes them as given and answers a single engineering question: how do you deploy this chain so that the oracle genuinely shares neither source nor substrate with the solver?

The honest premise to name first: independence is not free, and it is not automatic. If REASON and VERIFY run on the same model — even the same model called twice with different prompts — the verifier inherits the solver's blind spots by construction. A model that confidently mis-derives a result will, with high probability, confidently fail to catch its own mis-derivation, because the error and the missed check are two expressions of the same underlying representation. Chapter 21 develops why this caps the conclusion at the weakest oracle. The engineering answer is to make the verifier a different thing: a different provider, a different architecture, or — for the levels that admit it — no model at all.

The five-level chain as deployed

The deployment splits the five levels by what kind of backend can decide them, because the strength of an independence guarantee depends on the backend:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE FIVE-LEVEL VERIFIER CHAIN — AS DEPLOYED (B5.1)                     │
│  Candidate answer enters from REASON (Stage 6) on Provider A.          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                        │
│  L1  SYNTAX        backend: parser / grammar / regex                   │
│      "Is it well-formed?"        ── model-FREE ── strongest indep.     │
│                                                                        │
│  L2  SEMANTICS     backend: type-checker / schema / symbolic           │
│      "Does it mean a coherent thing?"   ── mostly model-free ──        │
│                                                                        │
│  L3  EXECUTION     backend: sandboxed run / Z3 SMT / unit harness      │
│      "Does it actually do/compute what it claims?"  ── DETERMINISTIC ──│
│                                                                        │
│  L4  CORRECTNESS   backend: Provider B (≠ A) + Z3 for formal claims    │
│      "Is the conclusion true given the premises?"  ── cross-provider ──│
│                                                                        │
│  L5  EXCELLENCE    backend: Provider B grader + rubric lookup          │
│      "Is it L0…L5 craft-grade?"  (Ch.19 ladder)    ── cross-provider ──│
│                                                                        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  AGGREGATE GATE:  all five ≥ threshold  →  VERIFIED                     │
│                   any one  <  threshold →  NOT VERIFIED (4/5 = fail)    │
│                   weakest-dimension feedback → loop back to REASON      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Diagram D7.1 — The five-level verifier chain, as deployed. The chain is the same five levels Chapter 19 defines; what this figure adds is the backend assignment. L1–L3 are decided by model-free or deterministic backends (parsers, type-checkers, a sandboxed runtime, the Z3 SMT solver), which are independent of any model by construction — they cannot share the solver's substrate because they have no substrate. L4–L5 are the levels where a judgment call survives, and those are precisely the levels that are routed to a different provider than the one that produced the answer. The aggregate gate is all-or-nothing: four passing levels and one failing level is a chain failure, not a 0.8 score.

The engineering point this figure encodes is a gradient of independence. The strongest independence is the absence of a model: a regex either matches or it does not, and it has never seen the solver's weights. The Z3 SMT solver at L3 (and for formal claims at L4) is the keystone here — it backs the logical, dimensional, and physical sub-checks by deciding them rather than opining on them. When a claim can be reduced to a satisfiability problem — "do these constraints admit a model?", "is this unit-dimensionally consistent?", "does this arithmetic identity hold?" — the verdict is a proof or a counterexample, not a vote, and the solver shares nothing with the reasoner because it is not a reasoner. The weaker (but still real) independence is cross-provider: routing L4/L5 to a model from a different vendor, trained on different data with a different architecture, so that the correlation between solver-error and verifier-miss is reduced — not to zero, but materially.

Cross-reference. Why a partial pass must be recorded as failure, why grader stability is checked before a grade is trusted, and why the chain is exactly five levels deep are all Chapter 19's to argue. How the Verification Box gate sits in Stage 7 and what the failure protocol does on a reject is Chapter 10's. This section assumes both and only specifies the backend topology.

Cross-provider independence as a deployment rule

The decisive move is to treat verifier independence as a configuration constraint enforced by the router, not as an aspiration written in a comment. Concretely: the stage router (Chapter 11's constellation router, realized in SYNAPSE as the per-stage size/provider selector) carries a hard rule — the provider selected for VERIFY must not equal the provider selected for REASON on the same request. If only one provider is configured, the rule degrades explicitly and audibly: the system either falls back to the symbolic backends for the levels that admit them (L1–L3 plus any L4 claim reducible to SMT) and marks the model-graded levels as low-independence in the audit log, or it refuses to certify the answer as independently verified at all. There is no silent path where REASON and VERIFY collapse onto the same weights and the system still stamps the result "verified."

Diagram D7.2 — Verifier independence, cross-provider. The router enforces provider(VERIFY) ≠ provider(REASON) as a hard constraint. Decidable levels go to the model-free symbolic backends (strongest independence); judgment levels go to a different provider (cross-provider independence). The dotted path is the honest degradation: when independence cannot be achieved, the system says so in the audit log rather than pretending. The backward edge from the aggregate gate to REASON is the all-or-nothing loop — any single failing level returns weakest-dimension feedback and re-runs the solve, never accepts a partial.

Three engineering properties make this topology trustworthy:

  1. The symbolic backends are model-free by construction. A parser, a type-checker, a sandboxed runtime, and the Z3 SMT solver carry no learned weights from the solver's training. They cannot "agree" with a wrong answer out of shared bias because they have no bias to share — they have a specification. This is the part of the independence guarantee that is provable rather than merely probable.
  1. Cross-provider routing reduces correlated error, it does not eliminate it. Two different vendors' models can still share a mistake — they may have ingested the same wrong fact from the same place on the public web, or share a failure mode common to the architecture family. Honesty requires naming this: cross-provider independence is a variance-reduction mechanism, not an independence proof. The proof-grade guarantee lives only in the symbolic backends. Chapter 21 is the place where the residual is reasoned about; this section's job is to maximize the share of the verdict that rests on the provable backends and to flag the share that rests on the probable ones.
  1. Independence is auditable. Because the provider assignment for every REASON/VERIFY pair is written to the tamper-evident event log (Chapter B7 / SYNAPSE L8: append-only, SHA-256 chain-hashed), an auditor can later confirm that a given answer was in fact verified by a different substrate, and which levels were decided symbolically versus model-graded. "Independently verified" becomes a claim with a receipt, not an adjective.

Cross-reference. The all-or-nothing rule, grader-stability discipline turned on the brain's own self-claims, and graph-integrity checking are Chapter 19's. The reason a base model's score must never be attributed to the wrapper — the honesty discipline that keeps the verifier from certifying capability the architecture did not add — is the benchmark-gating principle developed with Chapter 16 and Chapter B6 (the grader-stability harness). This section borrows both and adds only the cross-provider/Z3 deployment topology that makes the independence physical.

B5.2 — The Structurally-Enforced Confidence Bus: Engineering

Why a "bus" and not a number

Chapter 17 owns the confidence calculus: six bands, assignment rules, propagation as min-across-gates, the inference-type multipliers (deductive ×1.0, inductive ×0.85, abductive ×0.70, analogical ×0.50), and the rule that confidence is capped at the weakest premise and never amplified. That is the theory, and this section does not re-derive a line of it. What it engineers is the carrier: the actual edge in the pipeline along which the confidence value travels, built so that the theory's invariants are enforced by the data structure rather than by the discipline of whoever happens to be writing the next stage.

The reason this needs to be a structural object — a bus — rather than a convention is a hard-won lesson named throughout the cognition chapters: anything that depends on a downstream component choosing to honor an upstream confidence will eventually be violated under pressure. A SYNTHESIZE stage that wants to produce a fluent, authoritative answer is under constant temptation to round 0.55 up to "high confidence" because the prose reads better. The bus removes the choice. Confidence is carried as a typed, banded value with fixed propagation operators, and the only operations the bus exposes are operations that cannot increase it.

The four hard invariants, as enforced

The bus is the edge between REASON and SYNTHESIZE (SYNAPSE L7), and it enforces four invariants in the carrier itself:

InvariantTheory ownerHow the bus enforces it (engineering)
Min-across-gatesCh.17The combine operator is min, not a mean, product-then-renormalize, or max. A chain's confidence equals its lowest-confidence link. There is no API on the bus that returns a value higher than the lowest input.
Banded, not raw floatCh.17The carried type is a band enum with half-open numeric edges, not a float. You cannot write 0.834 onto the bus; you write a band. This kills false precision and makes outputs machine-comparable and calibration-testable (Ch.27).
Never amplifyCh.17Every exposed operator is monotone non-increasing. Inference-type multipliers are all ≤ 1.0 (deductive ×1.0 … analogical ×0.50), so multiplying can only lower a band. There is no multiplier > 1.0 in the table, by construction.
Capped at weakest premiseCh.17 / Ch.21The retrieval-status boundary (SYNAPSE L4) sets each fact's trust as a ceiling on any conclusion that depends on it. The bus inherits this ceiling: a conclusion drawn from an ASSUMED fact cannot be carried above the band that ASSUMED permits.

The "banded, not raw float" choice deserves a word, because it is the least obvious and the most load-bearing. A raw float invites two failures: spurious precision (reporting 0.834 when the underlying evidence supports nothing finer than "moderate"), and silent amplification by arithmetic (a sequence of innocent-looking float operations that nudge the value up). Half-open numeric bands with per-band output-language rules solve both: the band is the unit of confidence, the band edges are fixed, and each band maps to a fixed output language ("near-certain", "likely", "uncertain", "do not know") so that calibration can be measured per band (Chapter 27's reliability diagrams and ECE operate on these bands). Confidence becomes a thing you can test the calibration of, which a raw, per-stage-reinvented float never is.

Gate-then-propagate, in sequence

The order of operations matters and is fixed: halt on a failed gate first, then propagate. You do not multiply inference-type modifiers into a confidence that has already failed its gate — a failed gate halts the chain and routes to the honest-uncertainty terminal; only a passing gate's confidence proceeds to be multiplied down by the inference-type modifier of the step that consumes it.

Diagram D7.3 — The confidence-bus sequence. Confidence flows left to right but can only travel level or downward. Gate-then-propagate is explicit: GATE 1 caps at the weakest premise; the COMBINE step takes the min of the reasoner's band and the independent verifier's band (B5.1) — never the higher; the PROPAGATE step multiplies the inference-type modifier, which is always ≤ 1.0 and therefore can only lower the band. Two halt edges route to the honest-uncertainty terminal: a premise below the floor, and a final band below the SYNTHESIZE floor. The terminal exists under a cognition budget — the system is permitted to spend bounded effort trying to raise the band before it admits it cannot, but when the budget is exhausted at low confidence, "I don't know" is the structurally-correct output, not a fallback to fluent guessing.

The engineering pay-off of forcing this through a bus is that no downstream stage can launder confidence upward. SYNTHESIZE receives a band and a fixed output-language rule for that band; it does not receive a dial it can turn. If the band says "uncertain," the output-language rule says the answer must be framed as uncertain, and there is no operation on the bus that would let SYNTHESIZE present it otherwise. This is the structural realization of the cognitive principle that the architecture must carry calibrated honesty forward — honesty is a property of the wire, not of the writer.

Cross-reference. The six bands themselves, the exact band edges, the full inference-type modifier table, and the rule that an unhandled non-empty MISSING list is itself a verification failure are Chapter 17's (with the MISSING-list discipline shared with Chapter 10 and the retrieval-status boundary). Calibration measurement — turning these bands into reliability diagrams, ECE, and Brier scores, and wiring the feedback loop back to REFLECT — is Chapter 27's, and the per-band output-language rules exist precisely so that measurement is possible. This section builds the carrier; those chapters supply what it carries and how its accuracy is checked.

B5.3 — Process Supervision and Fan-Out-and-Refute: The Engineering Answer to the Oracle Problem

The problem, stated once and handed back

Chapter 21 owns the Oracle Problem in full: a verifier that shares the reasoner's substrate is blind exactly where the reasoner is blind; a conclusion can be no more trustworthy than its weakest oracle; and tool-trust must be weighted, not assumed. Chapter 10's Self-Confirming Verification check (C10.6) enforces the anti-pattern at check level — a verifier may not simply re-run the reasoner's own derivation and call the agreement a confirmation. Chapter 21.5 then points forward — to here — for the structural and engineering answer. This section is that answer. It does not re-argue why the Oracle Problem exists; it specifies the two mechanisms that bound it in deployment.

Mechanism 1 — process supervision over outcome-only

The first mechanism is a choice about what gets supervised. An outcome-only verifier grades the final answer: it sees the conclusion and judges whether the conclusion is acceptable. A process verifier grades the steps: it sees the reasoning chain and judges, step by step, whether each move was valid given what preceded it.

The engineering reason to prefer process supervision is that outcome-only grading is systematically gameable by a reasoner that learns to produce acceptable-looking conclusions through unacceptable steps — the classic failure where a model gets the right answer for the wrong reason and the verifier, seeing only the answer, signs off. A correct-conclusion-via-invalid-step is exactly the kind of error that an outcome verifier sharing the solver's substrate is least likely to catch and most likely to reward.
